# 1. Executive Summary
Owner: Eric Rash
[This manual exists to solve a simple problem: when an athlete gets hurt at Baylor, everyone involved in getting them back on the field needs to be on the same page. Right now, that process looks different depending on the sport, the clinician, and the injury. This manual changes that.]
[Start here. Lay out in plain terms what the HPI is, what this manual covers, and who it applies to. Name the target rollout date (soft launch June 1, 2026; full launch August 2026). State the scope: every sport, every injury type, every duration. Explain why standardization matters, not just for the athlete, but for the practitioners protecting them and the institution backing them. Note alignment with NCAA Performance Technology Best Practices.]
# 2. Purpose Statement
Owner: Eric Rash
[The core idea: every injured athlete at Baylor goes through the same evidence-based process before returning to play. No exceptions based on injury severity, sport, or timeline pressure. Answer three questions: (1) What problem does this solve? (2) Why now? (3) What does success look like?]
# 3. Return-to-Performance (RTP) Protocol Framework
Owner: Jeremy  |  Co-Pilot: Eric Rash
This is the backbone of the manual. It defines the framework governing how injured athletes move from the training room back to competition.
V3 Note: This section is largely complete based on existing documents. Remaining work is formatting for consistency with the rest of the manual.
## 3.1 Stage Overview
[Describe the five-stage return-to-performance framework. For each stage, state what happens, what the athlete needs to demonstrate before moving forward, and a general timeline. The stages are the same regardless of injury; the pace is not.]
## 3.2 Injury Classification & Tiered Response
V3 Change: Simplified to a concise, easily digestible table format with brief justification statements. The full supporting document with detailed explanations and literature references is available separately and referenced here. The goal is that someone can look at this table and immediately know which tier an injury falls into.
[TABLE]
| Tier | Time Frame | Testing Response | Justification |
| Tier 1 | < 2 weeks | Abbreviated. If still training: quality of movement and visual assessment. If not training: quick strength screen. | Minimal deconditioning within this window if training continues. Ref: [source] |
| Tier 2 | 2-4 weeks | Standard protocol. If training: force plate data + visual assessment. If not training: expanded objective testing battery. | Measurable strength/power changes begin in this range. Greater clinical judgment required. Ref: [source] |
| Tier 3 | 4+ weeks or surgical | Full protocol. All milestone checkpoints required including mental health, nutrition, physician clearance, and complete testing battery. | Significant deconditioning, psychological factors, and systemic effects. Full documentation essential. Ref: [source] |
[/TABLE]
[Brief narrative (2-3 sentences per tier) expanding on the table above. Reference the full classification document for detailed supporting evidence. Keep this section to one page maximum.]
## 3.3 Workload Reintegration Guidelines
Applies to both upper and lower body protocols. Modeled after professional team workload management practices.
[Define the workload reintegration model. Progression framework should address controlled workload-only environments before transitioning to full sport participation with its inherent chaos and unpredictability.]
Recommended Progression Model:
- Phase 1 (~70% workload): Controlled, sport-specific activity only. No live competition or unpredictable scenarios.
- Phase 2 (~90% workload): Increased volume and intensity in controlled settings. Introduction of limited live scenarios.
- Phase 3 (~110% controlled / 80% live): Overload in controlled environment to build reserve; drop to ~80% load upon reintegration into full, chaotic participation.
- Phase 4 (100% full participation): Unrestricted competition. Ongoing monitoring as appropriate.
[Strength and conditioning staff takes primary ownership at later stages. Sport coach determines competition readiness. For football and similar sports, workload may be managed in snap counts rather than percentage. Include guidance on communication between AT, strength coach, and sport coach at each phase.]
# 4. Lower Body RTP Protocol
Owner: Jeremy
V3 Note: This section is essentially the existing lower body rehab progression document. Content is in place. Remaining work is formatting for manual consistency and adding brief purpose statements.
## 4.1 Testing Battery
[List every test: force plate assessments (CMJ, rebound jump), hop tests, Y balance (anterior reach only), range of motion. For each: what it measures, how it is administered, what a passing result looks like.]
## 4.2 Rehabilitation Progression & Decision Framework
[Purpose statement for the rehab progression framework. The progression documents (maintained as separate working clinical documents) define stage-by-stage exercises, volumes, intensities, and milestone criteria. Intentionally kept flexible for clinical judgment.]
Milestone Checkpoints (embedded in progression documents):
- Mental health check-in at key stages (initial evaluation, mid-rehab, pre-clearance)
- Nutrition check-in at key stages
- Documentation collection (especially for external surgeons: surgical reports, imaging, outside physician records)
- Physician clearance checkpoint
- Subjective questionnaire (lower extremity functional scale or equivalent)
V3 Note: The fillable version of the progression checklist will be maintained as a separate editable file, not embedded in this manual. An example/screenshot is included here for reference only. See Section 10 for the testing record form.
# 5. Upper Body RTP Protocol
Owner: Jeremy  |  Co-Pilot: Jacob/Josh
V3 Note: This section is essentially the existing upper body rehab progression document, with sport-specific pathways added. Content is largely in place.
## 5.1 Testing Battery
- Strength testing (dynamometer/force-based)
- Y balance upper quarter (retained; CKC test removed per team consensus)
- Plyometric push-up (force plate-based; serves as both baseline intake and return-to-play measure)
- Sport-specific functional tests (throwing metrics, contact drills) as applicable
[For each test: what it measures, how it is administered, and benchmarks. Call out sport-specific considerations directly.]
## 5.2 Rehabilitation Progression & Decision Framework
[Same structure as Section 4.2. Purpose statement, milestone checkpoints (mental health, nutrition, documentation, physician clearance, subjective questionnaire). Reference Section 3.3 for workload reintegration.]
Biodex / Physician-Specific Testing:
[Some physicians require Biodex testing before clearance. Handled under the physician clearance checkpoint rather than as a standard protocol element. If the physician has not cleared, the protocol cannot be completed. Note current Biodex availability limitations on campus.]
## 5.3 Sport-Specific Pathways (Throwing, Contact, Overhead)
[Return-to-throw pathway: Acknowledge expertise shift to coaching staff at a certain point (spin rate, velocity, location as objective markers). Work with coaches to establish objective comparison points to pre-injury data. Note post-Tommy John velocity increase phenomenon and associated internal impingement risk.]
[Contact sports pathway: Strength criteria followed by non-contact to contact progression.]
# 6. Testing Program
Owner: Eric Rash  |  Co-Pilot: Jeremy
Consolidated from V1 Sections 6, 7, and 8. Quality Assurance folded into general testing guidelines.
## 6.1 Purpose Statement & Justification
[Why do we test? Testing gives practitioners objective data so clearance decisions are based on evidence. Explain how testing establishes baselines, tracks progress, identifies asymmetries, and supports the return-to-play call.]
## 6.2 Literature Review
[For each test, provide peer-reviewed evidence supporting its inclusion. Organize by domain: strength, power, balance, range of motion. Brief plain-language summaries alongside citations. In-text citations reference the full bibliography in Section 12.]
## 6.3 Sport-Specific Applications
Co-Pilot: Jacob/Josh (upper body specific)
[Connect each test to the specific demands of the sports at Baylor. If a coach asks why their athlete is doing a particular test, the answer should be in this section.]
## 6.4 Standard Operating Procedures
### 6.4.1 General Testing Guidelines
[Warm-up protocols, environment setup, equipment calibration, athlete preparation, data recording. QA measures: inter-rater reliability, equipment maintenance, SOP review cycle.]
### 6.4.2 Lower Body Test SOPs
[Per test: equipment, setup, positioning, verbal cues, trials, rest intervals, data capture, common mistakes. Include photos/diagrams.]
### 6.4.3 Upper Body Test SOPs
[Same format. Include sport-specific procedural notes for throwing athletes.]
## 6.5 Sport-Specific Intake Test Matrix
V3 Update: Intake testing coordination is a care team decision per sport. The strength coach and athletic trainer must collaborate on logistics. Some sports (e.g., football) may handle all intake testing internally.
[TABLE]
| Sport | CMJ | Rebound | Y Bal (Ant) | Plyo Push-Up | Strength | Notes |
| Football | X | X | X | X | X | All internal |
| Basketball (M/W) | X | X | X | X | X |  |
| Soccer | X | X | X | X | X |  |
| Volleyball | X | X | X | X | X |  |
| Baseball | X | X | X | X | X | Throwing path |
| Softball | X | X | X | X | X | Throwing path |
| Track (Sprint) | X | X | X | TBD | X |  |
| Track (Throws) | X | X | X | X* | X | *May modify |
| Cross Country | X | X | X | - | X |  |
| Tennis | X | X | X | X | X |  |
| Equestrian | X | TBD | X | TBD | X | Fall risk |
| Golf | X | - | X | - | X |  |
[/TABLE]
[Finalize matrix with input from all sport ATCs and strength coaches. TBD items to be resolved before June 1 soft launch. Anticipated question for May 7: 'Who coordinates intake testing?' Answer: Care team decision per sport, with AT and strength coach collaborating.]
## 6.6 Standardized Fallback & Regression Options
- Plyometric push-up: Regression to modified (from knees) with notation in records
- Dynamometer testing: If open-chain extension causes pain, closed-chain isometric squat test as alternative, with supervisor approval
- All regressions must be documented and noted as modified in the testing record
[Complete list of fallback options for each test. Any substitution discussed with supervising AT or strength coach before administration.]
# 7. Metric Descriptions & Normative Data
Owner: Eric Rash  |  Co-Pilot: Jeremy / Jacob
## 7.1 Metric Reference Table
[Table: Test Name, Metric, What It Measures, Why It Matters, Sport Application, Normative Range. Every metric collected during testing should have a row.]
## 7.2 Normative Data & Benchmarks
Data Source Hierarchy:
- Primary: Vault Systems published normative reports (larger, de-identified D1 datasets). Access via Vault Hub > Normative Reports.
- Secondary: Internal Baylor data. Currently robust for CMJ across most sports. Limited for other measures.
- Approach: Use Vault data as primary benchmark. Supplement with internal data for comparison. Update annually.
Clinical Application:
[Normative data serves as additional justification, not a standalone gating criterion. Example: both limbs above normative benchmark may support clearance even with elevated asymmetry index. Sport-specific normative data tables housed in Appendix C.]
## 7.3 Asymmetry Thresholds
[Acceptable side-to-side differences per test. Kidman Labs collaboration status. Contingency: develop internally if external timeline slips.]
# 8. Chain of Command, Personnel & Communication
Owner: Eric Rash  |  Co-Pilot: Jeremy
## 8.1 Roles & Responsibilities (RACI Framework)
[Define key roles: AT, S&C Coach, Mental Health Provider, Sports Nutritionist, Team Physician, Head Coach. RACI matrix showing Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed at each phase.]
Phase ownership progression:
- Early rehab: Athletic trainer leads
- Late rehab / return-to-training: Strength & conditioning staff leads
- Return-to-competition: Sport coach determines game readiness (with input from AT and S&C)
## 8.2 Communication Flow
[Map how information moves between people during a rehab case. Who reports to whom, documentation handoffs at each stage, escalation triggers.]
## 8.3 Care Team Meetings vs. Sport Performance Meetings
V3 Addition: Expanded from V2 to clearly distinguish the two meeting types and propose a framework for sport performance meetings. This distinction was a major discussion point across all four team meetings.
[TABLE]
|  | Care Team Meeting | Sport Performance Meeting |
| Purpose | What is going on. Awareness-level updates across all domains (medical, academic, mental health, character formation). | How it is being done. Performance-specific: periodization, nutrition planning, technology integration, workload management, rehab progression specifics. |
| Scope | Broad. Connect dots across domains (e.g., academic struggles + practice behavior). All athletes. | Deep. Drill into performance details for mid-to-long-term cases. May also cover healthy athlete programming. |
| Attendees | AT, S&C, Mental Health, Nutrition, Academics, Character Formation, Sport Coach rep. | AT, S&C, Nutrition, Sport Coach (position/event coach if relevant). |
| Format | Roster review, brief updates per athlete. Keep moving. No deep dives. | Structured agenda: injury report (mid/long-term only), training status updates, action items, follow-up from previous meeting. |
| Frequency | Weekly (established) | Weekly or biweekly (proposed; requires leadership mandate) |
| Authority | Established by administration | Proposed. Requires Kenny/Carrie to formalize and mandate. |
[/TABLE]
V3 Note: This group does not have the authority to mandate sport performance meetings. A proposed framework and recommendation will be presented to leadership (Kenny/Carrie) for formal approval. The framework must be scalable across sports of different sizes and staffing models. Without defined structure, these meetings risk becoming redundant with care team meetings or devolving into unproductive check-the-box exercises.
Proposed Performance Meeting Structure:
- Clear objectives defined for each meeting (not open-ended discussion)
- Agenda template: mid-to-long-term injury updates only (short-term handled in care team), training program discussion, technology/data review, action items
- Time-boxed (30-45 minutes maximum depending on sport size)
- Notes/action items documented and followed up on at next meeting
- Scalable: works for a 12-athlete roster (e.g., tennis) and a 120-athlete roster (e.g., football)
## 8.4 Clearance Authority & Procedures
V3 Update: The April 15 discussion reinforced that clearance is a collective decision. Physician documentation practices vary widely and need to be standardized at a leadership level.
[Clearance requires sign-off from some or all of the following: Athletic Trainer, Team Physician, S&C staff, supervising administrator. The specific combination depends on injury tier.]
Key distinctions:
- Physician clearance = clearance to begin participating and progressing back into full participation. It does not equal clearance for unrestricted competition.
- Full return-to-competition readiness is determined by AT and performance staff in conjunction with the sport coach, after the physician has provided initial clearance.
- Physician-specific testing requirements (e.g., Biodex) are handled under the physician clearance checkpoint.
Physician Clearance Documentation:
V3 Addition: Currently, physician clearance documentation is inconsistent. Some physicians provide written clearance letters on letterhead (common with external/outside physicians). Others clear verbally or instruct the AT to note the clearance in their own records, which creates documentation gaps.
- External physicians: Already providing written clearance on their letterhead. Continue this practice.
- Internal physicians: Need to provide a written note, dictated visit note, or signed form documenting clearance. A verbal instruction to 'put it in your notes' is insufficient from a documentation standpoint.
- This is a leadership conversation. Carrie/Kenny should address standardized clearance documentation expectations with the physician group before the manual is presented to the larger group.
- If a standardized clearance sign-off form is developed (see Section 10.2), it would need to be reviewed and approved through appropriate channels before implementation.
Mental Health in the Clearance Process:
V3 Addition: Addresses the intersection of mental health readiness and clearance authority.
- Mental health check-ins are milestone checkpoints within the rehab progression (checkbox: completed). The outcome of the check-in is documented in the mental health provider's own records system, separate from the athletic training files.
- For the purposes of this manual, the clearance process documents that the check-in occurred, not the clinical details.
- If a mental health concern affects clearance readiness, it is raised in the care team meeting and addressed through the physician. The manual does not need to prescribe specific language for this scenario; it is handled through the existing clinical care team structure.
- Detailed mental health documentation is not placed in the athlete's performance or AT file. It remains with the mental health provider.
Nutrition Accountability:
V3 Clarification: Nutrition referrals follow the same model as mental health. The milestone checklist confirms the referral and meeting occurred. The care team meeting serves as the accountability mechanism. No separate referral form is required; adding another form does not solve compliance issues if the underlying meetings are not happening. The care team is the check-and-balance.
## 8.5 Athlete & Parent Communication Protocols
[At the initiation of rehab, communicate to the athlete that physician clearance and full return-to-competition are separate milestones. Where the athlete consents, proactive communication with parents about the clearance process helps prevent misunderstandings. Document the protocol without being so prescriptive it creates compliance risk.]
# 9. Data Repository & Visualization
Owner: Eric Rash
## 9.1 Data Collection, Storage & Folder Ownership
Folder Ownership Hierarchy:
- Level 1: Team ATC (primary owner)
- Level 2: ATC Supervisor (co-owner)
- Level 3: Department-level administrator (master access, extreme situations only)
Injury Folder Management:
- Each injury event gets its own folder within the athlete's directory
- Resolved injuries moved to archive
- Flare-ups/re-aggravations within a close timeframe: continue in existing folder
- Re-injuries separated by significant time: new folder, treated as new case
## 9.2 Athlete Profile Template
[One-page at-a-glance view: athlete info, test results by metric, progress chart. The document pulled up when Carrie or leadership asks for the big picture on a specific athlete.]
## 9.3 Load Monitoring Integration
[For sports using wearables (Catapult/Connects): how load data feeds into the RTP picture and informs clearance.]
## 9.4 Reporting & Dashboards
[Available reports: individual athlete progress, team-level summaries, compliance tracking. Each report has a clear audience and purpose.]
# 10. Forms & Documentation
Owner: JB
V3 Change: Significantly pared down from V2. The injury intake form was removed (initial documentation is captured in the AT's existing note/record for that visit). Mental health and nutrition referral forms were removed; accountability for those referrals is managed through the care team meeting mechanism, not additional paperwork. Remaining items: testing record form and clearance sign-off form.
## 10.1 Testing Record Form
V3 Note: This form provides a single place to summarize all testing data for an athlete across the entire RTP process. It is the go-to document when leadership asks for the complete picture on where an athlete stands. All testing data eventually feeds into this form. This will be a separate, editable digital file.
[Insert or reference the testing record form template. Fields should include: athlete name, sport, injury description, date of injury, testing dates, all test metrics with results, normative comparison, asymmetry indices, and a summary status. Capture any test modifications or regressions used.]
## 10.2 Clearance Sign-Off Form
V3 Update: This form needs to be more concrete than what currently exists. Currently, physician clearance is often verbal or captured only in AT notes, which creates documentation gaps.
[Insert or reference the clearance sign-off form template. This is the document that says: this athlete has met every criterion and is cleared to return. Required elements:]
- Athlete information and injury summary
- All testing criteria met (checkbox with date)
- Physician clearance obtained (checkbox with date; physician's own written documentation attached or on file)
- Mental health check-in completed (checkbox with date; details remain in MH provider's records)
- Nutrition check-in completed (checkbox with date)
- Signatures from applicable personnel per Section 8.4
V3 Note: For external physicians, their existing clearance letter/note satisfies the physician clearance element. For internal physicians, a standardized expectation for written clearance documentation needs to be established at the leadership level (Carrie/Kenny conversation with physician group). This form may need legal review before finalization. The form itself can be used as-is by the AT; the physician component is their own documentation attached to it.
# 11. Audit, Review & Continuous Improvement
Owner: Eric Rash
V3 Reinforcement: The April 15 discussion surfaced a concrete example of an athlete going an entire year without meeting with either nutrition or mental health despite being in a long-term rehab. This underscores the need for a review mechanism beyond 'trusting the process.'
Components:
- Post-case review: After each Tier 3 case reaches full return, review process for completeness and outcome
- Care team accountability: Mid-to-long-term cases reviewed in care team meetings at defined intervals to confirm all milestone checkpoints (including nutrition and mental health referrals) are being completed on schedule
- Athlete satisfaction survey: Include question on whether all parties were appropriately informed and involved
- Periodic audit: Quarterly or semester-based review of a sample of cases to identify systemic gaps
- Protocol update cycle: Annual review of full manual, incorporating audit findings and updated normative data
- Testing process audit: Regular check on testing procedures for consistency across administrators
# 12. References & Literature Citations
Owner: Jeremy
V3 Clarification: This section is the full bibliography. Section 6.2 (Literature Review) contains the narrative write-ups with in-text citations. This section compiles all cited sources in APA 7th edition format, organized by topic.
[Compile all citations: return-to-play criteria, force plate testing, mental health screening in athletes, nutritional assessment, load monitoring, and any other relevant domains.]
# 13. Appendices
## Appendix A: NCAA Performance Technology Best Practices
[Include or reference the NCAA document. Show where Baylor's protocols align and exceed.]
## Appendix B: Rollout Timeline & Communication Plan
V3 Update: Timeline refined. Physician briefing added before large group presentation. June 3 training moved to morning. Communication plan expanded to address multi-audience delivery.
[TABLE]
| Date | Milestone | Owner |
| April 29 | Dry run presentation (5-10 min review) | Eric Rash |
| Late April | Physician briefing on manual content (before large group) | Carrie |
| May 7 | SAS meeting update presentation + Q&A session | Eric Rash / Team |
| May 7 | Section co-pilot assignments confirmed | All |
| May (TBD) | Staff training on evaluation and rehab system | Performance Staff |
| May (TBD) | Carrie/Kenny discussion with physicians re: written clearance documentation | Carrie / Kenny |
| June 1 | Soft launch: ~90% operational. Intake system running. Manual substantially complete. | All |
| June 3 (AM) | Emergency preparedness day: 60-90 min staff training session (morning, done by lunch; EP training runs 3-7pm) | AT / S&C |
| June 8 | Summer school begins; new athletes arrive | - |
| August 2026 | Hard launch: Full manual finalized and fully operational | All |
[/TABLE]
Communication Plan:
V3 Addition: The manual will be delivered in multiple formats tailored to the audience:
- Full manual (Word document): The definitive reference for leadership (Kenny), compliance, and legal defensibility.
- Infographic / one-pager: Condensed version for physicians, coaches, and team meetings. Straightforward and to the point. Can be generated via NotebookLM or similar tool once the full manual is finalized.
- Presentation / slide deck: For the May 7 SAS meeting (abbreviated), June 3 staff training (comprehensive), and future onboarding.
- Phased rollout: Initial briefing at the SAS meeting (awareness), followed by deeper training in May/June, scaling into full operation by August.
## Appendix C: Sport-Specific Normative Data Tables
[Sport-specific data tables from Vault Systems and internal Baylor data. Organize by sport. Update annually.]
## Appendix D: Glossary of Terms
Owner: Jacob/Josh
[Define key terms and abbreviations used throughout the manual in plain language. Include: medical abbreviations (ADL, FMS, IMTP, WNL, etc.), testing terminology, protocol-specific terms. The goal is that anyone, regardless of clinical background, can follow the document.]
## Appendix E: Multi-Format Deliverables Plan
V3 Addition: Tracks the different output formats of the manual.
[TABLE]
| Format | Audience | Purpose | Status |
| Full Manual (Word) | Leadership, Compliance, Legal | Definitive reference | In progress |
| Infographic / One-Pager | Physicians, Coaches | Quick reference, meetings | After manual finalized |
| Slide Deck | SAS Meeting, Staff Training | Presentation, onboarding | After manual finalized |
| Physician Brief | Team Physicians | Pre-rollout alignment | Carrie to coordinate |
[/TABLE]
## Appendix F: May 7 SAS Meeting Q&A Preparation
V3 Addition: Anticipated questions and prepared responses for the May 7 presentation.
[TABLE]
| Anticipated Question | Prepared Response |
| This changes my processes. | [Draft response: The manual standardizes the framework, not the clinical judgment. Your expertise is still central to every decision.] |

58	# 1. Executive Summary
59	[This manual exists to solve a simple problem: when an athlete gets hurt at Baylor, everyone involved in getting them back on the field needs to be on the same page. Right now, that process looks different depending on the sport, the clinician, and the injury. This manual changes that.]
60	[Start here. Lay out in plain terms what the HPI is, what this manual covers, and who it applies to. Name the target rollout date (soft launch June 1, 2026; full launch August 2026). State the scope: every sport, every injury type, every duration. Explain why standardization matters, not just for the athlete, but for the practitioners protecting them and the institution backing them. Note alignment with NCAA Performance Technology Best Practices.]
61	# 2. Purpose Statement
62	[The core idea: every injured athlete at Baylor goes through the same evidence-based process before returning to play. No exceptions based on injury severity, sport, or timeline pressure. This section should answer three questions in order: (1) What problem does this solve? Inconsistent clearance processes expose athletes to re-injury risk and the institution to liability. (2) Why now? Leadership has directed universal application of post-injury testing. (3) What does success look like? A system where physical, mental health, and nutritional readiness are all evaluated before clearance, every single time.]
63	# 3. Return-to-Performance (RTP) Protocol Framework
64	This is the backbone of the manual. It defines the framework governing how injured athletes move from the training room back to competition.
65	## 3.1 Stage Overview
66	[Describe the five-stage return-to-performance framework. For each stage, state what happens, what the athlete needs to demonstrate before moving forward, and a general timeline. Address the difference between a two-week ankle sprain and a nine-month ACL reconstruction. The stages are the same; the pace is not.]
67	## 3.2 Injury Classification & Tiered Response
68	Not every injury needs the full battery. This tiered system gives clinicians and strength coaches the flexibility to match the response to the severity while keeping everyone inside a consistent framework.
69	### Tier 1: Minor Injuries (< 2 weeks)
70	[Quick turnaround injuries. If the athlete was still training during this window, quality of movement and how they look in practice largely dictates readiness. If they were unable to train for the full period, a quick strength screen or similar objective measure may be warranted. Abbreviated testing pathway. Define what qualifies, what testing is required (and what can be skipped), and what documentation is needed.]
71	### Tier 2: Moderate Injuries (2-4 weeks)
72	[Standard protocol. More gray area here. If the athlete was still training, rely on force plate data combined with visual assessment in practice. If the athlete was unable to train during this window, more objective testing is warranted. Define criteria, required testing, and where mental health and nutrition checkpoints enter the picture.]
73	### Tier 3: Severe / Surgical Injuries (4+ weeks or surgical)
74	[Full protocol, no shortcuts. Beginning, middle, and end checkpoints. Mandatory mental health and nutrition assessments at defined stages. Include requirement for documentation from external surgeons (surgical report, imaging, all outside physician records). This tier exists because the longer an athlete is out, the more variables affect their return.]
75	## 3.3 Workload Reintegration Guidelines
76	V2 Addition: Applies to both upper and lower body protocols. Modeled after professional team workload management practices.
77	[Define the workload reintegration model for athletes returning to sport participation. The progression framework should address controlled workload-only environments before transitioning to full sport participation with its inherent chaos and unpredictability.]
78	Recommended Progression Model:
79	- Phase 1 (~70% workload): Controlled, sport-specific activity only. No live competition or unpredictable scenarios.
80	- Phase 2 (~90% workload): Increased volume and intensity in controlled settings. Introduction of limited live scenarios.
81	- Phase 3 (~110% controlled / 80% live): Overload in controlled environment to build reserve; drop to ~80% load upon reintegration into full, chaotic participation (games, scrimmages).
82	- Phase 4 (100% full participation): Unrestricted competition. Ongoing monitoring as appropriate.
83	[Note: The strength and conditioning staff takes primary ownership of workload management at the later stages, with the sport coach determining competition readiness. For sports like football where snap counts drive participation, workload thresholds may be managed in terms of live reps rather than percentage of total practice volume. Include guidance on communication between AT, strength coach, and sport coach at each phase.]
84	# 4. Lower Body RTP Protocol
85	[Insert the complete lower body return-to-performance protocol. This protocol is being developed by Jeremy and is currently in draft form.]
86	## 4.1 Testing Battery
87	[List every test in the lower body protocol. For each one, state plainly: what it measures, how it is administered, and what a passing result looks like. Include force plate assessments (CMJ, rebound jump), hop tests, Y balance (anterior reach only), range of motion. A new staff member should be able to read this section and know exactly what to do.]
88	V2 Note: Y balance testing for lower body will use the anterior reach only, as this was identified as the most predictive measure. Full three-direction Y balance is no longer required for either screening or evaluation.
89	## 4.2 Rehabilitation Progression & Decision Framework
90	V2 Change: Sections 4.2 and 4.3 from V1 (Rehabilitation Progression and Return-to-Play Decision Matrix) have been consolidated. The rehab progression documents themselves serve as the decision framework. This section provides the purpose statement and context for how the documents are used.
91	[Purpose statement: This rehabilitation progression framework exists to guide the decision-making process using objective information and scientifically validated methods. The progression documents (maintained separately as working clinical documents) define the stage-by-stage exercises, volumes, intensities, and milestone criteria. They are intentionally kept flexible to accommodate clinical judgment on a case-by-case basis.]
92	Milestone Checkpoints (embedded in progression documents):
93	- Mental health check-in at key stages (initial evaluation, mid-rehab, pre-clearance)
94	- Nutrition check-in at key stages
95	- Documentation collection (especially for external surgeons: surgical reports, imaging, outside physician records)
96	- Physician clearance checkpoint
97	- Subjective questionnaire (lower extremity functional scale or equivalent)
98	[Reference the workload reintegration guidelines in Section 3.3 for the return-to-sport phase of progression.]
99	# 5. Upper Body RTP Protocol
100	[Insert the complete upper body return-to-performance protocol. The upper body protocol is less prescriptive with range-of-motion numbers because variability across sports and injury types is much wider. A baseball pitcher and a football lineman have very different demands.]
101	## 5.1 Testing Battery
102	V2 Updates: The upper body testing battery is intentionally less extensive than the lower body battery. The following tests were confirmed during team review:
103	- Strength testing (dynamometer/force-based)
104	- Y balance upper quarter (retained; CKC closed kinetic chain test removed per team consensus)
105	- Plyometric push-up (force plate-based; serves as both baseline intake test and return-to-play measure)
106	- Sport-specific functional tests (throwing metrics, contact drills) as applicable
107	[For each test, state what it measures, how it is administered, and what the benchmarks are. Call out sport-specific considerations directly (throwing athletes, contact sports, overhead athletes). Do not bury them in footnotes.]
108	V2 Note: The push-up/row endurance test on the Kaiser machine was discussed but tabled due to technical difficulties with functional trainer force output readings. If resolved, this may be added in a future revision.
109	## 5.2 Rehabilitation Progression & Decision Framework
110	V2 Change: Consolidated from V1 Sections 5.2 and 5.3, mirroring the lower body approach.
111	[Same structure as Section 4.2. Purpose statement for the upper body rehab progression documents. Include the same milestone checkpoints (mental health, nutrition, documentation, physician clearance, subjective questionnaire). Reference Section 3.3 for workload reintegration.]
112	Non-throwing athlete endpoint:
113	[Once strength criteria are met and physician clearance is obtained, the primary remaining steps are subjective assessments and workload reintegration through non-contact to contact progression.]
114	Biodex / Physician-Specific Testing:
115	[Some physicians (e.g., Dr. G) require Biodex testing before providing clearance. Rather than building this into the standard protocol, handle it under the physician clearance checkpoint. If the physician has not cleared the athlete, the protocol cannot be completed regardless of other test results. Note current Biodex availability limitations on campus.]
116	## 5.3 Sport-Specific Pathways (Throwing, Contact, Overhead)
117	[For throwing athletes: Define the return-to-throw pathway. Acknowledge that at a certain point, expertise shifts to the coaching staff (spin rate, velocity, location as objective markers). The athletic training/performance staff should work with coaches to establish objective comparison points to pre-injury data. Note the common post-Tommy John velocity increase phenomenon and associated internal impingement risk that typically follows, especially in athletes with prior shoulder history.]
118	[For contact sports: Define the contact reintegration pathway. For non-throwing upper body injuries in contact sports (e.g., football), the progression is primarily strength criteria followed by non-contact to contact progression.]
119	# 6. Testing Program
120	V2 Change: Consolidated from V1 Sections 6, 7, and 8. The Testing Purpose Statement, Rationale & Test Justifications, and Test SOPs were combined into a single testing section to reduce redundancy. Quality Assurance is now folded into the general testing guidelines rather than standing as a separate subsection.
121	## 6.1 Purpose Statement & Justification
122	[Why do we test? Testing exists to give practitioners objective data so that clearance decisions are based on evidence, not gut feel. Explain how testing data establishes baselines, tracks progress during rehab, identifies asymmetries, and supports the final return-to-play call. Write it so that anyone from a head coach to a new GA understands the reasoning behind every test an athlete goes through.]
123	## 6.2 Literature Review
124	[For each test in the battery, provide the peer-reviewed evidence supporting its inclusion. Organize by domain: strength, power, balance, range of motion. Keep it accessible. A citation list is necessary, but a brief plain-language summary of what the research shows is just as important.]
125	## 6.3 Sport-Specific Applications
126	[Connect each test to the specific demands of the sports at Baylor. Why does this test matter for football? For soccer? For baseball? If a coach asks why their athlete is doing a particular test, the answer should be in this section.]
127	## 6.4 Standard Operating Procedures
128	V2 Change: Testing guidelines and SOPs have been combined into a single section, split by body region. Quality assurance (inter-rater reliability, equipment maintenance, SOP review cycle) is integrated into the general guidelines rather than standing alone.
129	### 6.4.1 General Testing Guidelines
130	[Cover the basics that apply to every test: warm-up protocols, environment setup, equipment calibration, athlete preparation, data recording procedures. Include quality assurance measures: inter-rater reliability procedures, equipment maintenance schedules, and the review cycle for updating SOPs as methods improve.]
131	### 6.4.2 Lower Body Test SOPs
132	[For each lower body test: equipment needed, setup instructions, athlete positioning, verbal cues, number of trials, rest intervals, data capture method, and common mistakes. Include photos or diagrams wherever they help.]
133	### 6.4.3 Upper Body Test SOPs
134	[For each upper body test: same format as 6.4.2. Include sport-specific procedural notes for throwing athletes where applicable.]
135	## 6.5 Sport-Specific Intake Test Matrix
136	V2 Addition: Not all sports require all intake tests. This matrix defines which baseline tests are administered for each sport.
137	[TABLE]
138	| Sport | CMJ | Rebound | Y Bal (Ant) | Plyo Push-Up | Strength | Notes |
139	| Football | X | X | X | X | X |  |
140	| Basketball (M/W) | X | X | X | X | X |  |
141	| Soccer | X | X | X | X | X |  |
142	| Volleyball | X | X | X | X | X |  |
143	| Baseball | X | X | X | X | X | Throwing pathway |
144	| Softball | X | X | X | X | X | Throwing pathway |
145	| Track & Field (Sprint) | X | X | X | TBD | X |  |
146	| Track & Field (Throws) | X | X | X | X* | X | *May modify |
147	| Cross Country | X | X | X | - | X |  |
148	| Tennis | X | X | X | X | X |  |
149	| Equestrian | X | TBD | X | TBD | X | Fall risk sport |
150	| Golf | X | - | X | - | X |  |
151	[/TABLE]
152	[Finalize this matrix with input from all sport ATCs and strength coaches. Designate which tests are mandatory vs. optional for each sport. TBD items to be resolved before June 1 soft launch.]
153	## 6.6 Standardized Fallback & Regression Options
154	V2 Addition: For athletes who cannot perform a standard test (e.g., limited upper body strength, post-surgical restrictions, physician-specific requirements), standardized regression options ensure consistent data collection.
155	- Plyometric push-up: Regression to modified (from knees) with notation in records
156	- Dynamometer testing: If open-chain extension causes pain, closed-chain isometric squat test (GR-specific knee isometric) as alternative, with supervisor approval
157	- All regressions must be documented and noted as modified in the testing record
158	[Define the complete list of fallback options for each test. Any substitution should be discussed with the supervising AT or strength coach before administration.]
159	# 7. Metric Descriptions & Normative Data
160	This section is the reference guide for every number that comes out of testing. If someone looks at a report and asks what a metric means or whether a value is good or bad, the answer should be here.
161	## 7.1 Metric Reference Table
162	[Build a table: Test Name, Metric, What It Measures, Why It Matters, Sport Application, and Normative Range. Every metric collected during testing should have a row. No orphan data points.]
163	## 7.2 Normative Data & Benchmarks
164	V2 Update: The normative data strategy was discussed at length and clarified as follows:
165	Data Source Hierarchy:
166	- Primary source: Vault Systems published normative reports. These provide larger, de-identified datasets across Division 1 populations. Available sports include football, men's basketball, women's basketball, baseball, softball, women's volleyball, soccer, track & field, and others. Access via Vault Hub > Normative Reports.
167	- Secondary source: Internal Baylor data. Currently robust for countermovement jump (CMJ) across most sports. Limited for rebound jump, force frame, and other measures.
168	- Approach: Use Vault data as the primary benchmark. Supplement with internal data where available for comparison. Do not exclusively rely on internal data until datasets are sufficient across all tests and sports.
169	Update Cadence:
170	[Normative data will be updated annually. Vault typically publishes updated reports each summer using data collected within that calendar year. Internal data should be refreshed on the same cycle. This is especially important given the ongoing changes in collegiate athletics (roster turnover, development timelines, NIL impacts on athlete populations).]
171	Clinical Application:
172	[Normative data serves as an additional justification tool, not a standalone gating criterion. Example: If an athlete shows an asymmetry index above the threshold but both limbs score above the normative benchmark for their population, that context may support a clearance decision. Normative data should not be used to hold an athlete out if all other criteria are met. Sport-specific normative data tables will be housed in Appendix C.]
173	Action Item: Coordinate with Vault Systems to obtain comprehensive, sport-specific normative data sets beyond what is currently published. Request pending as of April 2026.
174	## 7.3 Asymmetry Thresholds
175	[Define acceptable side-to-side differences for each relevant test (e.g., limb symmetry index). Explain what it means clinically when an athlete exceeds the threshold. Reference the Kidman Labs collaboration on asymmetry threshold development. Note current status: project has been handed to Kidman Labs with limited recent progress. Contingency: develop internally if external timeline slips further.]
176	# 8. Chain of Command, Personnel & Communication
177	V2 Change: Expanded from V1 Section 10 to include athlete/parent communication protocols and high performance meeting structure. Clearance authority is integrated here rather than standing as a separate concept.
178	## 8.1 Roles & Responsibilities (RACI Framework)
179	[Define the key roles: Athletic Trainer, Strength & Conditioning Coach, Mental Health Provider, Sports Nutritionist, Team Physician, Head Coach. For each role, state what they own in the RTP process and what decisions they can make. Incorporate a RACI-style matrix showing who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed at each phase of the rehab and return-to-play process. A new hire should know exactly where they fit on day one.]
180	Phase ownership progression:
181	- Early rehab: Athletic trainer leads
182	- Late rehab / return-to-training: Strength & conditioning staff leads
183	- Return-to-competition: Sport coach determines game readiness (with input from AT and S&C)
184	## 8.2 Communication Flow & High Performance Meetings
185	[Map out how information moves between people during a rehab case. Who reports to whom, what documentation gets handed off at each stage, and what triggers an escalation.]
186	High Performance Meetings:
187	V2 Addition: The high performance meeting (or care team plus meeting) is the primary mechanism for ensuring communication between athletic training, strength & conditioning, sport coaching, nutrition, and mental health during active rehab cases.
188	- Structure: Focused on performance and return-to-play specifics (distinct from higher-level care team meetings that address the 'what' not the 'how')
189	- Attendance: Recommendation is mandatory for all parties involved in active rehab cases
190	- Expectations and follow-up responsibilities need to be clearly defined
191	- Escalation path: Performance staff to bring structure/mandate recommendation to senior leadership (Kenny) for formal approval
192	## 8.3 Clearance Authority & Procedures
193	V2 Update: Clearance authority was a significant discussion point across both team meetings. The following framework balances specificity for legal defensibility with flexibility for clinical reality.
194	[Define clearance authority by tier. For Tier 3 injuries (4+ weeks or surgical), clearance requires communication and sign-off from some or all of the following personnel: Athletic Trainer, Team Physician, Strength & Conditioning staff, and supervising administrator.]
195	Key distinctions:
196	- Physician clearance = clearance to begin participating and progressing back into full participation. It does not equal clearance for full, unrestricted competition.
197	- Full return-to-competition readiness is determined by the athletic training and performance staff in conjunction with the sport coach, after the physician has provided initial clearance.
198	- Physician-specific testing requirements (e.g., Biodex for certain surgeons) are handled under the physician clearance checkpoint. If the physician has not cleared, the protocol is not complete.
199	[This distinction must be communicated to the athlete (and, where appropriate, parents) at the outset of the rehab process to manage expectations. See Section 8.4.]
200	## 8.4 Athlete & Parent Communication Protocols
201	V2 Addition: Addresses a gap identified during team discussion regarding miscommunication when physicians clear athletes for participation.
202	[At the initiation of the rehab process, clearly communicate to the athlete that physician clearance and full return-to-competition are separate milestones. The physician clears them to begin the return-to-sport progression; the performance and medical staff collectively determine when the athlete is ready for unrestricted competition.]
203	[Address parent communication: While FERPA/HIPAA considerations apply, in practice, parents are frequently involved. Where the athlete consents, proactive communication with parents about the clearance process helps prevent misunderstandings (e.g., 'the doctor said I'm cleared, why can't I play?'). Document this communication protocol without being so prescriptive that it creates compliance risk. Defer to Carrie/administration on legal boundaries.]
204	# 9. Data Repository & Visualization
205	## 9.1 Data Collection, Storage & Folder Ownership
206	V2 Update: Folder ownership hierarchy was discussed and defined.
207	[Walk through the data workflow from test day to the repository. How does data get entered? Where does it live? What are the naming conventions and folder structures? Who has access?]
208	Folder Ownership Hierarchy:
209	- Level 1: Team ATC (primary owner)
210	- Level 2: ATC Supervisor (co-owner)
211	- Level 3: Department-level administrator (master access, for extreme situations such as full team staff turnover)
212	Injury Folder Management:
213	- Each injury event gets its own folder within the athlete's directory
214	- Resolved injuries are moved to archive
215	- Flare-ups or re-aggravations within a close timeframe: continue in the existing folder
216	- Re-injuries separated by significant time (e.g., freshman injury recurring as a senior): new folder, treated as a new case
217	## 9.2 Athlete Profile Template
218	[Include the one-page athlete profile template. At-a-glance view: athlete info, test results by metric, progress chart. This is the document pulled up in meetings.]
219	## 9.3 Load Monitoring Integration
220	[For sports using wearable technology (Catapult/Connects), describe how load monitoring data feeds into the RTP picture and informs clearance decisions.]
221	## 9.4 Reporting & Dashboards
222	[Describe available reports and dashboards: individual athlete progress, team-level summaries, compliance tracking. Each report should have a clear audience and purpose.]
223	# 10. Forms & Documentation
224	V2 Change: Streamlined from V1 Section 12. Mental health and nutrition referral forms removed as standalone subsections. Referrals to nutrition and mental health are documented within the rehab progression milestone checkpoints (Sections 4.2/5.2) and noted in the athlete's case record. No separate referral form is needed at this time; referral documentation follows existing physician/clinical workflows.
225	## 10.1 Injury Intake Form
226	[Insert fillable injury intake form. This is the starting point for every case.]
227	## 10.2 Testing Record Form
228	[Insert fillable testing record form. One for each protocol stage. Include fields for documenting any test modifications or regressions used.]
229	## 10.3 Clearance Sign-Off Form
230	[Insert fillable clearance form. Include required signatures from applicable personnel per Section 8.3. Checkpoint confirmations for: all testing criteria met, physician clearance obtained, mental health check-in completed, nutrition check-in completed.]
231	# 11. Audit, Review & Continuous Improvement
232	V2 Addition: This section was added in response to team discussion about the need for a review mechanism to identify gaps and improve outcomes over time.
233	[Define the process for auditing rehab cases after completion. How frequently are cases reviewed? Who conducts the review? What is being evaluated (e.g., were all protocol steps followed, were outcomes consistent with expectations, were there communication breakdowns)?]
234	Components:
235	- Post-case review: After each Tier 3 case reaches full return, review the process for completeness and outcome
236	- Athlete satisfaction survey: Include a question on whether all parties were appropriately informed and involved in the process
237	- Periodic audit: Quarterly or semester-based review of a sample of cases to identify systemic gaps
238	- Protocol update cycle: Annual review of the full manual, incorporating audit findings and updated normative data
239	- Testing process audit: Regular check on testing procedures to ensure consistency across administrators
240	# 12. References & Literature Citations
241	[Every claim in this manual should trace back to a source. Compile all citations in APA 7th edition format, organized by topic: return-to-play criteria, force plate testing, mental health screening in athletes, nutritional assessment, load monitoring, and any other relevant domains. This section is what makes the manual defensible.]
242	# 13. Appendices
243	## Appendix A: NCAA Performance Technology Best Practices
244	[Include or reference the NCAA performance technology best practices document. Show where Baylor's protocols align and note any areas where we exceed the recommendations.]
245	## Appendix B: Rollout Timeline & Communication Plan
246	V2 Update: Timeline refined based on team discussions.
247	[TABLE]
248	| Date | Milestone | Owner |
249	| April 29 | Dry run presentation (5-10 min review) | Eric Rash |
250	| May 7 | SAS meeting update presentation | Eric Rash / Team |
251	| May 7 | Section co-pilot assignments due | All |
252	| May (TBD) | Staff training on evaluation and rehab system | Performance Staff |
253	| June 1 | Soft launch: Intake system operational | All |
254	| June 3 | Emergency preparedness day: 60-90 min staff training session | AT / S&C |
255	| June 8 | Summer school begins; new athletes arrive | - |
256	| August 2026 | Hard launch: Full manual complete and operational | All |
257	[/TABLE]
258	## Appendix C: Sport-Specific Normative Data Tables
259	V2 Addition: Centralized location for all normative data referenced in Section 7.2.
260	[Include sport-specific data tables from Vault Systems normative reports and internal Baylor data. Organize by sport. For each sport, include: data source, sample description (e.g., Division 1, calendar year), metrics reported, and percentile distributions. Update annually.]
261	## Appendix D: Glossary of Terms
262	[Define key terms used throughout this manual in plain language.]
263	## Appendix E: Revision History
264	[TABLE]
265	| Version | Date | Author | Changes |
266	| 1.0 | March 2026 | Eric Rash | Initial draft outline |
267	| 2.0 | April 15, 2026 | Eric Rash | Consolidated rehab progression & decision matrix sections; merged testing guidelines, SOPs, and QA into unified Testing Program section; added workload reintegration guidelines; added sport-specific intake test matrix; added standardized fallback/regression options; clarified normative data strategy (Vault primary, internal secondary); defined clearance authority framework; added athlete/parent communication protocols; added high performance meeting structure; defined folder ownership hierarchy and injury folder management; removed standalone referral form sections; added Audit & Continuous Improvement section; added sport-specific normative data appendix; updated rollout timeline |

# 1. Executive Summary
[This manual exists to solve a simple problem: when an athlete gets hurt at Baylor, everyone involved in getting them back on the field needs to be on the same page. Right now, that process looks different depending on the sport, the clinician, and the injury. This manual changes that.]
[Start here. Lay out in plain terms what the HPI is, what this manual covers, and who it applies to. Name the target rollout date (soft launch June 1, 2026; full launch August 2026). State the scope: every sport, every injury type, every duration. Explain why standardization matters, not just for the athlete, but for the practitioners protecting them and the institution backing them. Note alignment with NCAA Performance Technology Best Practices.]
# 2. Purpose Statement
[The core idea: every injured athlete at Baylor goes through the same evidence-based process before returning to play. No exceptions based on injury severity, sport, or timeline pressure. This section should answer three questions in order: (1) What problem does this solve? Inconsistent clearance processes expose athletes to re-injury risk and the institution to liability. (2) Why now? Leadership has directed universal application of post-injury testing. (3) What does success look like? A system where physical, mental health, and nutritional readiness are all evaluated before clearance, every single time.]
# 3. Return-to-Performance (RTP) Protocol Framework
This is the backbone of the manual. It defines the framework governing how injured athletes move from the training room back to competition.
## 3.1 Stage Overview
[Describe the five-stage return-to-performance framework. For each stage, state what happens, what the athlete needs to demonstrate before moving forward, and a general timeline. Address the difference between a two-week ankle sprain and a nine-month ACL reconstruction. The stages are the same; the pace is not.]
## 3.2 Injury Classification & Tiered Response
Not every injury needs the full battery. This tiered system gives clinicians and strength coaches the flexibility to match the response to the severity while keeping everyone inside a consistent framework.
### Tier 1: Minor Injuries (< 2 weeks)
[Quick turnaround injuries. If the athlete was still training during this window, quality of movement and how they look in practice largely dictates readiness. If they were unable to train for the full period, a quick strength screen or similar objective measure may be warranted. Abbreviated testing pathway. Define what qualifies, what testing is required (and what can be skipped), and what documentation is needed.]
### Tier 2: Moderate Injuries (2-4 weeks)
[Standard protocol. More gray area here. If the athlete was still training, rely on force plate data combined with visual assessment in practice. If the athlete was unable to train during this window, more objective testing is warranted. Define criteria, required testing, and where mental health and nutrition checkpoints enter the picture.]
### Tier 3: Severe / Surgical Injuries (4+ weeks or surgical)
[Full protocol, no shortcuts. Beginning, middle, and end checkpoints. Mandatory mental health and nutrition assessments at defined stages. Include requirement for documentation from external surgeons (surgical report, imaging, all outside physician records). This tier exists because the longer an athlete is out, the more variables affect their return.]
## 3.3 Workload Reintegration Guidelines
V2 Addition: Applies to both upper and lower body protocols. Modeled after professional team workload management practices.
[Define the workload reintegration model for athletes returning to sport participation. The progression framework should address controlled workload-only environments before transitioning to full sport participation with its inherent chaos and unpredictability.]
Recommended Progression Model:
- Phase 1 (~70% workload): Controlled, sport-specific activity only. No live competition or unpredictable scenarios.
- Phase 2 (~90% workload): Increased volume and intensity in controlled settings. Introduction of limited live scenarios.
- Phase 3 (~110% controlled / 80% live): Overload in controlled environment to build reserve; drop to ~80% load upon reintegration into full, chaotic participation (games, scrimmages).
- Phase 4 (100% full participation): Unrestricted competition. Ongoing monitoring as appropriate.
[Note: The strength and conditioning staff takes primary ownership of workload management at the later stages, with the sport coach determining competition readiness. For sports like football where snap counts drive participation, workload thresholds may be managed in terms of live reps rather than percentage of total practice volume. Include guidance on communication between AT, strength coach, and sport coach at each phase.]
# 4. Lower Body RTP Protocol
[Insert the complete lower body return-to-performance protocol. This protocol is being developed by Jeremy and is currently in draft form.]
## 4.1 Testing Battery
[List every test in the lower body protocol. For each one, state plainly: what it measures, how it is administered, and what a passing result looks like. Include force plate assessments (CMJ, rebound jump), hop tests, Y balance (anterior reach only), range of motion. A new staff member should be able to read this section and know exactly what to do.]
V2 Note: Y balance testing for lower body will use the anterior reach only, as this was identified as the most predictive measure. Full three-direction Y balance is no longer required for either screening or evaluation.
## 4.2 Rehabilitation Progression & Decision Framework
V2 Change: Sections 4.2 and 4.3 from V1 (Rehabilitation Progression and Return-to-Play Decision Matrix) have been consolidated. The rehab progression documents themselves serve as the decision framework. This section provides the purpose statement and context for how the documents are used.
[Purpose statement: This rehabilitation progression framework exists to guide the decision-making process using objective information and scientifically validated methods. The progression documents (maintained separately as working clinical documents) define the stage-by-stage exercises, volumes, intensities, and milestone criteria. They are intentionally kept flexible to accommodate clinical judgment on a case-by-case basis.]
Milestone Checkpoints (embedded in progression documents):
- Mental health check-in at key stages (initial evaluation, mid-rehab, pre-clearance)
- Nutrition check-in at key stages
- Documentation collection (especially for external surgeons: surgical reports, imaging, outside physician records)
- Physician clearance checkpoint
- Subjective questionnaire (lower extremity functional scale or equivalent)
[Reference the workload reintegration guidelines in Section 3.3 for the return-to-sport phase of progression.]
# 5. Upper Body RTP Protocol
[Insert the complete upper body return-to-performance protocol. The upper body protocol is less prescriptive with range-of-motion numbers because variability across sports and injury types is much wider. A baseball pitcher and a football lineman have very different demands.]
## 5.1 Testing Battery
V2 Updates: The upper body testing battery is intentionally less extensive than the lower body battery. The following tests were confirmed during team review:
- Strength testing (dynamometer/force-based)
- Y balance upper quarter (retained; CKC closed kinetic chain test removed per team consensus)
- Plyometric push-up (force plate-based; serves as both baseline intake test and return-to-play measure)
- Sport-specific functional tests (throwing metrics, contact drills) as applicable
[For each test, state what it measures, how it is administered, and what the benchmarks are. Call out sport-specific considerations directly (throwing athletes, contact sports, overhead athletes). Do not bury them in footnotes.]
V2 Note: The push-up/row endurance test on the Kaiser machine was discussed but tabled due to technical difficulties with functional trainer force output readings. If resolved, this may be added in a future revision.
## 5.2 Rehabilitation Progression & Decision Framework
V2 Change: Consolidated from V1 Sections 5.2 and 5.3, mirroring the lower body approach.
[Same structure as Section 4.2. Purpose statement for the upper body rehab progression documents. Include the same milestone checkpoints (mental health, nutrition, documentation, physician clearance, subjective questionnaire). Reference Section 3.3 for workload reintegration.]
Non-throwing athlete endpoint:
[Once strength criteria are met and physician clearance is obtained, the primary remaining steps are subjective assessments and workload reintegration through non-contact to contact progression.]
Biodex / Physician-Specific Testing:
[Some physicians (e.g., Dr. G) require Biodex testing before providing clearance. Rather than building this into the standard protocol, handle it under the physician clearance checkpoint. If the physician has not cleared the athlete, the protocol cannot be completed regardless of other test results. Note current Biodex availability limitations on campus.]
## 5.3 Sport-Specific Pathways (Throwing, Contact, Overhead)
[For throwing athletes: Define the return-to-throw pathway. Acknowledge that at a certain point, expertise shifts to the coaching staff (spin rate, velocity, location as objective markers). The athletic training/performance staff should work with coaches to establish objective comparison points to pre-injury data. Note the common post-Tommy John velocity increase phenomenon and associated internal impingement risk that typically follows, especially in athletes with prior shoulder history.]
[For contact sports: Define the contact reintegration pathway. For non-throwing upper body injuries in contact sports (e.g., football), the progression is primarily strength criteria followed by non-contact to contact progression.]
# 6. Testing Program
V2 Change: Consolidated from V1 Sections 6, 7, and 8. The Testing Purpose Statement, Rationale & Test Justifications, and Test SOPs were combined into a single testing section to reduce redundancy. Quality Assurance is now folded into the general testing guidelines rather than standing as a separate subsection.
## 6.1 Purpose Statement & Justification
[Why do we test? Testing exists to give practitioners objective data so that clearance decisions are based on evidence, not gut feel. Explain how testing data establishes baselines, tracks progress during rehab, identifies asymmetries, and supports the final return-to-play call. Write it so that anyone from a head coach to a new GA understands the reasoning behind every test an athlete goes through.]
## 6.2 Literature Review
[For each test in the battery, provide the peer-reviewed evidence supporting its inclusion. Organize by domain: strength, power, balance, range of motion. Keep it accessible. A citation list is necessary, but a brief plain-language summary of what the research shows is just as important.]
## 6.3 Sport-Specific Applications
[Connect each test to the specific demands of the sports at Baylor. Why does this test matter for football? For soccer? For baseball? If a coach asks why their athlete is doing a particular test, the answer should be in this section.]
## 6.4 Standard Operating Procedures
V2 Change: Testing guidelines and SOPs have been combined into a single section, split by body region. Quality assurance (inter-rater reliability, equipment maintenance, SOP review cycle) is integrated into the general guidelines rather than standing alone.
### 6.4.1 General Testing Guidelines
[Cover the basics that apply to every test: warm-up protocols, environment setup, equipment calibration, athlete preparation, data recording procedures. Include quality assurance measures: inter-rater reliability procedures, equipment maintenance schedules, and the review cycle for updating SOPs as methods improve.]
### 6.4.2 Lower Body Test SOPs
[For each lower body test: equipment needed, setup instructions, athlete positioning, verbal cues, number of trials, rest intervals, data capture method, and common mistakes. Include photos or diagrams wherever they help.]
### 6.4.3 Upper Body Test SOPs
[For each upper body test: same format as 6.4.2. Include sport-specific procedural notes for throwing athletes where applicable.]
## 6.5 Sport-Specific Intake Test Matrix
V2 Addition: Not all sports require all intake tests. This matrix defines which baseline tests are administered for each sport.

[/TABLE]
[Finalize this matrix with input from all sport ATCs and strength coaches. Designate which tests are mandatory vs. optional for each sport. TBD items to be resolved before June 1 soft launch.]
## 6.6 Standardized Fallback & Regression Options
V2 Addition: For athletes who cannot perform a standard test (e.g., limited upper body strength, post-surgical restrictions, physician-specific requirements), standardized regression options ensure consistent data collection.
- Plyometric push-up: Regression to modified (from knees) with notation in records
- Dynamometer testing: If open-chain extension causes pain, closed-chain isometric squat test (GR-specific knee isometric) as alternative, with supervisor approval
- All regressions must be documented and noted as modified in the testing record
[Define the complete list of fallback options for each test. Any substitution should be discussed with the supervising AT or strength coach before administration.]
# 7. Metric Descriptions & Normative Data
This section is the reference guide for every number that comes out of testing. If someone looks at a report and asks what a metric means or whether a value is good or bad, the answer should be here.
## 7.1 Metric Reference Table
[Build a table: Test Name, Metric, What It Measures, Why It Matters, Sport Application, and Normative Range. Every metric collected during testing should have a row. No orphan data points.]
## 7.2 Normative Data & Benchmarks
V2 Update: The normative data strategy was discussed at length and clarified as follows:
Data Source Hierarchy:
- Primary source: Vault Systems published normative reports. These provide larger, de-identified datasets across Division 1 populations. Available sports include football, men's basketball, women's basketball, baseball, softball, women's volleyball, soccer, track & field, and others. Access via Vault Hub > Normative Reports.
- Secondary source: Internal Baylor data. Currently robust for countermovement jump (CMJ) across most sports. Limited for rebound jump, force frame, and other measures.
- Approach: Use Vault data as the primary benchmark. Supplement with internal data where available for comparison. Do not exclusively rely on internal data until datasets are sufficient across all tests and sports.
Update Cadence:
[Normative data will be updated annually. Vault typically publishes updated reports each summer using data collected within that calendar year. Internal data should be refreshed on the same cycle. This is especially important given the ongoing changes in collegiate athletics (roster turnover, development timelines, NIL impacts on athlete populations).]
Clinical Application:
[Normative data serves as an additional justification tool, not a standalone gating criterion. Example: If an athlete shows an asymmetry index above the threshold but both limbs score above the normative benchmark for their population, that context may support a clearance decision. Normative data should not be used to hold an athlete out if all other criteria are met. Sport-specific normative data tables will be housed in Appendix C.]
Action Item: Coordinate with Vault Systems to obtain comprehensive, sport-specific normative data sets beyond what is currently published. Request pending as of April 2026.
## 7.3 Asymmetry Thresholds
[Define acceptable side-to-side differences for each relevant test (e.g., limb symmetry index). Explain what it means clinically when an athlete exceeds the threshold. Reference the Kidman Labs collaboration on asymmetry threshold development. Note current status: project has been handed to Kidman Labs with limited recent progress. Contingency: develop internally if external timeline slips further.]
# 8. Chain of Command, Personnel & Communication
V2 Change: Expanded from V1 Section 10 to include athlete/parent communication protocols and high performance meeting structure. Clearance authority is integrated here rather than standing as a separate concept.
## 8.1 Roles & Responsibilities (RACI Framework)
[Define the key roles: Athletic Trainer, Strength & Conditioning Coach, Mental Health Provider, Sports Nutritionist, Team Physician, Head Coach. For each role, state what they own in the RTP process and what decisions they can make. Incorporate a RACI-style matrix showing who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed at each phase of the rehab and return-to-play process. A new hire should know exactly where they fit on day one.]
Phase ownership progression:
- Early rehab: Athletic trainer leads
- Late rehab / return-to-training: Strength & conditioning staff leads
- Return-to-competition: Sport coach determines game readiness (with input from AT and S&C)
## 8.2 Communication Flow & High Performance Meetings
[Map out how information moves between people during a rehab case. Who reports to whom, what documentation gets handed off at each stage, and what triggers an escalation.]
High Performance Meetings:
V2 Addition: The high performance meeting (or care team plus meeting) is the primary mechanism for ensuring communication between athletic training, strength & conditioning, sport coaching, nutrition, and mental health during active rehab cases.
- Structure: Focused on performance and return-to-play specifics (distinct from higher-level care team meetings that address the 'what' not the 'how')
- Attendance: Recommendation is mandatory for all parties involved in active rehab cases
- Expectations and follow-up responsibilities need to be clearly defined
- Escalation path: Performance staff to bring structure/mandate recommendation to senior leadership (Kenny) for formal approval
## 8.3 Clearance Authority & Procedures
V2 Update: Clearance authority was a significant discussion point across both team meetings. The following framework balances specificity for legal defensibility with flexibility for clinical reality.
[Define clearance authority by tier. For Tier 3 injuries (4+ weeks or surgical), clearance requires communication and sign-off from some or all of the following personnel: Athletic Trainer, Team Physician, Strength & Conditioning staff, and supervising administrator.]
Key distinctions:
- Physician clearance = clearance to begin participating and progressing back into full participation. It does not equal clearance for full, unrestricted competition.
- Full return-to-competition readiness is determined by the athletic training and performance staff in conjunction with the sport coach, after the physician has provided initial clearance.
- Physician-specific testing requirements (e.g., Biodex for certain surgeons) are handled under the physician clearance checkpoint. If the physician has not cleared, the protocol is not complete.
[This distinction must be communicated to the athlete (and, where appropriate, parents) at the outset of the rehab process to manage expectations. See Section 8.4.]
## 8.4 Athlete & Parent Communication Protocols
V2 Addition: Addresses a gap identified during team discussion regarding miscommunication when physicians clear athletes for participation.
[At the initiation of the rehab process, clearly communicate to the athlete that physician clearance and full return-to-competition are separate milestones. The physician clears them to begin the return-to-sport progression; the performance and medical staff collectively determine when the athlete is ready for unrestricted competition.]
[Address parent communication: While FERPA/HIPAA considerations apply, in practice, parents are frequently involved. Where the athlete consents, proactive communication with parents about the clearance process helps prevent misunderstandings (e.g., 'the doctor said I'm cleared, why can't I play?'). Document this communication protocol without being so prescriptive that it creates compliance risk. Defer to Carrie/administration on legal boundaries.]
# 9. Data Repository & Visualization
## 9.1 Data Collection, Storage & Folder Ownership
V2 Update: Folder ownership hierarchy was discussed and defined.
[Walk through the data workflow from test day to the repository. How does data get entered? Where does it live? What are the naming conventions and folder structures? Who has access?]
Folder Ownership Hierarchy:
- Level 1: Team ATC (primary owner)
- Level 2: ATC Supervisor (co-owner)
- Level 3: Department-level administrator (master access, for extreme situations such as full team staff turnover)
Injury Folder Management:
- Each injury event gets its own folder within the athlete's directory
- Resolved injuries are moved to archive
- Flare-ups or re-aggravations within a close timeframe: continue in the existing folder
- Re-injuries separated by significant time (e.g., freshman injury recurring as a senior): new folder, treated as a new case
## 9.2 Athlete Profile Template
[Include the one-page athlete profile template. At-a-glance view: athlete info, test results by metric, progress chart. This is the document pulled up in meetings.]
## 9.3 Load Monitoring Integration
[For sports using wearable technology (Catapult/Connects), describe how load monitoring data feeds into the RTP picture and informs clearance decisions.]
## 9.4 Reporting & Dashboards
[Describe available reports and dashboards: individual athlete progress, team-level summaries, compliance tracking. Each report should have a clear audience and purpose.]
# 10. Forms & Documentation
V2 Change: Streamlined from V1 Section 12. Mental health and nutrition referral forms removed as standalone subsections. Referrals to nutrition and mental health are documented within the rehab progression milestone checkpoints (Sections 4.2/5.2) and noted in the athlete's case record. No separate referral form is needed at this time; referral documentation follows existing physician/clinical workflows.
## 10.1 Injury Intake Form
[Insert fillable injury intake form. This is the starting point for every case.]
## 10.2 Testing Record Form
[Insert fillable testing record form. One for each protocol stage. Include fields for documenting any test modifications or regressions used.]
## 10.3 Clearance Sign-Off Form
[Insert fillable clearance form. Include required signatures from applicable personnel per Section 8.3. Checkpoint confirmations for: all testing criteria met, physician clearance obtained, mental health check-in completed, nutrition check-in completed.]
# 11. Audit, Review & Continuous Improvement
V2 Addition: This section was added in response to team discussion about the need for a review mechanism to identify gaps and improve outcomes over time.
[Define the process for auditing rehab cases after completion. How frequently are cases reviewed? Who conducts the review? What is being evaluated (e.g., were all protocol steps followed, were outcomes consistent with expectations, were there communication breakdowns)?]
Components:
- Post-case review: After each Tier 3 case reaches full return, review the process for completeness and outcome
- Athlete satisfaction survey: Include a question on whether all parties were appropriately informed and involved in the process
- Periodic audit: Quarterly or semester-based review of a sample of cases to identify systemic gaps
- Protocol update cycle: Annual review of the full manual, incorporating audit findings and updated normative data
- Testing process audit: Regular check on testing procedures to ensure consistency across administrators
# 12. References & Literature Citations
[Every claim in this manual should trace back to a source. Compile all citations in APA 7th edition format, organized by topic: return-to-play criteria, force plate testing, mental health screening in athletes, nutritional assessment, load monitoring, and any other relevant domains. This section is what makes the manual defensible.]
# 13. Appendices
## Appendix A: NCAA Performance Technology Best Practices

Programming the Process (Gameplan)
- Gaps

- Not reverse engineering the process
