# BAYLOR HEALTH & WELLNESS
# RTP Working Group 2025-26
# Athlete Testing and Assessment Protocols
- SFMA (Selective Functional Movement Assessment)
Purpose: Baseline movement screening and identification of mobility/stability limitations.
Implementation:
Who: All incoming athletes (intake), plus targeted reassessments (injury, RTP).
How: Administered by trained staff following SFMA guidelines.
When:
Intake/pre-season baseline.
Post-injury and return-to-play checkpoints.
Mid-season check for flagged athletes.
Technology: Integrate VALD HumanTrak for kinematic capture where available.
- Force Plate Assessments
Purpose: Neuromuscular profiling, fatigue monitoring, asymmetry detection.
Testing Battery:
Countermovement Jump (CMJ):
Frequency: 1x/week.
Primary monitoring tool for load/fatigue readiness.
Rebound Jump (RJ):
Frequency: 1x/week (first month) to establish repeatability/reliability.
Ongoing testing as needed for elastic/reactive strength profiles.
Isometric Mid-Thigh Pull (IMTP) or Belt Squat Isometric:
Frequency: 1x/month.
Focus on maximal force capacity and asymmetry.
- Nordic Hamstring Test
Purpose: Hamstring strength, asymmetry monitoring, RTP clearance.
Implementation:
Timing:
Intake baseline.
Post-season reassessment.
Periodic monitoring for flagged athletes (injury history).
Thresholds:
Target: 1.75x bodyweight force output.
Track asymmetry thresholds closely.
Contextualization: Adjust cadence based on sport demands, facility resources, and seasonal timing.
- DXA (Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry)
Purpose: Comprehensive body composition analysis.
Key Metrics:
Limb mass asymmetry (for strength balance monitoring).
Trunk-to-limb ratio (structural balance).
Visceral fat mass (health & performance risk factor).
Timing: Intake, mid-year, and post-season (or after major rehab periods).

- SFMA (Selective Functional Movement Assessment)
Purpose: Baseline movement screening and identification of mobility/stability limitations.

How: Administered by trained staff following SFMA guidelines.

Post-injury and return-to-play checkpoints.
Mid-season check for flagged athletes.

Purpose: Neuromuscular profiling, fatigue monitoring, asymmetry detection.
Testing Battery:
Countermovement Jump (CMJ):
Frequency: 1x/week.
Primary monitoring tool for load/fatigue readiness.
Rebound Jump (RJ):
Frequency: 1x/week (first month) to establish repeatability/reliability.
Ongoing testing as needed for elastic/reactive strength profiles.
Isometric Mid-Thigh Pull (IMTP) or Belt Squat Isometric:
Frequency: 1x/month.
Focus on maximal force capacity and asymmetry.
- Nordic Hamstring Test
Purpose: Hamstring strength, asymmetry monitoring, RTP clearance.
Implementation:
Timing:
Intake baseline.
Post-season reassessment.
Periodic monitoring for flagged athletes (injury history).
Thresholds:
Target: 1.75x bodyweight force output.

Contextualization: Adjust cadence based on sport demands, facility resources, and seasonal timing.

Purpose: Comprehensive body composition analysis.

Limb mass asymmetry (for strength balance monitoring).
Trunk-to-limb ratio (structural balance).
Visceral fat mass (health & performance risk factor).
Timing: Intake, mid-year, and post-season (or after major rehab periods).

BAYLOR UNIVERSITY
High Performance Initiative
Return-to-Performance Manual
Effective Date: June 1, 2026
Version 1.0 | Draft
# Table of Contents
# 1. Executive Summary
[This manual exists to solve a simple problem: when an athlete gets hurt at Baylor, everyone involved in getting them back on the field needs to be on the same page. Right now, that process looks different depending on the sport, the clinician, and the injury. This manual changes that.]
[Start here. Lay out in plain terms what the HPI is, what this manual covers, and who it applies to. Name the target rollout date (June 1, 2026). State the scope: every sport, every injury type, every duration. Explain why standardization matters, not just for the athlete, but for the practitioners protecting them and the institution backing them. Note alignment with NCAA Performance Technology Best Practices.]
# 2. Purpose Statement
[The core idea: every injured athlete at Baylor goes through the same evidence-based process before returning to play. No exceptions based on injury severity, sport, or timeline pressure. This section should answer three questions in order: (1) What problem does this solve? Inconsistent clearance processes expose athletes to re-injury risk and the institution to liability. (2) Why now? Leadership has directed universal application of post-injury testing. (3) What does success look like? A system where physical, mental health, and nutritional readiness are all evaluated before clearance, every single time.]
# 3. Return-to-Performance (RTP) Protocols
This is the backbone of the manual. It defines the framework that governs how injured athletes move from the training room back to competition.
## 3.1 Protocol Framework
[Describe the five-stage return-to-performance framework. For each stage, state what happens, what the athlete needs to demonstrate before moving forward, and a general timeline. Keep it concrete. A reader should be able to look at any athlete and say: they are in Stage 3, and here is what needs to happen before Stage 4. Address the difference between a two-week ankle sprain and a nine-month ACL reconstruction. The stages are the same; the pace is not.]
## 3.2 Injury Classification & Tiered Response
Not every injury needs the full battery. A sprained ankle and an ACL tear are not the same, and the protocol should reflect that. This tiered system gives clinicians and strength coaches the flexibility to match the response to the severity, while still keeping everyone inside a consistent framework.
### Tier 1: Minor Injuries (< 2 weeks)
[Quick turnaround injuries. Abbreviated testing pathway. Define what qualifies, what testing is required (and what can be skipped), and what documentation is needed. The goal: keep it simple without cutting corners.]
### Tier 2: Moderate Injuries (2-6 weeks)
[Standard protocol. Define criteria, required testing, and where mental health and nutrition checkpoints enter the picture. This is the middle ground where most injuries will land.]
### Tier 3: Severe / Surgical Injuries (6+ weeks or surgical)
[Full protocol, no shortcuts. Beginning, middle, and end checkpoints. Mandatory mental health and nutrition assessments at defined stages. This tier exists because the longer an athlete is out, the more variables affect their return, and all of them need to be tracked.]
# 4. Lower Body RTP Protocols
[Insert the complete lower body return-to-performance protocol. This protocol is being developed by Jeremy and is currently in draft form. Everything below should follow his structure and content once finalized.]
## 4.1 Testing Battery
[List every test in the lower body protocol. For each one, state plainly: what it measures, how it is administered, and what a passing result looks like. Think force plate assessments, hop tests, balance and stability work, range of motion. No ambiguity. A new staff member should be able to read this section and know exactly what to do.]
## 4.2 Rehabilitation Progression
[Walk through the rehab stages for lower body injuries. What exercises, at what volume and intensity, with what progression criteria between stages. Write it so a practitioner can hand this to a colleague and say: follow this.]
## 4.3 Return-to-Play Decision Matrix
[This is where testing data turns into a yes-or-no decision. Provide the decision matrix or flowchart. Include asymmetry thresholds, normative comparison benchmarks, and the specific criteria that must all be met before clearance. No gray areas.]
# 5. Upper Body RTP Protocols
[Insert the complete upper body return-to-performance protocol. Important note: the upper body protocol is less prescriptive with range-of-motion numbers because variability across sports and injury types is much wider here. A baseball pitcher and a football lineman have very different demands. The protocol should account for that without becoming vague.]
## 5.1 Testing Battery
[Same format as the lower body section. Every test, what it measures, how it is done, and what the benchmarks are. Call out sport-specific considerations directly (throwing athletes, contact sports, overhead athletes). Do not bury them in footnotes.]
## 5.2 Rehabilitation Progression
[Stage-by-stage rehab progression for upper body injuries. Include sport-specific pathways where they diverge (return-to-throwing, return-to-contact). Each pathway should be its own clearly labeled subsection.]
## 5.3 Return-to-Play Decision Matrix
[Decision matrix for upper body clearance. Range of motion standards, strength benchmarks, and sport-specific functional testing. Same principle as Section 4.3: testing data in, clearance decision out.]
# 6. Testing Purpose Statement
[Why do we test? Answer that question directly. Testing is not a box to check. It exists to give practitioners objective data so that clearance decisions are based on evidence, not gut feel. This section should explain how testing data establishes baselines before injury, tracks progress during rehab, identifies asymmetries that signal risk, and ultimately supports the final return-to-play call. Write it so that anyone reading this manual, from a head coach to a new GA, understands the reasoning behind every test an athlete will go through.]
# 7. Rationale & Test Justifications
Every test in this manual was selected for a reason. This section lays out those reasons so that the protocol is transparent, defensible, and grounded in research.
## 7.1 Literature Review
[For each test in the battery, provide the peer-reviewed evidence supporting its inclusion. Organize by domain: strength, power, balance, range of motion, and so on. Keep it accessible. A citation list is necessary, but a brief plain-language summary of what the research shows is just as important. Practitioners need to understand why, not just that.]
## 7.2 Sport-Specific Applications
[Connect each test to the specific demands of the sports at Baylor. Why does this test matter for football? For soccer? For baseball? This section bridges the gap between the research and the practice. If a coach asks why their athlete is doing a particular test, the answer should be in this section.]
# 8. Test Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs)
Consistency matters. If two different practitioners run the same test on the same athlete and get different results because of setup differences, the data is useless. This section ensures everyone administers every test the same way, every time.
## 8.1 General Testing Guidelines
[Cover the basics that apply to every test: warm-up protocols, environment setup, equipment calibration, how to prepare the athlete, and how to record data. These are the non-negotiables.]
## 8.2 Test-Specific SOPs
[For each test, spell out: equipment needed, setup instructions, athlete positioning, verbal cues to use, number of trials, rest intervals between trials, how to capture and record data, and common mistakes to watch for. Include photos or diagrams wherever they help. The goal is that someone who has never run this test before can follow these instructions and get reliable results.]
## 8.3 Quality Assurance
[How do we make sure the data stays reliable over time? Cover inter-rater reliability procedures (how we check that different practitioners get consistent results), equipment maintenance schedules, and a review cycle for updating these SOPs as methods improve.]
# 9. Metric Descriptions & Normative Data
This section is the reference guide for every number that comes out of testing. If someone looks at a report and asks what a metric means or whether a value is good or bad, the answer should be here.
## 9.1 Metric Reference Table
[Build a table with these columns: Test Name, Metric, What It Measures, Why It Matters, Sport Application, and Normative Range. Every metric collected during testing should have a row in this table. No orphan data points.]
## 9.2 Normative Data & Benchmarks
[Provide reference data for the Baylor athlete population. Sport-specific norms where we have them, general collegiate norms for comparison where we do not. Be clear about sample sizes and how this data was collected. Include a plan for how normative data gets updated as we accumulate more results over time.]
## 9.3 Asymmetry Thresholds
[Define acceptable side-to-side differences for each relevant test (e.g., limb symmetry index). Explain what it means clinically when an athlete exceeds the threshold, and how asymmetry factors into the clearance decision. This is one of the most important pieces of the puzzle, so be specific.]
# 10. Chain of Command & Personnel
People change. Roles do not. This section is written around roles so that it holds up through staff turnover without needing a rewrite every time someone leaves or joins.
## 10.1 Roles & Responsibilities
[Define the key roles: Athletic Trainer, Strength & Conditioning Coach, Mental Health Provider, Sports Nutritionist, Team Physician, Head Coach. For each role, state what they own in the RTP process and what decisions they can make. Keep it clear enough that a new hire knows exactly where they fit on day one.]
## 10.2 Communication Flow
[Map out how information moves between people during a rehab case. Who reports to whom, what documentation gets handed off at each stage, and what triggers an escalation. A missed handoff is where things fall through the cracks, so this section needs to be airtight.]
## 10.3 Clearance Authority
[Who makes the final call? Define clearance authority for each injury tier. Outline the collaborative decision-making process and any required sign-offs. The goal: no ambiguity about who can and cannot clear an athlete to return.]
# 11. Data Repository & Visualization
Good data is only useful if people can find it and understand it. This section covers how testing data gets collected, stored, and turned into something practitioners can actually use to make decisions.
## 11.1 Data Collection & Storage
[Walk through the data workflow from test day to the repository. How does data get entered? Where does it live? What are the naming conventions and folder structures? Who has access? Keep it practical. If someone needs to pull up an athlete's test history, they should be able to do it in under a minute.]
## 11.2 Athlete Profile Template
[Include the one-page athlete profile template. This is the at-a-glance view: athlete info at the top, test results organized by metric, and a simple chart showing progress over time (bar or line). This is the document that gets pulled up in a meeting when someone asks how an athlete is tracking. Design it to answer questions, not create them.]
## 11.3 Load Monitoring Integration
[For sports that use wearable technology (football, soccer, and others with Catapult/Connects), describe how load monitoring data feeds into the RTP picture. Load data without context is noise. This section should explain how it connects to testing data and informs clearance decisions.]
## 11.4 Reporting & Dashboards
[Describe what reports and dashboards are available: individual athlete progress, team-level summaries, compliance tracking for administration. Each report should have a clear audience and a clear purpose. If a report does not help someone make a better decision, cut it.]
# 12. Fillable Forms & Documentation
These are the working documents that move through the RTP process. Each form is designed for digital completion and long-term archival.
## 12.1 Injury Intake Form
[Insert fillable injury intake form. This is the starting point for every case.]
## 12.2 Testing Record Form
[Insert fillable testing record form. One for each protocol stage so that data capture is standardized from start to finish.]
## 12.3 Clearance Sign-Off Form
[Insert fillable clearance form. Include required signatures and checkpoint confirmations. This is the document that says: this athlete has met every criterion and is cleared to return.]
## 12.4 Mental Health Assessment Referral
[Insert the form used to document the mental health checkpoint. For Tier 2 and Tier 3 injuries, this is mandatory. The form should capture the referral, the assessment outcome, and any follow-up actions.]
## 12.5 Nutrition Assessment Referral
[Insert the form used to document the nutrition checkpoint. Same structure as the mental health form: referral, assessment, follow-up.]
# 13. References & Literature Citations
[Every claim in this manual should trace back to a source. Compile all citations in APA 7th edition format, organized by topic: return-to-play criteria, force plate testing, mental health screening in athletes, nutritional assessment, load monitoring, and any other relevant domains. This section is what makes the manual defensible.]
# 14. Appendices
## Appendix A: NCAA Performance Technology Best Practices
[Include or reference the NCAA performance technology best practices document. Show where Baylor's protocols align with these guidelines and note any areas where we exceed the recommendations.]
## Appendix B: Rollout Communication Plan
[The June 1, 2026 rollout needs to be communicated clearly to coaching staff, athletes, and the broader Health & Wellness department. Include the messaging plan, timeline, and who is responsible for each communication touchpoint.]
## Appendix C: Glossary of Terms
[Define key terms used throughout this manual. Write definitions in plain language so that anyone, regardless of clinical background, can follow the document.]
## Appendix D: Revision History
[Track every update: date, author, what changed, and why. This manual is a living document, and the revision history is how we keep it accountable.]=========ORIG

[The core idea: every injured athlete at Baylor goes through the same evidence-based process before returning to play. No exceptions based on injury severity, sport, or timeline pressure. This section should answer three questions in order: (1) What problem does this solve? Inconsistent clearance processes expose athletes to re-injury risk and the institution to liability. (2) Why now? Leadership has directed universal application of post-injury testing. (3) What does success look like? A system where physical, mental health, and nutritional readiness are all evaluated before clearance, every single time.]
# 3. Return-to-Performance (RTP) Protocols
This is the backbone of the manual. It defines the framework that governs how injured athletes move from the training room back to competition.
## 3.1 Protocol Framework
[Describe the five-stage return-to-performance framework. For each stage, state what happens, what the athlete needs to demonstrate before moving forward, and a general timeline. Keep it concrete. A reader should be able to look at any athlete and say: they are in Stage 3, and here is what needs to happen before Stage 4. Address the difference between a two-week ankle sprain and a nine-month ACL reconstruction. The stages are the same; the pace is not.]
## 3.2 Injury Classification & Tiered Response
Not every injury needs the full battery. A sprained ankle and an ACL tear are not the same, and the protocol should reflect that. This tiered system gives clinicians and strength coaches the flexibility to match the response to the severity, while still keeping everyone inside a consistent framework.
### Tier 1: Minor Injuries (< 2 weeks)
[Quick turnaround injuries. Abbreviated testing pathway. Define what qualifies, what testing is required (and what can be skipped), and what documentation is needed. The goal: keep it simple without cutting corners.]
### Tier 2: Moderate Injuries (2-6 weeks)
[Standard protocol. Define criteria, required testing, and where mental health and nutrition checkpoints enter the picture. This is the middle ground where most injuries will land.]
### Tier 3: Severe / Surgical Injuries (6+ weeks or surgical)
[Full protocol, no shortcuts. Beginning, middle, and end checkpoints. Mandatory mental health and nutrition assessments at defined stages. This tier exists because the longer an athlete is out, the more variables affect their return, and all of them need to be tracked.]
# 4. Lower Body RTP Protocols

Think force plate assessments, hop tests, balance and stability work, range of motion. No ambiguity. A new staff member should be able to read this section and know exactly what to do.]
## 4.2 Rehabilitation Progression
[Walk through the rehab stages for lower body injuries. What exercises, at what volume and intensity, with what progression criteria between stages. Write it so a practitioner can hand this to a colleague and say: follow this.]
## 4.3 Return-to-Play Decision Matrix
[This is where testing data turns into a yes-or-no decision. Provide the decision matrix or flowchart. Include asymmetry thresholds, normative comparison benchmarks, and the specific criteria that must all be met before clearance. No gray areas.]
# 5. Upper Body RTP Protocols
[Insert the complete upper body return-to-performance protocol. Important note: the upper body protocol is less prescriptive with range-of-motion numbers because variability across sports and injury types is much wider here. A baseball pitcher and a football lineman have very different demands. The protocol should account for that without becoming vague.]
## 5.1 Testing Battery
[Same format as the lower body section. Every test, what it measures, how it is done, and what the benchmarks are. Call out sport-specific considerations directly (throwing athletes, contact sports, overhead athletes). Do not bury them in footnotes.]

[Decision matrix for upper body clearance. Range of motion standards, strength benchmarks, and sport-specific functional testing. Same principle as Section 4.3: testing data in, clearance decision out.]
# 6. Testing Purpose Statement
[Why do we test? Answer that question directly. Testing is not a box to check. It exists to give practitioners objective data so that clearance decisions are based on evidence, not gut feel. This section should explain how testing data establishes baselines before injury, tracks progress during rehab, identifies asymmetries that signal risk, and ultimately supports the final return-to-play call. Write it so that anyone reading this manual, from a head coach to a new GA, understands the reasoning behind every test an athlete will go through.]

Every test in this manual was selected for a reason. This section lays out those reasons so that the protocol is transparent, defensible, and grounded in research.

A citation list is necessary, but a brief plain-language summary of what the research shows is just as important. Practitioners need to understand why, not just that.]

1	# Matt Jordan’s Approach to Force Plate CMJ Metrics for ACL Return-to-Play
2	## Overview of Matt Jordan’s Neuromuscular Recovery Framework Post-ACL Injury
3	Matt Jordan emphasizes a comprehensive, long-term approach to monitoring neuromuscular recovery after ACL injury. Rather than relying on a single “clearance” test at 9–12 months, Jordan advocates continuous monitoring across the return-to-health, return-to-sport, return-to-competition, and return-to-performance phases[1][2]. He stresses the use of objective neuromuscular tests (especially force-plate jump tests) to uncover “hidden” deficits that may not be visible to the coach’s eye[3][2]. In particular, vertical jump force-plate assessments (like the countermovement jump) serve as a cornerstone for tracking recovery, because they are reliable, quick to administer, and sensitive to lingering deficits in neuromuscular function[4][5]. Jordan’s framework involves an expansive battery of tests targeting movement competency, strength capacity, and sport-specific demands – with the vertical jump providing key clues about asymmetries and explosive power recovery[6][7].
4	A key concept in Jordan’s approach is using phase-specific analysis of the CMJ force-time curve to detect neuromuscular asymmetries[8][9]. By partitioning the jump into phases – the eccentric deceleration phase (braking/downward phase) and the concentric propulsive phase (upward push-off) – Jordan measures each limb’s force contribution over time in each phase[8][9]. This allows calculation of a force-time asymmetry index for each phase, typically based on the difference in impulse (area under the force-time curve) produced by the injured vs. uninjured limb[10]. Jordan coined the term “kinetic impulse asymmetry index” (KIAI) to describe this measure[11]. His research found that CMJ asymmetry indices are highly sensitive to an athlete’s musculoskeletal status through rehab – often revealing deficits well before they show up in simple performance metrics[4]. For example, in elite skiers returning from ACL reconstruction, the vertical jump asymmetry (especially during the eccentric phase) tracked closely with rehab progress and even predicted future injury risk[12][13]. Jordan’s framework therefore integrates bilateral dual-force-plate CMJ tests (to compute interlimb asymmetries in real time) and unilateral CMJ tests (to assess each leg’s independent explosive capacity) as complementary tools for decision-making in ACL rehab.
5	Crucially, Jordan cautions that no single metric guarantees readiness or predicts reinjury on its own[2]. Instead, practitioners should “be like Sherlock Holmes” – gathering multiple clues (strength tests, jump metrics, psychological readiness, etc.) and using informed reasoning to build a holistic picture[14]. In Jordan’s words, it’s an n=1 game: each athlete’s recovery profile is unique, so coaches should use Bayesian thinking – update expectations with each new test result – rather than chasing any one “magic” variable[14]. Nonetheless, force-plate CMJ testing has emerged as one of the most informative components of this holistic monitoring system. The following sections outline the specific CMJ force-plate metrics that Jordan’s research highlights for ACL return-to-play, along with the rationale and practical implications for each.
6	## Recommended Force Plate CMJ Metrics (Bilateral & Unilateral)
7	Jordan’s research and publications identify several CMJ-derived metrics as particularly useful for monitoring ACL recovery. These include metrics obtained from bilateral CMJ tests using dual force plates (which enable direct left-right comparisons during a two-leg jump), as well as metrics from unilateral CMJ tests performed on each leg separately. Below is an overview of the key metrics, grouped by bilateral vs. unilateral CMJ assessments:
8	### Bilateral CMJ Metrics (Dual-Plate Assessment)
9	Eccentric Deceleration Impulse Asymmetry: Difference between limbs in impulse (force × time area) during the braking phase of a bilateral CMJ[10]. This phase-specific asymmetry index (KIAI for the eccentric phase) quantifies how evenly the athlete accepts load on the way down.
10	Concentric Impulse Asymmetry: Difference between limbs in impulse during the propulsive (upward) phase of the CMJ[10]. This asymmetry index for the concentric phase reflects imbalance in force output when jumping off.
11	Peak Eccentric Power: The peak negative mechanical power (force × velocity) reached in the eccentric phase on each limb[15]. This indicates how powerfully the athlete can decelerate. It can be examined for asymmetry between legs or tracked for the injured limb.
12	Total Jump Height (bilateral): The jump height achieved in a countermovement jump (derived from takeoff velocity)[16]. While not an asymmetry metric itself (both legs contribute), jump height is a fundamental outcome to track recovery of overall power. Jordan often pairs jump height with time metrics (see below) to assess efficiency.
13	Jump Contraction Time: The total duration of the movement (from start of downward motion to take-off) in the CMJ[17]. This indicates how quickly the athlete can produce the jump. It’s especially telling when considered alongside jump height (e.g. a normal jump height achieved with abnormally long time may indicate a compensatory, slow strategy).
14	Modified Reactive Strength Index (RSI_Mod): Ratio of jump height to contraction time[18]. This metric, essentially jump height per unit time, encapsulates explosiveness of the stretch-shortening cycle. A lower RSI_Mod suggests impaired explosive capacity post-ACL, even if jump height alone appears acceptable[19][15].
15	Eccentric Phase Stiffness: Calculated as the change in vertical force divided by change in center-of-mass displacement during the eccentric deceleration phase[18]. This “lower limb stiffness” metric reflects how stiff or compliant the athlete’s landing/countermovement strategy is. Changes in stiffness can indicate adaptations – e.g. an athlete might adopt a more compliant (low stiffness) strategy post-ACL to reduce knee load[20][21].
16	Unweighting (Unloading) Impulse: The impulse during the initial unweighting phase (when the athlete quickly reduces force to initiate the downward movement)[22]. This metric can reveal subtle side-to-side shifts at movement onset – for instance, if the athlete favors the uninjured leg immediately when starting the counter-movement. Jordan’s work found the unloading impulse (and its asymmetry) to be among the top features distinguishing ACL-reconstructed athletes from uninjured controls[23].
17	### Unilateral CMJ Metrics (Single-Leg Jump Assessment)
18	Single-Leg Jump Height & LSI: Jump height performed on the injured leg versus the uninjured leg, often expressed as a Limb Symmetry Index (injured limb height as a percentage of the contralateral limb)[7]. This is a direct measure of functional performance per leg. An LSI approaching 90–100% is typically desired; persistent deficits in single-leg jump height indicate incomplete recovery of power on the involved side.
19	Single-Leg Concentric Impulse / Peak Power: The propulsive impulse or peak concentric power achieved by the injured limb, compared to the contralateral side. Like the bilateral test, this gauges the recovered force-time output of the surgical limb in isolation. Jordan’s analyses highlight that even at ~6 months post-ACL, athletes often show lower concentric impulse and power on the reconstructed side, which should improve over time[24]. Comparing against the healthy leg (or pre-injury benchmarks) helps determine if the involved leg’s explosive output is sufficient for return to play.
20	Eccentric Deceleration RFD (Single-Leg): The rate of force development during the eccentric phase of a unilateral CMJ on each leg. In practice, this can be observed via the force-time curve’s slope as the athlete brakes during the countermovement. A markedly blunted eccentric RFD on the injured limb (i.e. taking more time to decelerate and reverse direction) is a red flag for residual neuromuscular inhibition or fear of loading[21]. Jordan’s case studies have shown injured skiers exhibiting reduced eccentric RFD and reduced knee flexion on the involved side, indicative of a protective strategy[21]. Improvement in eccentric RFD suggests the athlete is regaining confidence and capacity in load acceptance on that limb.
21	Time to Peak Power (Single-Leg): The time it takes for the single leg to reach its peak concentric power output during the jump. A prolonged time-to-peak on the injured side can indicate a slower force production profile (possibly due to impaired rapid force capacity in the knee extensors). Jordan et al. identified this as a useful metric; athletes with ACL history often exhibit longer time to peak power compared to uninjured athletes[15]. A shortening of this time toward normative values is a positive sign for return-to-play readiness.
22	(Note: Many of the above unilateral metrics are also relevant in bilateral jumps when each limb’s contribution is analyzed separately. In Jordan’s methodology, a dual-force-plate CMJ can effectively provide both the bilateral overall outcomes and the side-specific metrics via decomposed force-time data[10]. For clarity, we list them under unilateral context since they reflect one limb’s capacity, but they may be measured in either format.)
23	## Rationale Behind Each Key Metric
24	Each of the above metrics offers a specific window into the athlete’s neuromuscular status post-ACL, aligning with Jordan’s research findings. Below we explain the rationale for why each metric is valuable for return-to-play monitoring:
25	Eccentric Deceleration Impulse Asymmetry (Bilateral CMJ): This metric directly assesses load acceptance asymmetry, which is critical after ACL injury. The eccentric impulse (area under the force curve in the downward phase) tells us how much force each leg is absorbing during landing and countermovement. A large asymmetry (injured leg contributing significantly less impulse) signals that the athlete is offloading the surgical limb during the braking phase[8][9]. This often reflects quadriceps weakness or fear of loading that limb. Jordan’s 2015 study demonstrated that ACL-reconstructed skiers had significantly higher eccentric impulse asymmetries than uninjured athletes[8]. Monitoring this metric helps ensure the athlete relearns to confidently absorb force on the injured side – a prerequisite for safe decelerations and landings in sport.
26	Concentric Impulse Asymmetry (Bilateral CMJ): This captures asymmetry in the propulsive phase, i.e. the ability of the injured leg to produce upward force relative to the healthy leg. Even if total jump performance seems normal, a high concentric impulse asymmetry indicates the uninjured leg is compensating to generate take-off force[25]. Jordan notes that athletes can often maintain jump height by favoring the stronger limb, masking deficits[25]. Thus, the concentric asymmetry index is a sensitive marker of lingering power deficits in the affected limb. A decreasing asymmetry over time indicates recovery of explosive force production on the surgical side. In Jordan’s practice, the concentric asymmetry index has emerged as one of the top metrics to flag neuromuscular deficits that are hidden from basic hop tests[26] (athletes may pass single-leg hop distance tests yet still show a high force asymmetry in a bilateral CMJ).
27	Peak Eccentric Power (Negative Power) and RFD: These metrics relate to how quickly and forcefully the athlete can brake during the countermovement, which is an aspect of dynamic knee stability. A reduced peak eccentric power on the injured side (or overall, in a bilateral jump) suggests the athlete is either avoiding a rapid descent or lacking eccentric strength to control it[15]. Similarly, a slower eccentric rate of force development indicates a cautious strategy – the athlete is taking more time to decelerate, often to minimize knee stress[27]. Jordan’s work highlights cases where an athlete post-ACL shows a much gentler slope in the force-time curve during eccentric loading on the surgical leg, corresponding with reduced knee flexion angle[21]. Restoring high eccentric power and RFD is important because it underpins reactive athletic movements (e.g. cutting, landing from a jump). These metrics tie into the concept of “load acceptance” – the faster and more powerfully a limb can absorb force, the more prepared it is for sports demands.
28	Jump Contraction Time & Time to Peak Power: These time-based metrics provide insight into the athlete’s explosive temporal profile. Jump contraction time (the total movement time) tends to be longer if an athlete uses a slower, strength-dominant strategy (perhaps due to impaired explosive capacity or hesitancy)[20]. Time to peak concentric power specifically homes in on the propulsive explosiveness – a longer time to peak power on the injured limb suggests the athlete cannot generate force rapidly, possibly due to residual neuromuscular inhibition or fiber-type shifts during rehab[15]. Jordan’s recent analysis found time-to-peak-power to be a distinguishing feature for athletes with ACL reconstruction[15]. The rationale for tracking these metrics is to ensure the athlete is not only regaining quantity of force, but also the rate of force development, which is crucial for agile, high-speed sports movements. As rehab progresses, one should see contraction times shorten and time to peak power get closer to that of healthy athletes.
29	Vertical Jump Height (Outcome) and Modified RSI: Jump height remains a simple indicator of overall power output and is often the first thing athletes and coaches look at. After ACL reconstruction, jump height on the injured side (single-leg CMJ) will usually be depressed; it should gradually improve to near baseline/pre-injury levels. In bilateral jumps, total jump height might recover faster – sometimes even before true symmetry is achieved, due to compensations[25]. Therefore, jump height is best interpreted alongside the asymmetry and timing metrics above. The modified RSI (jump height divided by time) adds context by accounting for how quickly that height was achieved[20]. Jordan supports RSI_Mod as a valuable metric because it captures deficits in stretch-shortening cycle efficiency that pure height might miss[20]. A low RSI_Mod (e.g. normal height but taking too long to produce it) flags that the athlete is not yet back to optimal explosiveness. The rationale for including jump height and RSI_Mod is that, together with force asymmetry measures, they give a balanced view of performance and strategy – ensuring the athlete eventually regains both sufficient power and efficient mechanics.
30	Lower Limb Stiffness (Eccentric Stiffness): Jordan includes stiffness as a metric to evaluate the movement strategy during the countermovement. Stiffness in this context is how much force is generated per unit displacement of the center of mass in the eccentric phase[18]. An athlete with a very low stiffness (i.e. large depth with relatively low force) might be relying on a deeper, slower squat to compensate for reduced knee extensor strength, whereas an excessively high stiffness (minimal bend, high forces) might indicate they are avoiding knee flexion and absorbing impact through a stiffer leg. Both extremes can be concerning; post-ACL, some athletes adopt a “stiffer” strategy to protect the knee[21]. Monitoring eccentric stiffness helps tailor feedback: for instance, if stiffness is too high on the injured side (indicating they aren’t using a normal range of motion to absorb load), the therapist might work on improving confidence in deeper knee flexion. Ultimately, a normalization of stiffness between limbs and versus normative data is desired, reflecting a return to a normal jumping strategy[20].
31	Unilateral Performance and Symmetry (Single-Leg CMJ metrics): The rationale for testing single-leg jumps in addition to bilateral is to expose deficits that bilateral tests can mask. A classic example is an athlete who can squat jump or CMJ nearly to their pre-injury height using both legs, but when asked to jump off the injured leg alone, they achieve significantly less height or force. Jordan’s studies (and others) consistently show that unilateral jump LSIs are often <90% at return-to-sport if thorough rehab hasn’t been done[7]. By measuring single-leg jump height, peak power, and impulse directly, one can determine if the involved limb has restored the necessary output for sport. Moreover, unilateral tests eliminate the “cheating” that can occur in bilateral tests (where the healthy leg compensates)[25]. A high-quality return-to-play protocol will typically require that single-leg metrics (e.g. jump height, or peak force normalized to body weight) of the injured side reach some threshold of the uninvolved side (often 90% or greater). Jordan’s approach uses single-leg CMJs to verify symmetric explosive performance and to identify which aspect of the force-time curve is lacking in the injured limb. For instance, if the injured leg’s jump height is close to the good leg but time to take-off is much longer, it indicates an underlying explosive speed deficit despite recovered jump capacity. Each unilateral metric thus feeds into a targeted intervention – e.g. addressing eccentric strength if eccentric impulse or RFD is low, or plyometric training if concentric power is lagging.
32	In summary, each metric is chosen for its ability to illuminate a particular dimension of neuromuscular recovery: asymmetry (between-limb deficits), load acceptance/braking (eccentric control), force-time characteristics (timing, RFD, power curve shape), and interlimb comparisons (performance of one leg vs the other). Jordan’s peer-reviewed studies underscore that using a phase-specific, multi-metric analysis of CMJ data gives a much more complete picture than raw jump height or isolated strength tests[28][15]. By combining these metrics, practitioners can detect whether an athlete is truly ready for the demands of sport or if subtle deficits remain.
33	## Practical Implications for Return-to-Play Decision Making
34	Implementing Jordan’s CMJ metrics in return-to-play decisions can significantly enhance the safety and effectiveness of the process. These force-plate metrics translate to actionable criteria for clinicians and coaches:
35	Identifying Hidden Deficits: One of the most important implications is catching deficits that traditional tests might miss. For example, an athlete may pass standard hop distance tests and have a nearly symmetric quadriceps strength ratio, yet still exhibit a 15% concentric impulse asymmetry and a blunted eccentric RFD on force-plate testing[25][21]. Jordan’s research warns that such an athlete is not truly symmetric in function – the force-plate is revealing a neuromuscular deficit that could predispose to re-injury if left unaddressed[25][13]. Thus, in practice, if meaningful asymmetries or power deficits show up in CMJ metrics, the return-to-play should be delayed or modified to target those deficits, even if classical criteria are met.
36	Guiding Targeted Rehab Interventions: Each metric can point to specific rehab needs. A high eccentric impulse asymmetry or low injured-limb eccentric power, for instance, tells the practitioner to focus on eccentric strength and deceleration training (e.g. eccentric squat programs, landing drills) to build load acceptance capacity. If jump contraction time or time to peak power is prolonged, plyometric and explosive training might be emphasized to improve rapid force development. By routinely testing these metrics, practitioners can form “training hypotheses” (as Jordan calls them) and then re-test to see if the deficits resolve[29][30]. This creates a feedback loop ensuring the rehab is effectively targeting the athlete’s weak links.
37	Informing Clearance and Risk Assessment: Force-plate CMJ metrics add quantitative rigor to return-to-play clearance decisions. Many programs use an LSI > 90% on hop tests as a criterion; Jordan’s approach would similarly advocate that CMJ asymmetry indices be within acceptable range (e.g. below ~10% asymmetry, acknowledging some day-to-day variability) before full return to sport. Moreover, absolute performance metrics should be back to baseline: for instance, if a jumper’s pre-injury bilateral CMJ height was 50 cm, but at 9 months post-op it’s 40 cm (even if symmetric), that indicates residual global power deficit. In such a case, pushing the athlete into high-level competition may invite injury due to inadequate capacity (Jordan notes that two weak but symmetric limbs are not desirable[31]). Practically, this means both symmetry and adequate magnitude of force/power must be achieved. Coaches should ensure the athlete’s injured limb is not just within X% of the other leg, but that both limbs are near their normative or pre-injury benchmarks[31].
38	Predicting Re-injury Risk: Perhaps the most compelling practical aspect is the potential to forecast injury risk. Emerging evidence (including work cited by Jordan) suggests that certain jump metrics correlate with re-injury. For example, one study found that in male athletes, those who sustained a second ACL injury had exhibited longer ground contact times, lower jump heights, and lower RSI in a drop jump test, whereas traditional single-leg hop distances and quad strength LSI did not predict re-injury[32]. This aligns with Jordan’s own findings that dynamic asymmetry and explosive deficits can linger despite “passing” simpler tests[13]. In practice, this means a return-to-play committee should weigh these force-plate findings heavily: an athlete with ongoing jump asymmetries or SSC (stretch-shortening cycle) deficits should be flagged as higher risk and possibly kept in rehabilitation or a modified training program longer. Over time, as data accumulates, an organization can even develop its own “profiles” for safe return – for instance, using Jordan’s generalized additive modeling approach to forecast neuromuscular recovery timelines[33]. If an athlete’s recovery curve for concentric impulse asymmetry is behind the expected trajectory, the staff might extend the rehab duration proactively.
39	Communication and Motivation: Jordan points out the importance of using these metrics to educate and motivate the athlete (and inform coaches) during the process[34][35]. Because the CMJ metrics are objective and trackable, they can be shown to athletes to validate their progress or highlight areas that need work. For example, showing an athlete that their injured leg produces, say, 20% less concentric impulse than their healthy leg can underscore the need for continued rehab – this can combat the impatience or false confidence that often occurs around the typical 6–9 month mark. Conversely, demonstrating improvements (e.g. “your eccentric impulse on the surgical side improved from 60% to 85% of the other leg in the last 6 weeks”) can boost confidence and buy-in. By translating the complex force-time data into simple charts or scores, practitioners can keep the athlete and coaching staff informed about readiness indicators, making the return-to-play decision a collaborative and transparent process rather than a subjective call.
40	Long-Term Athlete Monitoring: Finally, Jordan advocates extending these assessments well beyond the initial return to sport – into the return to performance phase and even for injury prevention in uninjured athletes[1][6]. The practical implication is that force-plate CMJ testing becomes part of routine monitoring for all athletes. For an ACL rehab case, even after the athlete is back in competition, continued periodic testing can catch any regressions (e.g. fatigue or overuse causing asymmetry to creep up again) and ensure that full performance potential is restored. Notably, Jordan’s team found that some deficits (like reduced rapid torque capacity) persisted 18+ months post-ACL despite meeting conventional criteria[36][7]. Ongoing monitoring helps confirm when the athlete has truly returned to pre-injury performance level, not just cleared the minimum standards. It also may alert staff to compensations that could lead to other injuries (e.g. if an athlete chronically offloads one side, they might be at risk of injuring the opposite limb – a common occurrence with second ACL injuries on the contralateral knee[37]).
41	Incorporating Matt Jordan’s force-plate CMJ metrics thus leads to a more data-driven and nuanced return-to-play decision. It ensures that the athlete not only passes a checklist but is genuinely prepared – symmetrically strong, explosively powerful, and confident in both limbs. Practitioners who adopt this approach can better safeguard athletes from premature return and re-injury, ultimately facilitating a safer progression back to full competition.
42	## Summary Tables: Key CMJ Metrics and Their Use in ACL Monitoring
43	The tables below summarize the primary force-plate CMJ metrics recommended in Jordan’s research, along with their definitions and practical use cases for ACL return-to-play monitoring.

Even if jump height is similar, lower peak power or impulse on the injured side suggests a less efficient force generation[24]. Improving this is key for reactive ability – the athlete must quickly brace and reverse from a jump or landing on that leg. While not always done in practice, Jordan’s case work used loaded jumps to see if the injured limb has specific weakness (low F₀ suggests strength deficit; low V₀ suggests explosive speed deficit)[39]. In rehab, this can fine-tune training focus (strength vs. power) for the injured leg. |

65	Each of these metrics is supported by Matt Jordan’s research and applied work, giving practitioners a robust toolkit for monitoring ACL recovery. By combining bilateral asymmetry indices with unilateral performance measures, one can triangulate the athlete’s readiness: confirming the once-injured limb is both symmetric in contribution and independently capable. This dual lens – looking at interlimb symmetry and absolute limb capacity – is at the heart of Jordan’s return-to-play testing paradigm. As evidence grows, these metrics are becoming integral in high-performance settings to reduce re-injury rates and optimize athletes’ return to their pre-injury performance levels[40][41].
66	Sources: Primary findings and recommendations are drawn from Matt Jordan’s publications and presentations, including his 2015 phase-specific asymmetry study[8], the 2022 Aspetar consensus on explosive strength after ACL[9][23], his case-study and medium articles on ACL return-to-sport testing[42][10], and related works by his collaborators. These sources provide detailed evidence for the metrics and their relevance to ACL rehabilitation and return-to-play decision-making. Each metric above is grounded in peer-reviewed research where Jordan is a lead or contributing author, ensuring that the recommendations are scientifically supported and practitioner-vetted.
