# Matt Jordan’s Approach to Force Plate CMJ Metrics for ACL Return-to-Play
## Overview of Matt Jordan’s Neuromuscular Recovery Framework Post-ACL Injury
Matt Jordan emphasizes a comprehensive, long-term approach to monitoring neuromuscular recovery after ACL injury. Rather than relying on a single “clearance” test at 9–12 months, Jordan advocates continuous monitoring across the return-to-health, return-to-sport, return-to-competition, and return-to-performance phases[1][2]. He stresses the use of objective neuromuscular tests (especially force-plate jump tests) to uncover “hidden” deficits that may not be visible to the coach’s eye[3][2]. In particular, vertical jump force-plate assessments (like the countermovement jump) serve as a cornerstone for tracking recovery, because they are reliable, quick to administer, and sensitive to lingering deficits in neuromuscular function[4][5]. Jordan’s framework involves an expansive battery of tests targeting movement competency, strength capacity, and sport-specific demands – with the vertical jump providing key clues about asymmetries and explosive power recovery[6][7].
A key concept in Jordan’s approach is using phase-specific analysis of the CMJ force-time curve to detect neuromuscular asymmetries[8][9]. By partitioning the jump into phases – the eccentric deceleration phase (braking/downward phase) and the concentric propulsive phase (upward push-off) – Jordan measures each limb’s force contribution over time in each phase[8][9]. This allows calculation of a force-time asymmetry index for each phase, typically based on the difference in impulse (area under the force-time curve) produced by the injured vs. uninjured limb[10]. Jordan coined the term “kinetic impulse asymmetry index” (KIAI) to describe this measure[11]. His research found that CMJ asymmetry indices are highly sensitive to an athlete’s musculoskeletal status through rehab – often revealing deficits well before they show up in simple performance metrics[4]. For example, in elite skiers returning from ACL reconstruction, the vertical jump asymmetry (especially during the eccentric phase) tracked closely with rehab progress and even predicted future injury risk[12][13]. Jordan’s framework therefore integrates bilateral dual-force-plate CMJ tests (to compute interlimb asymmetries in real time) and unilateral CMJ tests (to assess each leg’s independent explosive capacity) as complementary tools for decision-making in ACL rehab.
Crucially, Jordan cautions that no single metric guarantees readiness or predicts reinjury on its own[2]. Instead, practitioners should “be like Sherlock Holmes” – gathering multiple clues (strength tests, jump metrics, psychological readiness, etc.) and using informed reasoning to build a holistic picture[14]. In Jordan’s words, it’s an n=1 game: each athlete’s recovery profile is unique, so coaches should use Bayesian thinking – update expectations with each new test result – rather than chasing any one “magic” variable[14]. Nonetheless, force-plate CMJ testing has emerged as one of the most informative components of this holistic monitoring system. The following sections outline the specific CMJ force-plate metrics that Jordan’s research highlights for ACL return-to-play, along with the rationale and practical implications for each.
## Recommended Force Plate CMJ Metrics (Bilateral & Unilateral)
Jordan’s research and publications identify several CMJ-derived metrics as particularly useful for monitoring ACL recovery. These include metrics obtained from bilateral CMJ tests using dual force plates (which enable direct left-right comparisons during a two-leg jump), as well as metrics from unilateral CMJ tests performed on each leg separately. Below is an overview of the key metrics, grouped by bilateral vs. unilateral CMJ assessments:
### Bilateral CMJ Metrics (Dual-Plate Assessment)
Eccentric Deceleration Impulse Asymmetry: Difference between limbs in impulse (force × time area) during the braking phase of a bilateral CMJ[10]. This phase-specific asymmetry index (KIAI for the eccentric phase) quantifies how evenly the athlete accepts load on the way down.
Concentric Impulse Asymmetry: Difference between limbs in impulse during the propulsive (upward) phase of the CMJ[10]. This asymmetry index for the concentric phase reflects imbalance in force output when jumping off.
Peak Eccentric Power: The peak negative mechanical power (force × velocity) reached in the eccentric phase on each limb[15]. This indicates how powerfully the athlete can decelerate. It can be examined for asymmetry between legs or tracked for the injured limb.
Total Jump Height (bilateral): The jump height achieved in a countermovement jump (derived from takeoff velocity)[16]. While not an asymmetry metric itself (both legs contribute), jump height is a fundamental outcome to track recovery of overall power. Jordan often pairs jump height with time metrics (see below) to assess efficiency.
Jump Contraction Time: The total duration of the movement (from start of downward motion to take-off) in the CMJ[17]. This indicates how quickly the athlete can produce the jump. It’s especially telling when considered alongside jump height (e.g. a normal jump height achieved with abnormally long time may indicate a compensatory, slow strategy).
Modified Reactive Strength Index (RSI_Mod): Ratio of jump height to contraction time[18]. This metric, essentially jump height per unit time, encapsulates explosiveness of the stretch-shortening cycle. A lower RSI_Mod suggests impaired explosive capacity post-ACL, even if jump height alone appears acceptable[19][15].
Eccentric Phase Stiffness: Calculated as the change in vertical force divided by change in center-of-mass displacement during the eccentric deceleration phase[18]. This “lower limb stiffness” metric reflects how stiff or compliant the athlete’s landing/countermovement strategy is. Changes in stiffness can indicate adaptations – e.g. an athlete might adopt a more compliant (low stiffness) strategy post-ACL to reduce knee load[20][21].
Unweighting (Unloading) Impulse: The impulse during the initial unweighting phase (when the athlete quickly reduces force to initiate the downward movement)[22]. This metric can reveal subtle side-to-side shifts at movement onset – for instance, if the athlete favors the uninjured leg immediately when starting the counter-movement. Jordan’s work found the unloading impulse (and its asymmetry) to be among the top features distinguishing ACL-reconstructed athletes from uninjured controls[23].
### Unilateral CMJ Metrics (Single-Leg Jump Assessment)
Single-Leg Jump Height & LSI: Jump height performed on the injured leg versus the uninjured leg, often expressed as a Limb Symmetry Index (injured limb height as a percentage of the contralateral limb)[7]. This is a direct measure of functional performance per leg. An LSI approaching 90–100% is typically desired; persistent deficits in single-leg jump height indicate incomplete recovery of power on the involved side.
Single-Leg Concentric Impulse / Peak Power: The propulsive impulse or peak concentric power achieved by the injured limb, compared to the contralateral side. Like the bilateral test, this gauges the recovered force-time output of the surgical limb in isolation. Jordan’s analyses highlight that even at ~6 months post-ACL, athletes often show lower concentric impulse and power on the reconstructed side, which should improve over time[24]. Comparing against the healthy leg (or pre-injury benchmarks) helps determine if the involved leg’s explosive output is sufficient for return to play.
Eccentric Deceleration RFD (Single-Leg): The rate of force development during the eccentric phase of a unilateral CMJ on each leg. In practice, this can be observed via the force-time curve’s slope as the athlete brakes during the countermovement. A markedly blunted eccentric RFD on the injured limb (i.e. taking more time to decelerate and reverse direction) is a red flag for residual neuromuscular inhibition or fear of loading[21]. Jordan’s case studies have shown injured skiers exhibiting reduced eccentric RFD and reduced knee flexion on the involved side, indicative of a protective strategy[21]. Improvement in eccentric RFD suggests the athlete is regaining confidence and capacity in load acceptance on that limb.
Time to Peak Power (Single-Leg): The time it takes for the single leg to reach its peak concentric power output during the jump. A prolonged time-to-peak on the injured side can indicate a slower force production profile (possibly due to impaired rapid force capacity in the knee extensors). Jordan et al. identified this as a useful metric; athletes with ACL history often exhibit longer time to peak power compared to uninjured athletes[15]. A shortening of this time toward normative values is a positive sign for return-to-play readiness.
(Note: Many of the above unilateral metrics are also relevant in bilateral jumps when each limb’s contribution is analyzed separately. In Jordan’s methodology, a dual-force-plate CMJ can effectively provide both the bilateral overall outcomes and the side-specific metrics via decomposed force-time data[10]. For clarity, we list them under unilateral context since they reflect one limb’s capacity, but they may be measured in either format.)
## Rationale Behind Each Key Metric
Each of the above metrics offers a specific window into the athlete’s neuromuscular status post-ACL, aligning with Jordan’s research findings. Below we explain the rationale for why each metric is valuable for return-to-play monitoring:
Eccentric Deceleration Impulse Asymmetry (Bilateral CMJ): This metric directly assesses load acceptance asymmetry, which is critical after ACL injury. The eccentric impulse (area under the force curve in the downward phase) tells us how much force each leg is absorbing during landing and countermovement. A large asymmetry (injured leg contributing significantly less impulse) signals that the athlete is offloading the surgical limb during the braking phase[8][9]. This often reflects quadriceps weakness or fear of loading that limb. Jordan’s 2015 study demonstrated that ACL-reconstructed skiers had significantly higher eccentric impulse asymmetries than uninjured athletes[8]. Monitoring this metric helps ensure the athlete relearns to confidently absorb force on the injured side – a prerequisite for safe decelerations and landings in sport.
Concentric Impulse Asymmetry (Bilateral CMJ): This captures asymmetry in the propulsive phase, i.e. the ability of the injured leg to produce upward force relative to the healthy leg. Even if total jump performance seems normal, a high concentric impulse asymmetry indicates the uninjured leg is compensating to generate take-off force[25]. Jordan notes that athletes can often maintain jump height by favoring the stronger limb, masking deficits[25]. Thus, the concentric asymmetry index is a sensitive marker of lingering power deficits in the affected limb. A decreasing asymmetry over time indicates recovery of explosive force production on the surgical side. In Jordan’s practice, the concentric asymmetry index has emerged as one of the top metrics to flag neuromuscular deficits that are hidden from basic hop tests[26] (athletes may pass single-leg hop distance tests yet still show a high force asymmetry in a bilateral CMJ).
Peak Eccentric Power (Negative Power) and RFD: These metrics relate to how quickly and forcefully the athlete can brake during the countermovement, which is an aspect of dynamic knee stability. A reduced peak eccentric power on the injured side (or overall, in a bilateral jump) suggests the athlete is either avoiding a rapid descent or lacking eccentric strength to control it[15]. Similarly, a slower eccentric rate of force development indicates a cautious strategy – the athlete is taking more time to decelerate, often to minimize knee stress[27]. Jordan’s work highlights cases where an athlete post-ACL shows a much gentler slope in the force-time curve during eccentric loading on the surgical leg, corresponding with reduced knee flexion angle[21]. Restoring high eccentric power and RFD is important because it underpins reactive athletic movements (e.g. cutting, landing from a jump). These metrics tie into the concept of “load acceptance” – the faster and more powerfully a limb can absorb force, the more prepared it is for sports demands.
Jump Contraction Time & Time to Peak Power: These time-based metrics provide insight into the athlete’s explosive temporal profile. Jump contraction time (the total movement time) tends to be longer if an athlete uses a slower, strength-dominant strategy (perhaps due to impaired explosive capacity or hesitancy)[20]. Time to peak concentric power specifically homes in on the propulsive explosiveness – a longer time to peak power on the injured limb suggests the athlete cannot generate force rapidly, possibly due to residual neuromuscular inhibition or fiber-type shifts during rehab[15]. Jordan’s recent analysis found time-to-peak-power to be a distinguishing feature for athletes with ACL reconstruction[15]. The rationale for tracking these metrics is to ensure the athlete is not only regaining quantity of force, but also the rate of force development, which is crucial for agile, high-speed sports movements. As rehab progresses, one should see contraction times shorten and time to peak power get closer to that of healthy athletes.
Vertical Jump Height (Outcome) and Modified RSI: Jump height remains a simple indicator of overall power output and is often the first thing athletes and coaches look at. After ACL reconstruction, jump height on the injured side (single-leg CMJ) will usually be depressed; it should gradually improve to near baseline/pre-injury levels. In bilateral jumps, total jump height might recover faster – sometimes even before true symmetry is achieved, due to compensations[25]. Therefore, jump height is best interpreted alongside the asymmetry and timing metrics above. The modified RSI (jump height divided by time) adds context by accounting for how quickly that height was achieved[20]. Jordan supports RSI_Mod as a valuable metric because it captures deficits in stretch-shortening cycle efficiency that pure height might miss[20]. A low RSI_Mod (e.g. normal height but taking too long to produce it) flags that the athlete is not yet back to optimal explosiveness. The rationale for including jump height and RSI_Mod is that, together with force asymmetry measures, they give a balanced view of performance and strategy – ensuring the athlete eventually regains both sufficient power and efficient mechanics.
Lower Limb Stiffness (Eccentric Stiffness): Jordan includes stiffness as a metric to evaluate the movement strategy during the countermovement. Stiffness in this context is how much force is generated per unit displacement of the center of mass in the eccentric phase[18]. An athlete with a very low stiffness (i.e. large depth with relatively low force) might be relying on a deeper, slower squat to compensate for reduced knee extensor strength, whereas an excessively high stiffness (minimal bend, high forces) might indicate they are avoiding knee flexion and absorbing impact through a stiffer leg. Both extremes can be concerning; post-ACL, some athletes adopt a “stiffer” strategy to protect the knee[21]. Monitoring eccentric stiffness helps tailor feedback: for instance, if stiffness is too high on the injured side (indicating they aren’t using a normal range of motion to absorb load), the therapist might work on improving confidence in deeper knee flexion. Ultimately, a normalization of stiffness between limbs and versus normative data is desired, reflecting a return to a normal jumping strategy[20].
Unilateral Performance and Symmetry (Single-Leg CMJ metrics): The rationale for testing single-leg jumps in addition to bilateral is to expose deficits that bilateral tests can mask. A classic example is an athlete who can squat jump or CMJ nearly to their pre-injury height using both legs, but when asked to jump off the injured leg alone, they achieve significantly less height or force. Jordan’s studies (and others) consistently show that unilateral jump LSIs are often <90% at return-to-sport if thorough rehab hasn’t been done[7]. By measuring single-leg jump height, peak power, and impulse directly, one can determine if the involved limb has restored the necessary output for sport. Moreover, unilateral tests eliminate the “cheating” that can occur in bilateral tests (where the healthy leg compensates)[25]. A high-quality return-to-play protocol will typically require that single-leg metrics (e.g. jump height, or peak force normalized to body weight) of the injured side reach some threshold of the uninvolved side (often 90% or greater). Jordan’s approach uses single-leg CMJs to verify symmetric explosive performance and to identify which aspect of the force-time curve is lacking in the injured limb. For instance, if the injured leg’s jump height is close to the good leg but time to take-off is much longer, it indicates an underlying explosive speed deficit despite recovered jump capacity. Each unilateral metric thus feeds into a targeted intervention – e.g. addressing eccentric strength if eccentric impulse or RFD is low, or plyometric training if concentric power is lagging.
In summary, each metric is chosen for its ability to illuminate a particular dimension of neuromuscular recovery: asymmetry (between-limb deficits), load acceptance/braking (eccentric control), force-time characteristics (timing, RFD, power curve shape), and interlimb comparisons (performance of one leg vs the other). Jordan’s peer-reviewed studies underscore that using a phase-specific, multi-metric analysis of CMJ data gives a much more complete picture than raw jump height or isolated strength tests[28][15]. By combining these metrics, practitioners can detect whether an athlete is truly ready for the demands of sport or if subtle deficits remain.
## Practical Implications for Return-to-Play Decision Making
Implementing Jordan’s CMJ metrics in return-to-play decisions can significantly enhance the safety and effectiveness of the process. These force-plate metrics translate to actionable criteria for clinicians and coaches:
Identifying Hidden Deficits: One of the most important implications is catching deficits that traditional tests might miss. For example, an athlete may pass standard hop distance tests and have a nearly symmetric quadriceps strength ratio, yet still exhibit a 15% concentric impulse asymmetry and a blunted eccentric RFD on force-plate testing[25][21]. Jordan’s research warns that such an athlete is not truly symmetric in function – the force-plate is revealing a neuromuscular deficit that could predispose to re-injury if left unaddressed[25][13]. Thus, in practice, if meaningful asymmetries or power deficits show up in CMJ metrics, the return-to-play should be delayed or modified to target those deficits, even if classical criteria are met.
Guiding Targeted Rehab Interventions: Each metric can point to specific rehab needs. A high eccentric impulse asymmetry or low injured-limb eccentric power, for instance, tells the practitioner to focus on eccentric strength and deceleration training (e.g. eccentric squat programs, landing drills) to build load acceptance capacity. If jump contraction time or time to peak power is prolonged, plyometric and explosive training might be emphasized to improve rapid force development. By routinely testing these metrics, practitioners can form “training hypotheses” (as Jordan calls them) and then re-test to see if the deficits resolve[29][30]. This creates a feedback loop ensuring the rehab is effectively targeting the athlete’s weak links.
Informing Clearance and Risk Assessment: Force-plate CMJ metrics add quantitative rigor to return-to-play clearance decisions. Many programs use an LSI > 90% on hop tests as a criterion; Jordan’s approach would similarly advocate that CMJ asymmetry indices be within acceptable range (e.g. below ~10% asymmetry, acknowledging some day-to-day variability) before full return to sport. Moreover, absolute performance metrics should be back to baseline: for instance, if a jumper’s pre-injury bilateral CMJ height was 50 cm, but at 9 months post-op it’s 40 cm (even if symmetric), that indicates residual global power deficit. In such a case, pushing the athlete into high-level competition may invite injury due to inadequate capacity (Jordan notes that two weak but symmetric limbs are not desirable[31]). Practically, this means both symmetry and adequate magnitude of force/power must be achieved. Coaches should ensure the athlete’s injured limb is not just within X% of the other leg, but that both limbs are near their normative or pre-injury benchmarks[31].
Predicting Re-injury Risk: Perhaps the most compelling practical aspect is the potential to forecast injury risk. Emerging evidence (including work cited by Jordan) suggests that certain jump metrics correlate with re-injury. For example, one study found that in male athletes, those who sustained a second ACL injury had exhibited longer ground contact times, lower jump heights, and lower RSI in a drop jump test, whereas traditional single-leg hop distances and quad strength LSI did not predict re-injury[32]. This aligns with Jordan’s own findings that dynamic asymmetry and explosive deficits can linger despite “passing” simpler tests[13]. In practice, this means a return-to-play committee should weigh these force-plate findings heavily: an athlete with ongoing jump asymmetries or SSC (stretch-shortening cycle) deficits should be flagged as higher risk and possibly kept in rehabilitation or a modified training program longer. Over time, as data accumulates, an organization can even develop its own “profiles” for safe return – for instance, using Jordan’s generalized additive modeling approach to forecast neuromuscular recovery timelines[33]. If an athlete’s recovery curve for concentric impulse asymmetry is behind the expected trajectory, the staff might extend the rehab duration proactively.
Communication and Motivation: Jordan points out the importance of using these metrics to educate and motivate the athlete (and inform coaches) during the process[34][35]. Because the CMJ metrics are objective and trackable, they can be shown to athletes to validate their progress or highlight areas that need work. For example, showing an athlete that their injured leg produces, say, 20% less concentric impulse than their healthy leg can underscore the need for continued rehab – this can combat the impatience or false confidence that often occurs around the typical 6–9 month mark. Conversely, demonstrating improvements (e.g. “your eccentric impulse on the surgical side improved from 60% to 85% of the other leg in the last 6 weeks”) can boost confidence and buy-in. By translating the complex force-time data into simple charts or scores, practitioners can keep the athlete and coaching staff informed about readiness indicators, making the return-to-play decision a collaborative and transparent process rather than a subjective call.
Long-Term Athlete Monitoring: Finally, Jordan advocates extending these assessments well beyond the initial return to sport – into the return to performance phase and even for injury prevention in uninjured athletes[1][6]. The practical implication is that force-plate CMJ testing becomes part of routine monitoring for all athletes. For an ACL rehab case, even after the athlete is back in competition, continued periodic testing can catch any regressions (e.g. fatigue or overuse causing asymmetry to creep up again) and ensure that full performance potential is restored. Notably, Jordan’s team found that some deficits (like reduced rapid torque capacity) persisted 18+ months post-ACL despite meeting conventional criteria[36][7]. Ongoing monitoring helps confirm when the athlete has truly returned to pre-injury performance level, not just cleared the minimum standards. It also may alert staff to compensations that could lead to other injuries (e.g. if an athlete chronically offloads one side, they might be at risk of injuring the opposite limb – a common occurrence with second ACL injuries on the contralateral knee[37]).
Incorporating Matt Jordan’s force-plate CMJ metrics thus leads to a more data-driven and nuanced return-to-play decision. It ensures that the athlete not only passes a checklist but is genuinely prepared – symmetrically strong, explosively powerful, and confident in both limbs. Practitioners who adopt this approach can better safeguard athletes from premature return and re-injury, ultimately facilitating a safer progression back to full competition.
## Summary Tables: Key CMJ Metrics and Their Use in ACL Monitoring
The tables below summarize the primary force-plate CMJ metrics recommended in Jordan’s research, along with their definitions and practical use cases for ACL return-to-play monitoring.
Table 1. Bilateral CMJ Metrics (Dual-Force-Plate) for ACL Rehabilitation
[TABLE]
| Metric | Definition / Calculation | Use Case in ACL Monitoring |
| Eccentric Deceleration Impulse Asymmetry | Difference between limbs in impulse (force–time integral) during the CMJ eccentric (braking) phase[10]. Often expressed as an asymmetry index (% difference). | Indicates uneven load acceptance. A high asymmetry means the injured limb is absorbing significantly less force during descent, signaling protective behavior or weakness[8][9]. Used to ensure the athlete can safely decelerate loads on the surgical side before RTS. |
| Concentric Impulse Asymmetry | Difference between limbs in impulse during the concentric (propulsive) phase of a bilateral CMJ[10]. Calculated similarly as % difference in upward impulse. | Indicates imbalance in force output during take-off. High values denote the uninjured leg compensating for a weaker surgical leg[25]. Monitored to ensure power symmetry is restored, as persistent asymmetry is linked to neuromuscular deficits post-ACL[25]. |
| Peak Eccentric Power | The maximum negative power (force × velocity) during the CMJ deceleration phase, measured for each leg (in a dual-plate setup)[15]. | Reflects the limb’s powerful braking ability. Lower eccentric power on the injured side indicates cautious, slow descent or limited strength[15]. Improving this is crucial for reactive movements (cutting, landing); used to gauge if the athlete can handle high-force stops. |
| Jump Height (Total) | Height achieved in a CMJ (usually via take-off velocity)[16]. In bilateral jumps this is a combined result of both legs; can also be measured per leg in unilateral tests. | Key outcome for overall explosiveness. In rehab, reduced jump height indicates lingering power deficits. However, normal jump height with other asymmetries could mean compensation[25]. Thus, it’s tracked alongside asymmetry and timing metrics to ensure quality of movement, not just quantity, is back to pre-injury level. |
| Jump Contraction Time | Total time from start of movement (onset of unweighting) to toe-off in the CMJ[17]. Essentially the duration of eccentric + concentric phases. | Serves as an indicator of explosiveness and strategy. A longer time suggests a slower force development (or a deliberate slow countermovement)[20]. Monitored so that the athlete’s jump execution becomes quicker as they recover, reflecting normalized SSC function. |
| Modified RSI (CMJ) | Ratio of jump height to contraction time (often denoted RSI_Mod)[18]. Example: if 0.5 m jump height in 0.5 s, RSI_Mod = 1.0 (m/s). | Captures explosive performance efficiency. Lower values post-ACL indicate the athlete spends longer to produce a given jump height (diminished reactive strength)[20]. Used to track improvements in stretch-shortening cycle capacity; rising RSI_Mod implies better explosive return. |
| Eccentric Phase Stiffness | Ratio of change in force to change in center-of-mass displacement during the eccentric phase (ΔF/Δx over the decel phase)[18]. A higher value = stiffer, less displacement for given force. | Assesses movement strategy for load absorption. Low stiffness (excessive sink) might mean using a deeper bend to compensate for weakness; very high stiffness (minimal bend) might mean avoiding knee flexion[21]. Balanced stiffness suggests a more normal countermovement strategy. This metric helps ensure the athlete isn’t adopting a risky strategy to achieve performance (too stiff or too compliant). |
| Unloading Impulse | Impulse during the unweighting phase at movement initiation (when force dips below body weight as the athlete initiates downward motion)[22]. Can be measured per limb on dual plates. | Reveals subtle side-to-side weight shift at jump start. An injured athlete might unload the injured side less vigorously. In Jordan’s work, unloading impulse ranked highly in identifying ACL vs. healthy athletes[23]. Coaches watch this to ensure symmetric intent and explosiveness from the very start of the movement, indicating psychological and neuromuscular readiness. |
[/TABLE]
Table 2. Unilateral CMJ Metrics (Single-Leg Jumps) for ACL Rehabilitation
[TABLE]
| Metric | Definition / How Measured | Use Case in ACL Monitoring |
| Single-Leg Jump Height & LSI | CMJ height performed on each leg separately; Limb Symmetry Index (LSI) = injured leg height ÷ uninjured leg height × 100%. | Fundamental measure of single-leg power. An LSI below ~90% indicates the affected leg hasn’t regained jump performance[7]. Used as a return-to-play criterion (e.g. require ≥90–95%). Also provides psychological reassurance to athlete and coach when near parity is achieved. |
| Single-Leg Concentric Impulse / Peak Power | The impulse or peak power output of the isolated injured limb vs. the healthy limb during the upward phase of CMJ. Typically expressed in absolute terms (N·s or W) and via LSI. | Gauges the restored explosive capacity of the knee extensors and hip extensors in the injured leg. Even if jump height is similar, lower peak power or impulse on the injured side suggests a less efficient force generation[24]. This metric guides programming (e.g. if power is low, incorporate more power training) and ensures the athlete’s injured limb can produce the necessary force for sport actions (sprinting, jumping off that leg). |
| Eccentric RFD (Single-Leg) | Rate of force development in the eccentric phase for the single leg CMJ, often measured as the slope of the force–time curve or force attained at a short time interval. | Indicates speed of load acceptance on the individual limb. A slow eccentric RFD on the surgical leg reflects guarded movement or neuromuscular deficits[21]. Improving this is key for reactive ability – the athlete must quickly brace and reverse from a jump or landing on that leg. Clinicians use this to identify need for eccentric-focused training and to judge when the injured leg’s reactive strength is back to sport-ready levels. |
| Time to Peak Power (Single-Leg) | Time from start of upward movement to the point of peak concentric power for that leg’s jump. Measured in seconds (or milliseconds) for each leg. | A measure of explosive timing. Longer time on the injured side means the athlete reaches peak power more slowly[15], potentially problematic for rapid athletic moves. Coaches look for this to decrease to near the uninjured side’s timing. It helps confirm the athlete can generate power quickly (not just eventually), which is critical in fast sports scenarios. |
| Force–Velocity Profile Metrics (optional) | Advanced metrics like extrapolated max force (F₀) and velocity (V₀) from loaded single-leg CMJs[38]. Require multiple loads. | Provide deeper insight into whether the deficit is more force-related or velocity-related. While not always done in practice, Jordan’s case work used loaded jumps to see if the injured limb has specific weakness (low F₀ suggests strength deficit; low V₀ suggests explosive speed deficit)[39]. In rehab, this can fine-tune training focus (strength vs. power) for the injured leg. |
[/TABLE]
Each of these metrics is supported by Matt Jordan’s research and applied work, giving practitioners a robust toolkit for monitoring ACL recovery. By combining bilateral asymmetry indices with unilateral performance measures, one can triangulate the athlete’s readiness: confirming the once-injured limb is both symmetric in contribution and independently capable. This dual lens – looking at interlimb symmetry and absolute limb capacity – is at the heart of Jordan’s return-to-play testing paradigm. As evidence grows, these metrics are becoming integral in high-performance settings to reduce re-injury rates and optimize athletes’ return to their pre-injury performance levels[40][41].
Sources: Primary findings and recommendations are drawn from Matt Jordan’s publications and presentations, including his 2015 phase-specific asymmetry study[8], the 2022 Aspetar consensus on explosive strength after ACL[9][23], his case-study and medium articles on ACL return-to-sport testing[42][10], and related works by his collaborators. These sources provide detailed evidence for the metrics and their relevance to ACL rehabilitation and return-to-play decision-making. Each metric above is grounded in peer-reviewed research where Jordan is a lead or contributing author, ensuring that the recommendations are scientifically supported and practitioner-vetted.

# Force Plate Reporting System — Project Context

## Purpose

This system supports the Baylor Health & Wellness Applied Performance team in collecting, storing, analyzing, and presenting force plate data for athlete monitoring and return-to-play (RTP) decision-making. It is designed to serve practitioners, coaching staff, and athletics administration with outputs that range from raw data management to presentation-ready visual reports.

## Organizational Context

The system sits within the RTP Working Group's Intake/Assessment pillar, one of four pillars defined by the group (alongside Programming the Process, Medical Admin, and Staff Education). Assessment protocols include SFMA, Force Plates, Nordic Hamstring testing, and DXA scanning. Force plate testing is the most data-rich of these and drives the primary reporting infrastructure described here.

Key stakeholders who receive reports include athletic trainers, strength and conditioning staff, team physicians, and coaching staff. Not all of these audiences have a biomechanics background, which is why the system pairs visual reports with a plain-language metric appendix.

## Architecture

The system has three layers:

**Layer 1 — Data Ingestion (`force_plate_manager.py`)**
A Python CLI tool that manages the pipeline from raw ForceDecks CSV exports to a unified master database. It handles format detection, column standardization, duplicate prevention (via file hashing), and import logging. Processed files are automatically archived.

Key commands:
- `setup` — Creates the folder structure (`csv_inbox/`, `csv_processed/`, `reports/`)
- `combine` — Ingests new CSVs from the inbox into `master_database.csv`
- `report` — Generates a tabular progress report (baseline, latest, best, % change, trend)
- `status` — Shows current database summary

**Layer 2 — Master Database (`master_database.csv`)**
A flat CSV file. One row per athlete per session per test type. Currently built around bilateral CMJ metrics from ForceDecks. The schema includes identity columns (Name, Date, Test Type, Trial), optional metadata (Sport, Position, Body Mass), and all numeric metric columns exported from ForceDecks. Internal tracking columns (`_source_file`, `_import_timestamp`) support audit trails.

The current master DB was generated from sample data for development. It contains 90 rows across multiple simulated athletes and sessions.

**Layer 3 — Visual Reports (HTML + React `.jsx` artifacts)**
Presentation-layer components that render multi-panel dashboards with Baylor branding (green `#154734`, gold `#FFB81C`). These are currently populated with hardcoded data parsed from CSV files during each work session. Five report templates exist; V5 HTML is the production reference. HTML files open directly in any browser with no build step.

**Companion Document — Metric Appendix (`Force_Plate_Metric_Appendix.docx`)**
A Word document defining every metric on the report in plain language with practical examples in a power/speed sport context. Organized into four categories: Output, Driver, Strategy, Asymmetry. Intended to accompany any visual report so non-technical readers can interpret the data.

## Workflow (Current State)

1. **Export** — Practitioner runs force plate test, exports CSV from ForceDecks with selected metrics. File goes into `csv_inbox/`.
2. **Ingest** — Run `python force_plate_manager.py combine`. Script hashes for duplicates, cleans and standardizes columns, appends to `master_database.csv`, moves originals to `csv_processed/`.
3. **Tabular Report** — Run `python force_plate_manager.py report --athlete "Name"`. Pulls from master DB, calculates baseline, latest, best, percent change, and 3-session trend per metric. Saves summary CSV to `reports/`.
4. **Visual Report** — HTML template (`MaikolPerezReport_v5.html`) is manually populated with data. Renders multi-panel dashboard with KPI blocks + sparklines, 4-column session data tables for CMJ bilateral metrics, paired L/R bar charts for SL CMJ, asymmetry color-coding, and RTP symmetry flags. Athlete headshot loaded from same folder as HTML file.
5. **Appendix** — `Force_Plate_Metric_Appendix.docx` accompanies the report as a reference for each metric.

**Current gap:** Steps 1–3 are automated. Step 4 is manual. The next build priority is a pipeline that queries the master DB by athlete name and auto-populates the visual template.

## File Inventory

| File | Type | Purpose |
|------|------|---------|
| `force_plate_manager.py` | Python | Data ingestion, master DB management, tabular reporting |
| `generate_sample_data.py` | Python | Creates simulated athlete data for development/testing |
| `master_database.csv` | CSV | Unified data store (currently sample data) |
| `ForcePlayerReport.jsx` | React | Template V1 — KPI cards, sparklines, bilateral CMJ focus (superseded) |
| `DidiStyleReport.jsx` | React | Template V2 — Multi-panel grid matching DiDi Richards Excel layout (superseded) |
| `MaikolPerezReport.jsx` | React | Template V3 — Real athlete data (Maikcol Perez), headshot, bar charts, L/R splits (superseded) |
| `MaikolPerezReport_v4.html` | HTML | Template V4 — First hybrid HTML mockup (superseded) |
| `MaikolPerezReport_v5.html` | HTML | **Template V5 — Production reference.** Full RTP banner, KPI cards + sparkline, CMJ bilateral panels use 4-column data table (Session/Value/vs Baseline/vs Best) instead of bar charts, SL CMJ panels retain paired L/R bar charts, athlete headshot from `MP_Headshot.png` with initials fallback, 6px rounded corners, 13px body font, 1400px max-width, no footer |
| `Force_Plate_Metric_Appendix.docx` | Word | Plain-language metric descriptions for practitioners |

## Data Sources

Force plate data comes from ForceDecks via CSV export. Two export formats have been used:

- **Bilateral CMJ export** — One row per session. Columns include jump height (inches), eccentric braking impulse, concentric mean power/BM, concentric mean force, eccentric peak velocity, and eccentric braking impulse asymmetry (as "X.X L" or "X.X R").
- **Single-leg CMJ export** — One row per session. Columns include bilateral average plus L/R splits and asymmetry for jump height (cm), eccentric braking impulse, eccentric peak velocity, concentric mean force/BM, and countermovement depth.

The manager script's `CORE_METRICS` list was originally built around bilateral CMJ. The SL CMJ paired-column format (metric, metric (L), metric (R), metric (Asym)) has not yet been formally integrated into the master DB schema.

## Branding

All visual outputs use the Baylor University athletic identity:
- Primary green: `#154734`
- Gold accent: `#FFB81C`
- Light green background for data rows: `#eef3e8`
- Page background: `#f5f5f0`
- Monospace font for data tables (Consolas/Courier New)
- Sans-serif for headers and labels (Segoe UI/Arial)

## Clinical Thresholds

Asymmetry color coding:
- ≤5%: Normal (green `#059669`)
- 5–10%: Monitor (amber `#b45309`)
- 10–15%: Elevated (orange `#ea580c`)
- >15%: Flag (red `#dc2626`)

RTP symmetry thresholds (from RTP Working Group):
- Reconstruction phase: ≥80% symmetry (≤20% asymmetry)
- Reintegration phase: ≥90% symmetry (≤10% asymmetry)

## Metric Categories

# Force Plate Reporting System — Project Context

## Purpose

This system supports the Baylor Health & Wellness Applied Performance team in collecting, storing, analyzing, and presenting force plate data for athlete monitoring and return-to-play (RTP) decision-making. It is designed to serve practitioners, coaching staff, and athletics administration with outputs that range from raw data management to presentation-ready visual reports.

## Organizational Context

The system sits within the RTP Working Group's Intake/Assessment pillar, one of four pillars defined by the group (alongside Programming the Process, Medical Admin, and Staff Education). Assessment protocols include SFMA, Force Plates, Nordic Hamstring testing, and DXA scanning. Force plate testing is the most data-rich of these and drives the primary reporting infrastructure described here.

Key stakeholders who receive reports include athletic trainers, strength and conditioning staff, team physicians, and coaching staff. Not all of these audiences have a biomechanics background, which is why the system pairs visual reports with a plain-language metric appendix.

## Architecture

The system has three layers:

**Layer 1 — Data Ingestion (`force_plate_manager.py`)**
A Python CLI tool that manages the pipeline from raw ForceDecks CSV exports to a unified master database. It handles format detection, column standardization, duplicate prevention (via file hashing), and import logging. Processed files are automatically archived.

Key commands:
- `setup` — Creates the folder structure (`csv_inbox/`, `csv_processed/`, `reports/`)
- `combine` — Ingests new CSVs from the inbox into `master_database.csv`
- `report` — Generates a tabular progress report (baseline, latest, best, % change, trend)
- `status` — Shows current database summary

**Layer 2 — Master Database (`master_database.csv`)**
A flat CSV file. One row per athlete per session per test type. Currently built around bilateral CMJ metrics from ForceDecks. The schema includes identity columns (Name, Date, Test Type, Trial), optional metadata (Sport, Position, Body Mass), and all numeric metric columns exported from ForceDecks. Internal tracking columns (`_source_file`, `_import_timestamp`) support audit trails.

The current master DB was generated from sample data for development. It contains 90 rows across multiple simulated athletes and sessions.

**Layer 3 — Visual Reports (HTML + React `.jsx` artifacts)**
Presentation-layer components that render multi-panel dashboards with Baylor branding (green `#154734`, gold `#FFB81C`). These are currently populated with hardcoded data parsed from CSV files during each work session. Five report templates exist; V5 HTML is the production reference. HTML files open directly in any browser with no build step.

**Companion Document — Metric Appendix (`Force_Plate_Metric_Appendix.docx`)**
A Word document defining every metric on the report in plain language with practical examples in a power/speed sport context. Organized into four categories: Output, Driver, Strategy, Asymmetry. Intended to accompany any visual report so non-technical readers can interpret the data.

## Workflow (Current State)

1. **Export** — Practitioner runs force plate test, exports CSV from ForceDecks with selected metrics. File goes into `csv_inbox/`.
2. **Ingest** — Run `python force_plate_manager.py combine`. Script hashes for duplicates, cleans and standardizes columns, appends to `master_database.csv`, moves originals to `csv_processed/`.
3. **Tabular Report** — Run `python force_plate_manager.py report --athlete "Name"`. Pulls from master DB, calculates baseline, latest, best, percent change, and 3-session trend per metric. Saves summary CSV to `reports/`.
4. **Visual Report** — HTML template (`MaikolPerezReport_v5.html`) is manually populated with data. Renders multi-panel dashboard with KPI blocks + sparklines, 4-column session data tables for CMJ bilateral metrics, paired L/R bar charts for SL CMJ, asymmetry color-coding, and RTP symmetry flags. Athlete headshot loaded from same folder as HTML file.
5. **Appendix** — `Force_Plate_Metric_Appendix.docx` accompanies the report as a reference for each metric.

**Current gap:** Steps 1–3 are automated. Step 4 is manual. The next build priority is a pipeline that queries the master DB by athlete name and auto-populates the visual template.

## File Inventory

| File | Type | Purpose |
|------|------|---------|
| `force_plate_manager.py` | Python | Data ingestion, master DB management, tabular reporting |
| `generate_sample_data.py` | Python | Creates simulated athlete data for development/testing |
| `master_database.csv` | CSV | Unified data store (currently sample data) |
| `ForcePlayerReport.jsx` | React | Template V1 — KPI cards, sparklines, bilateral CMJ focus (superseded) |
| `DidiStyleReport.jsx` | React | Template V2 — Multi-panel grid matching DiDi Richards Excel layout (superseded) |
| `MaikolPerezReport.jsx` | React | Template V3 — Real athlete data (Maikcol Perez), headshot, bar charts, L/R splits (superseded) |
| `MaikolPerezReport_v4.html` | HTML | Template V4 — First hybrid HTML mockup (superseded) |
| `MaikolPerezReport_v5.html` | HTML | **Template V5 — Production reference.** Full RTP banner, KPI cards + sparkline, CMJ bilateral panels use 4-column data table (Session/Value/vs Baseline/vs Best) instead of bar charts, SL CMJ panels retain paired L/R bar charts, athlete headshot from `MP_Headshot.png` with initials fallback, 6px rounded corners, 13px body font, 1400px max-width, no footer |
| `Force_Plate_Metric_Appendix.docx` | Word | Plain-language metric descriptions for practitioners |

## Data Sources

Force plate data comes from ForceDecks via CSV export. Two export formats have been used:

- **Bilateral CMJ export** — One row per session. Columns include jump height (inches), eccentric braking impulse, concentric mean power/BM, concentric mean force, eccentric peak velocity, and eccentric braking impulse asymmetry (as "X.X L" or "X.X R").
- **Single-leg CMJ export** — One row per session. Columns include bilateral average plus L/R splits and asymmetry for jump height (cm), eccentric braking impulse, eccentric peak velocity, concentric mean force/BM, and countermovement depth.

The manager script's `CORE_METRICS` list was originally built around bilateral CMJ. The SL CMJ paired-column format (metric, metric (L), metric (R), metric (Asym)) has not yet been formally integrated into the master DB schema.

## Branding

All visual outputs use the Baylor University athletic identity:
- Primary green: `#154734`
- Gold accent: `#FFB81C`
- Light green background for data rows: `#eef3e8`
- Page background: `#f5f5f0`
- Monospace font for data tables (Consolas/Courier New)
- Sans-serif for headers and labels (Segoe UI/Arial)

## Clinical Thresholds

Asymmetry color coding:
- ≤5%: Normal (green `#059669`)
- 5–10%: Monitor (amber `#b45309`)
- 10–15%: Elevated (orange `#ea580c`)
- >15%: Flag (red `#dc2626`)

RTP symmetry thresholds (from RTP Working Group):
- Reconstruction phase: ≥80% symmetry (≤20% asymmetry)
- Reintegration phase: ≥90% symmetry (≤10% asymmetry)

## Metric Categories

Metrics are classified into four types, following the DiDi Richards template convention:
- **Output** — Performance results (Jump Height, Power/BM, RSI-modified)
- **Driver** — Force capacities (Concentric Mean Force, Eccentric Braking Impulse)
- **Strategy** — Movement organization (Eccentric Peak Velocity, CM Depth, Phase Durations)
- **Asymmetry** — L/R imbalance (% favoring L or R, reported per metric)

## Next Steps

- Build automated pipeline from master DB to visual report template (the Layer 2 → Layer 3 bridge)
- Integrate SL CMJ paired-column schema into master database
- Add bar charts for longitudinal progress visualization across all templates
- Expand to additional test types (Nordic Hamstring / Nordbord, IMTP)
- Develop risk stratification models using historical injury data
- Finalize metric list for production reports (current lists differ across templates)

Baylor Athletics staff use these department names, and Eric corrects the generic ones (2026-09-16):

- **Athletic Performance**, not "strength and conditioning" / S&C
- **Athletic Medicine**, not "sports medicine"
- **Applied Performance**, not "sport science" / sports science (also Eric's own department)

**Why:** deliverables go to Baylor staff and leadership; generic industry names read as outside-written.
**How to apply:** use these names in any staff-facing deck, email, report, or role list. Weekly_Research_Review enforces them in `tools/build.js` (ROLES list). Related: [[prioritization-slate]].
---
name: admin-docs-house-style
description: Every document going to administration uses the Baylor house style (Baylor_Doc_Style) — no local sizes/margins; ask before breaking a page limit
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: cc670342-87f8-4b63-a0f3-1542a985e260
  modified: 2026-09-29T20:49:32.873Z
---

Every document going to Baylor Athletics administration (leadership, admin, Kenny Boyd,
Chris Ruf) is built with the house style in `~/DEV/Baylor_Doc_Style`
(`baylor_docstyle.py`, `BaylorDoc`; exemplar is the Software & Technology Management
Framework draft, chosen 2026-08-30). Use only its components (`section`, `table`, `note`,
`para`, `bullets`) and its defaults: Calibri 10.5, 9.5pt tables, 0.80/0.90in margins.
No local font sizes, margins, Normal-style overrides or hand-built tables.

**Why:** on 2026-09-29 I shrank the Tech Inventory by-unit list (7.5pt, 0.6in margins,
custom table) to force one page. Eric: "the docs should have the same baylor styling
we've been using in other documentation. make a note that future docs going to
administration should use it also." When asked, he chose two pages in house style over
one page that broke it.

**How to apply:** if content won't fit a page limit in house style, ask Eric (more pages,
or cut content) instead of shrinking below house sizes. Word COM is the page-count
authority (`doc_platform.word_pdf` in Tech_Inventory_Analysis). Related:
[[tech-inventory-refresh]], [[kenny-boyd-doc-review-preferences]],
[[baylor-department-names]].
---
name: kenny-boyd-doc-review-preferences
description: "Kenny Boyd's editorial constraints on Athletics policy/framework docs — no language implying past incompetence, no judgmental tier labels, name the seniority of reviewers"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 126c5de4-d928-4658-88d2-1922d2464a29
  modified: 2026-08-11T23:13:32.529Z
---

Kenny Boyd (reviewer on the Baylor Athletics Software and Technology Management
Framework) consistently pushes back on three things in draft policy language:

1. **No language that implies the department was previously incompetent.** He cut
   "so the department stops discovering it is in the final year of an agreement
   with no time to act" for exactly this reason. Rewrite as forward-looking
   capability ("advance visibility of contract end dates and the lead time to
   evaluate options"), not as a problem being fixed.
2. **No judgmental or ranking-flavored labels.** He rejected the Light / Standard /
   Elevated review tiers. Neutral, descriptive, escalating names work better —
   Level 1 Standard / Level 2 Enhanced / Level 3 Comprehensive Review. He floated
   Basic / Intermediate / Advanced, which reads as sophistication of the
   *technology* rather than depth of *review*.
3. **Name the seniority of the reviewer, not just the office.** For ITS he wanted
   it clear that a supervisory-level person with authority to commit resources is
   involved, not a line technician. Frame this as decision authority the request
   requires, never as competence of the staff.

He also wants Baylor branding carried through headers/footers and draft status
marked on every page.

**Why:** These are tone constraints, not content ones — the same facts land or
fail on phrasing. Getting them wrong costs a full review cycle.

**How to apply:** Before sending any Athletics policy or framework draft for his
review, scan for blame-implying rationale, ranking adjectives on process tiers,
and unqualified office names where seniority matters.

Related: [[status-report-sourcing]]

NCAA Performance Technologies Recommendations

# What the NCAA Document Says
The NCAA Sport Science Institute brought together experts for a summit on performance technologies. The result is a consensus document organized around foundational concepts, recommendations, and implementation strategies. The document boils down to having a written plan. The plan should cover four things: education, data management, technology selection, and continuous improvement.

Worth noting:
- The definition of "performance technology" is intentionally broad. If it collects biometric or performance data, it counts. That includes cameras, surveys, and apps, not only wearables.
- Student-athlete rights are front and center. Informed consent, data privacy, and compliance were addressed.
- These tools can cause unintended harm. The document specifically calls out mental health effects: anxiety, fixation on numbers, and body image issues.

# Five Recommendations
Recommendation 1 (Policy) is to have a written plan. Recommendations 2 through 5 are what that plan needs to cover. The table below displays each recommendation and what we should do about it.


| Recommendation | NCAA Strategy | Baylor Action Step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Policy | Create a written plan. Build it with a multidisciplinary team (student-athletes, sports medicine, coaches, admin, legal, IT). Review it regularly. | Form a MDT (Multi-disciplinary Team) or a Performance Technology Working Group, draft the plan, and present it to S-A Services Staff for input. |
| 2. Education | Train everyone at least once a year. Tailor content by audience. Cover limitations, data privacy, informed consent, and departmental policies. | Add a performance technology module to existing compliance sessions and new student-athletes' onboarding. Different content for coaches, Athletic Medicine, Athletics Performance, and student-athletes, etc. |
| 3. Data Management | Establish who owns the data, where it lives, who can see it, and what it can be used for. Plan for transfer student-athletes. | Run a full technology inventory across all sports. Work with legal and IT to establish ownership, access, and transfer protocols. Develop a data rights/release consent template. |
| 4. Tech Selection | Evaluate quality (accuracy, reliability, validity) before you buy. Use evidence-based frameworks. Decisions should be made by a cross-functional group. | Build a Technology Evaluation Checklist. Route all new purchases through the Working Group (MDT). Establish a scalable review process with documentation |
| 5. Continuous Improvement | Collect feedback from student-athletes, coaches, and staff on a regular basis. Student-athlete feedback is not optional. Use it to update the plan. | Annual student-athlete survey. The Working Group runs an annual review. Each technology gets a continuation, modification, or discontinuation decision. |

# Sports Science Research Grounding

## Purpose

Ground normal domain conversations in the user's research library without requiring a paper title or special
command. This skill is harness-neutral: use the `zotero-research` MCP server when available, or the shared
`zotero-bridge` CLI as the operational fallback.

Do not use this skill for routine coding, scheduling, or administrative questions merely because the repository
contains sport-science material.

## Evidence workflow

1. Resolve material applicability context before retrieval: sport code, sex, age or competition level, and injury
   region or type. In this user's Baylor performance context, interpret unqualified `football` as `collegiate
   American football` unless the question says soccer, association football, Australian football, or another code.
   Pass that explicit context in the question sent to the evidence-pack tool.
2. Call `build_research_evidence_pack` with the contextualized question, `limit=5`, and `extract=false`.
3. Read `required_context`, `applicability_alignment`, `coverage`, `coverage_reason`, and every paper's
   `applicability_alignment`, matches, conflicts, evidence status, citation, DOI, snippet, and page hits.
4. Prefer `page-located` evidence. If a high-value local match is `pending-extraction` and its findings matter to
   the answer, call the evidence-pack tool again with `extract=true`, or use `search_paper_evidence` and
   `get_paper_pages` after preparation.
5. If coverage is `thin` or `none`, use the current harness's native research/search capability to locate primary
   peer-reviewed literature. Label each such citation `[External]`. Never imply an external paper is in Zotero.
6. If external research is unavailable, say that the local coverage is incomplete and identify the gap.

## Answer contract

- Lead with the practical answer, then show the research basis.
- Distinguish direct study findings, cross-paper synthesis, and practitioner interpretation.
- Include population, setting, study design, outcomes, and material limitations when they affect transfer.
- Cite local evidence as `[Zotero: ITEM_KEY, p. N]` when a page is available; include DOI or full citation.
- Cite external fallback as `[External]` and link the primary source.
- Treat systematic reviews and strong designs as higher-weight evidence, not automatic truth.
- Explain genuine disagreement, thin evidence, and uncertainty instead of averaging it away.
- Never use a Graphify-inferred or ambiguous edge as primary evidence. Verify graph-proposed links against the
  original paper evidence.

## Existing memory and SecondBrain

The Zotero index is retrieval memory, not a replacement for personal or project memory. Use the harness's normal
memory system for relevant user context and prior decisions, but do not cite memory as research evidence and do
not copy the paper corpus into memory. Reviewed Paper Briefs and multi-paper syntheses belong in SecondBrain.
Only write durable memory through the user's existing memory workflow or when explicitly asked.

## Full-library processing

When asked to ingest or continue the library:

1. Read [batch-model-routing.md](references/batch-model-routing.md) and apply its automatic routing policy.
2. Call `list_library_backlog`; the queue is the priority lane, not the boundary.
3. Work in a bounded batch. Skip `ingested`, review `update_available`, extract `pending_extraction`, and create
   claims-free Reference Stubs only for `reference_stub` records.
4. Use `prepare_paper_brief`, bounded evidence searches/pages, and the repository Paper Brief contract before
   calling `save_paper_brief` or `save_reference_stub`.
5. Do not overwrite locally edited notes, mutate Zotero, or silently commit SecondBrain changes.

## CLI fallback

From the `ZoteroInjestion` repo under the machine's DEV root (`~/Desktop/DEV` on Windows; `~/DEV` on macOS):

```powershell
uv run zotero-bridge ground "<question>" --limit 5
uv run zotero-bridge backlog --limit 50 --offset 0
```

{"result":[{"page":4,"text":"Stokes KA et al. Returning to Play after …  Int J Sports Med 
Review
Thieme
blood volume, interferes with heart rate and blood pressure regu-
lation, induces cardiac muscle atrophy and impairs myocardial me-
chanics and stroke volume. Though the time course and severity 
of some of these responses has not been precisely delineated, their 
integrated nature rapidly impairs oxygen (and nutrient) delivery 
and tissue extraction, and can be expected within < 4 weeks [52].
Skeletal muscle appears to be particularly susceptible to disuse-
induced deconditioning, with substantial impairments in markers 
of metabolic health (reflecting declining muscle tissue quantity 
and quality) within just one week [53, 54]. Disuse also almost im-
mediately reduces daily muscle protein synthesis rates [55], large-
ly driven by a reduced ability of the inactive tissue to extract die-
tary derived amino acids from the circulation following each meal 
[56] and utilize them for the construction of new proteins [57]. The 
resulting loss of muscle mass can be nearly 100 g after only two 
days of limb immobilization [55]. This increases to  > 250 g after 
one week, while one week of bed-rest results in ~1.5 kg of whole 
body muscle loss [53]. Strikingly, muscle strength and force gen-
erating capacity of a muscle group subjected to extreme disuse de-
clines by ~1.5–2 % per day [58], around 3-fold higher than the loss 
of muscle mass alone [59].
Muscles (groups) of a higher ‘training status’ within an individual 
(i. e. higher habitual gravitational loading and mechanical work-
load) typically decondition more rapidly. For example, the quadri-
ceps atrophy more rapidly than the hamstrings [60], and the large 
postural and gross motor movement muscles of the legs, trunk and 
back atrophy more quickly than the arms or other smaller muscles 
more attuned to fine movements [61]. In the event that disuse is 
brought about by any type of acute injury, which would typically 
elicit a local and systemic inflammatory response, muscle loss may 
be further accelerated over rest alone [62]. At the single fiber level, 
muscle disuse atrophy is characterized by a decrease in cross-sec-
tional area of all muscle fiber types, though type II fibers appear 
particularly susceptible [63]. Skeletal muscle fiber atrophy is ac-
companied by considerable and disproportionately large declines 
in function at the level of the muscle fiber. Despite this, some evi-
dence points towards deconditioning bringing about a ‘faster’ over-
all muscle phenotype, seemingly due to increased expression in 
the faster isoforms of muscle myosin heavy chain across fiber types 
[64] rather than any ‘fiber type switching’.
Bone demineralization also occurs within a week of unloading 
[65], while tendon and connective tissues such as ligaments appear 
to be more resistant to short-term muscle disuse [66, 67], likely 
due to considerably lower protein turnover rates. However, within 
a month of detraining, impairments in tendon and ligament ten-
sile strength and functionality can be expected [68]. Decondition-
ing of the tendon and ligament tissue also impacts on metabolic 
and functional performance [66, 67]. The crucial structural role of 
these collagen-rich tissues within the musculoskeletal system (par-
ticularly within joint stabilization) contributes heavily to movement 
and force generation, and therefore their deconditioning also con-
tributes to the degeneration of physical performance.
It is clear that the extreme models of disuse described above do 
not reflect the experiences of athletes during most periods of train-
ing restriction. However, case-study data on elite footballers sug-
gest that injury induced periods of disuse (e. g. Anterior cruciate 
ligament [ACL] surgery) lead to rapid tissue and performance det-
riments that reflect the changes seen in laboratory trials (e. g. loss 
of muscle mass and function, gain in fat tissue and alterations in 
metabolic rate) [69, 70]. Such effects are evident despite ‘best prac-
tice’ in terms of nutritional and physical therapy countermeasures 
being applied. Furthermore, elite athletes reducing training at the 
end of their competitive season can expect rapid (within 5 weeks) 
declines in function, with the extent being related to the level of 
withdrawal from training [71]. Such data brings into stark focus the 
challenges that those involved in collision sports face, if athletes 
undergo enforced periods of reduced or absent training load.
Maintaining muscle mass and function during 
enforced modified training
Fortunately, even in extreme physiological models of disuse, small 
amounts of exercise can mitigate losses in muscle size and func-
tion. For example, eighty-four days of bed rest in healthy men re-
sulted in a 17 % reduction in muscle size and around 40 % reduction 
in muscle strength and power [72]. However, when maximal con-
centric supine squats were performed every third day, muscle size, 
strength and power were maintained [72]. In 60 days of bed rest, 
just three minutes of “supine jumps” on 5–6 days per week main-
tained leg lean mass and strength, compared with reductions of 
around 10 % without exercise [73]. These examples are important 
in illustrating the concept of mitigating losses in muscle mass and 
function during deconditioning, but cannot be translated directly 
into sports settings.
A key question when access to training facilities is limited is 
whether heavy loads during resistance training are required for the 
development, or maintenance, of muscle mass and strength. Dur-
ing resistance exercise all motor units are recruited at momentary 
muscular failure, regardless of the load used [74]. In turn, rates of 
muscle protein synthesis for up to 24 hours after exercise were sim-
ilar when healthy men performed knee extension at 30 % of one 
repetition maximum (1RM) to failure compared with 90 % 1RM to 
failure [75]. Taking this further, 10 weeks of knee-extension train-
ing to failure at 30 % 1RM and 80 % 1RM in healthy young men re-
sulted in a similar change in quadriceps volume (hypertrophy), al-
though gains in strength as assessed by 1RM was significantly high-
er following training at 80 % 1RM [76]. Other studies have also 
reported similar hypertrophy responses in lower-load and higher-
load resistance training, with smaller gains in strength in lower-load 
training [77, 78]. Furthermore, 12 weeks of whole-body resistance 
training at either 30–50 % 1RM or 75–90 % 1RM in trained individ-
uals resulted in similar changes in whole body lean mass [79]. How-
ever, in this study, 1RM strength was tested every third week, es-
sentially allowing a small amount of high load training in both 
groups, and the strength outcomes were similar in all tests other 
than bench press for which there was a small but significantly su-
perior gain in the 75–90 % 1RM group. Incorporating plyometric 
training might also be beneficial, given that eccentric muscle ac-
tions have the potential to induce neural adaptations, even in the 
absence of heavy loads, and that both concentric and eccentric 
peak torque were better maintained during detraining following 
coupled concentric and eccentric resistance training than concen-
tric training alone [80]. Furthermore, although evidence is mixed, 
meta-analysis showed small-to-moderate effects of plyometric 
training on maximal strength in healthy adults [81].

riments that reflect the changes seen in laboratory trials (e. g. loss 
of muscle mass and function, gain in fat tissue and alterations in 
metabolic rate) [69, 70]. Such effects are evident despite ‘best prac-
tice’ in terms of nutritional and physical therapy countermeasures 
being applied. Furthermore, elite athletes reducing training at the 
end of their competitive season can expect rapid (within 5 weeks) 
declines in function, with the extent being related to the level of 
withdrawal from training [71]. Such data brings into stark focus the 
challenges that those involved in collision sports face, if athletes 
undergo enforced periods of reduced or absent training load.
Maintaining muscle mass and function during 
enforced modified training
Fortunately, even in extreme physiological models of disuse, small 
amounts of exercise can mitigate losses in muscle size and func-
tion. For example, eighty-four days of bed rest in healthy men re-
sulted in a 17 % reduction in muscle size and around 40 % reduction 
in muscle strength and power [72]. However, when maximal con-
centric supine squats were performed every third day, muscle size, 
strength and power were maintained [72]. In 60 days of bed rest, 
just three minutes of “supine jumps” on 5–6 days per week main-
tained leg lean mass and strength, compared with reductions of 
around 10 % without exercise [73]. These examples are important 
in illustrating the concept of mitigating losses in muscle mass and 
function during deconditioning, but cannot be translated directly 
into sports settings.
A key question when access to training facilities is limited is 
whether heavy loads during resistance training are required for the 
development, or maintenance, of muscle mass and strength. Dur-
ing resistance exercise all motor units are recruited at momentary 
muscular failure, regardless of the load used [74]. In turn, rates of 
muscle protein synthesis for up to 24 hours after exercise were sim-
ilar when healthy men performed knee extension at 30 % of one 
repetition maximum (1RM) to failure compared with 90 % 1RM to 
failure [75]. Taking this further, 10 weeks of knee-extension train-
ing to failure at 30 % 1RM and 80 % 1RM in healthy young men re-
sulted in a similar change in quadriceps volume (hypertrophy), al-
though gains in strength as assessed by 1RM was significantly high-
er following training at 80 % 1RM [76]. Other studies have also 
reported similar hypertrophy responses in lower-load and higher-
load resistance training, with smaller gains in strength in lower-load 
training [77, 78]. Furthermore, 12 weeks of whole-body resistance 
training at either 30–50 % 1RM or 75–90 % 1RM in trained individ-
uals resulted in similar changes in whole body lean mass [79]. How-
ever, in this study, 1RM strength was tested every third week, es-
sentially allowing a small amount of high load training in both 
groups, and the strength outcomes were similar in all tests other 
than bench press for which there was a small but significantly su-
perior gain in the 75–90 % 1RM group. Incorporating plyometric 
training might also be beneficial, given that eccentric muscle ac-
tions have the potential to induce neural adaptations, even in the 
absence of heavy loads, and that both concentric and eccentric 
peak torque were better maintained during detraining following 
coupled concentric and eccentric resistance training than concen-
tric training alone [80]. Furthermore, although evidence is mixed, 
meta-analysis showed small-to-moderate effects of plyometric 
training on maximal strength in healthy adults [81].

However, it remains unclear which vertical tests (bilateral or unilateral) and which metrics (kinetics or performance) are most effective in informing the rehabilitation status and readiness for return to sport. We aimed to investigate the status of athletes during vertical jump testing at return to sport after ACLR.\nMethods A dual force platform system was used to evaluate jumping performance of 126 recreational and professional athletes at the time of return to sport after ACLR, as well as 532 healthy control participants. Performance and kinetic metrics were collected during four jump tests: double-leg countermovement jump, single-leg countermovement jump, double-leg 30 cm drop jump and single-leg 15 cm drop jump. Between-limb and between-group differences were explored using mixed models analyses.\nResults At the time of return to sport after ACLR, athletes still presented significant differences favouring the uninvolved side, particularly in the symmetry of the concentric impulse (p<0.001) in all jumps compared with the control group.
