# 1. Executive Summary

Owner: Eric Rash

The High Performance Initiative (HPI) brings Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, Applied Performance, Nutrition and Mental Health together around one goal: every Baylor student-athlete who is injured returns to competition healthy, prepared and confident. This manual is the operating guide for that return. It describes how an injured athlete moves from the athletic training room back to full competition, who is responsible at each step, which tests show readiness, and how each decision is recorded.

The manual applies to every sport, every injury and every length of time lost. A two-week ankle sprain and a nine-month knee reconstruction follow the same six-phase framework (Section 3.1). What changes is the pace and the depth of testing, which scale with the injury tier (Section 3.2).

A shared framework does three things. It gives the athlete a clear, predictable path and the same standard of care in every sport. It gives practitioners a common language, objective criteria and a written record of the decisions they make. It gives the department a documented, evidence-based process that holds up to review. Clinical judgment stays central. The manual standardizes the framework and the documentation, not the clinician's decisions inside it.

The manual follows the NCAA Sport Science Institute recommendations on performance technology: a written plan, staff education, clear data ownership, evidence-based test selection and regular review (Appendix A).

The manual takes effect on [CONFIRM: Eric]. Full operation, including all forms and reports, is planned for [CONFIRM: Eric]. Appendix B records the rollout to date.

# 2. Purpose Statement

Owner: Eric Rash

Every injured athlete at Baylor goes through the same evidence-based process before returning to competition. Injury severity, sport and the pressure of the calendar change the pace of that process. They do not change whether it happens.

**What this manual addresses.** Returning an athlete to sport involves several professionals, often working in different buildings and on different schedules. This manual gives them one plan to work from. The plan starts from the demands of the sport: what the athlete must be able to do and withstand to compete safely. It then works backward to the testing and training that build and confirm that capacity. Each phase has named milestones, each milestone has an owner, and each decision is documented.

**Why now.** Health & Wellness leadership has directed that post-injury testing apply to every injury type and duration. The department now has the tools to do this well: force plates, a shared data repository and an established care team structure. A written framework turns those tools into a consistent process.

**What success looks like.** Before every athlete is cleared, physical, mental health and nutritional readiness have all been checked, and the record shows it. Clearance decisions rest on objective data that any member of the care team can read. Handoffs between athletic training, Athletic Performance and the sport coach happen on schedule and in writing. Section 11 describes how the department will measure this.

# 3. Return-to-Performance (RTP) Protocol Framework

DRAFT FOR JEREMY REVIEW

Owner: Jeremy | Co-Pilot: Eric Rash

This section sets out the framework every RTP case follows: six phases, three injury tiers and a four-step workload reintegration model. Sections 4 and 5 apply it to lower and upper body injuries.

## 3.1 Stage Overview

Every case moves through the same six phases. The phases are the same for every injury; the pace is not. An athlete moves forward when the milestones for the current phase are met, not when a set number of days has passed. Block durations within each phase are set by the physician's protocol and the lead clinician for that injury.

| Phase | Focus | What happens | Milestones to move forward (summary) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Healing | Prepare for activity: recovery | Control pain and swelling, restore range of motion within the physician's protocol, restore muscle activation. Aerobic conditioning and training of uninjured regions begin. Surgical reports and imaging are collected. First mental health and nutrition check-ins. | Pain below 3/10; range of motion progressing per protocol; muscle activation; swelling graded |
| 2. Foundation | Prepare to train: range of motion and movement quality | Restore full range of motion, normal gait or pain-free daily activity, balance and basic loading. | Range of motion symmetrical to the uninvolved side; movement screen and balance criteria (Sections 4.1, 5.1) |
| 3. Reconstruction | Prepare for practice: strength, symmetry, fitness | Rebuild strength and symmetry, return to the weight room, introduce low-level plyometrics and, for upper body cases, throwing or hitting progressions. | Strength and functional symmetry at or above 80% (lower body) or 90% (upper body) of the uninvolved side |
| 4. Reintegration | Prepare for game speed: rate of force development, change of direction, technical skill | Agility, cutting, reactive plyometrics, sport-specific work and non-contact practice. Workload reintegration (Section 3.3) begins. | Strength and hop symmetry at or above 90%; force plate jump testing; workload checkpoint |
| 5. Evaluation | Prepare for competition: maximal and sustained outputs | Full practice, game-like demands, psychological readiness. Final testing, subjective questionnaire, physician clearance, final mental health and nutrition check-ins. | Speed and change-of-direction tests; workload at 100%; questionnaire; physician clearance |
| 6. Competition | Maintenance and load management | Return to competition with ongoing monitoring of soreness, swelling and load. | Competition tolerated without pain or swelling |

Source: Baylor LE and UE Rehab Program Templates (phase names, focus and milestones).

The progression from controlled work to unpredictable, game-like work follows the control-chaos continuum (Taberner et al., 2019). Drills move from high control (planned, closed, low intensity) to high chaos (reactive, open, game speed) as the athlete progresses. The lower body template marks these steps: high to moderate control in Reconstruction, moderate control to moderate chaos in Reintegration, and moderate to high chaos in Evaluation.

## 3.2 Injury Classification and Tiered Response

The injury tier sets how much testing and documentation a case needs. The athletic trainer assigns the tier at the initial evaluation, based on expected time lost. If the expected time changes, the tier changes with it.

| Tier | Expected time lost | Testing response | Justification |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 1: Abbreviated | Less than 2 weeks | If still training: movement quality and visual assessment in practice. If not training: a quick strength screen. | Short absences cause little deconditioning when the athlete keeps training. Disuse without training causes measurable muscle loss within one week (Stokes et al., 2020). |
| Tier 2: Standard | 2 to 4 weeks | If training: force plate data plus visual assessment. If not training: the expanded objective battery for the injured region. | Cardiovascular deconditioning can be expected within 4 weeks of reduced training, and athletes show declines in function within 5 weeks of reduced training (Stokes et al., 2020). Objective testing is needed to see these changes. |
| Tier 3: Comprehensive | More than 4 weeks, or any surgery | Full protocol. Every milestone checkpoint, including mental health, nutrition, physician clearance and the complete testing battery. | Tendon and ligament strength declines within a month of detraining, on top of muscle and cardiovascular losses (Stokes et al., 2020). Psychological factors also shape return after longer absences (Ardern et al., 2013). Full documentation is required. |

Tier boundaries of 2 and 4 weeks were set by the RTP Working Group (Outline V2–V3). The cited evidence explains why deconditioning grows with time away; it does not set the exact cut points.

**Tier 1.** Most Tier 1 cases keep training in some form. Their return is judged mainly by how the athlete moves in practice. If the athlete could not train at all, a short strength screen of the injured region confirms readiness. The athletic trainer's note records the tier and the result.

**Tier 2.** Tier 2 calls for more judgment. If the athlete trained throughout, force plate jump data combined with practice observation is usually enough. If the athlete could not train, the athlete completes the objective tests for the injured region from Section 4.1 or 5.1. Mental health and nutrition check-ins are offered and recorded.

**Tier 3.** Tier 3 cases complete the full protocol with no shortened steps. They have checkpoints at the beginning, middle and end of rehabilitation, and mandatory mental health and nutrition check-ins at each. Outside surgeons' records, including the surgical report, imaging and physician notes, are collected in the Healing phase. Every Tier 3 case receives a post-case review (Section 11).

The longer supporting classification document is held by Athletic Medicine. Location: [CONFIRM: Eric].

## 3.3 Workload Reintegration Guidelines

Workload reintegration applies to both upper and lower body cases. It begins in the Reintegration phase and moves the athlete from controlled, predictable work into full participation with its unplanned demands. The steps below are called Load Steps so they are not confused with the six rehabilitation phases.

| Load Step | Target workload | Setting | Typical phase |
|---|---|---|---|
| Load Step 1 | About 70% | Controlled, sport-specific activity only. No live or unpredictable scenarios. | Reintegration |
| Load Step 2 | About 90% | More volume and intensity in controlled settings. Limited live scenarios introduced. | Reintegration to Evaluation |
| Load Step 3 | About 110% controlled, about 80% live | Overload in the controlled setting to build a reserve. Drop to about 80% when the athlete enters full, unpredictable participation such as scrimmages. | Evaluation |
| Load Step 4 | 100% | Unrestricted participation and competition, with ongoing monitoring. | Competition |

Source: RTP Working Group model (Outline V2–V3), based on professional team workload practice. The step percentages have no published source yet (Open Item O12).

Workload is expressed as a percentage of the athlete's typical pre-injury practice load for the same position and training day. The workload milestones in the rehab templates are checkpoints within these steps: 80% at the end of Reintegration (upper body) and 100% in Evaluation (both). The general principle, that an athlete returning to play needs enough recent training load to tolerate competition, is supported in the literature (Blanch & Gabbett, 2016; Taberner et al., 2022). The acute:chronic workload ratio that Blanch and Gabbett proposed has since been criticized on statistical grounds (Impellizzeri et al., 2019). This manual therefore uses it only as one input to the decision, never as a gate.

**Who leads.** The athletic trainer leads through the early phases. Athletic Performance staff take primary ownership of workload from Reintegration onward. The sport coach decides competition readiness, with input from the athletic trainer and Athletic Performance.

**Handoffs at each step.** At each Load Step the athletic trainer, the Athletic Performance coach and the sport coach agree on the next step's target and record it in the athlete's case notes. The athletic trainer confirms there are no new symptoms. The Athletic Performance coach confirms the load was completed and tolerated. The sport coach confirms which practice activities fit the next step.

**Sports measured in reps or snaps.** In football and similar sports, workload is managed in live reps or snap counts rather than a percentage of practice volume. Where wearable data are available, they are used alongside rep counts (Section 9.3).

# 4. Lower Body RTP Protocol

DRAFT FOR JEREMY REVIEW

Owner: Jeremy

This section applies the framework in Section 3 to lower body injuries. The Baylor LE Rehab Program Template is the working clinical document for each case. This section explains the tests and criteria it uses.

## 4.1 Testing Battery

The lower body battery is built from the LE Rehab Program Template. Tests are listed in the phase where they first act as a milestone. Section 6.4.2 gives the procedure for each test, Section 7.1 defines each metric and Section 7.3 explains the thresholds.

| Test | What it measures | Phase | Passing result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Range of motion | Joint motion compared with the uninvolved side | Healing, Foundation | Symmetrical to the uninvolved limb | LE template |
| Gait assessment | Walking pattern | Foundation | Normal and pain-free | LE template |
| Single-leg stance balance (SLSB), eyes open and closed | Static balance (total excursion, mm) | Foundation | At or above 90% of the uninvolved side | LE template |
| Y-Balance, anterior reach | Dynamic balance and reach | Foundation | At or above 90% of the uninvolved side | LE template; Smith et al. (2015) |
| Squat assessment (force plate) | Squat symmetry, depth and competency | Foundation | Symmetry at or above 90% | LE template |
| Functional Movement Screen (FMS) | Whole-body movement quality (7 tests, scored 0–21) | Foundation | Composite score above 14 | LE template; Kiesel et al. (2007) |
| Hand-held dynamometry (HHD) | Isometric strength of the injured muscle groups | Reconstruction, Reintegration | Limb symmetry index (LSI) at or above 80%, then 90% | LE template; Brinlee et al. (2022) |
| Isometric mid-thigh pull (IMTP) or isometric belt squat | Maximal force (N/kg) and force symmetry | Reconstruction, Reintegration | At or above 80%, then 90% | LE template |
| Hop test battery (hopscotch, single-leg broad jump, single-leg triple jump, 6 m speed hop) | Single-leg power, distance and time | Reconstruction, Reintegration | LSI at or above 80%, then 90% | LE template; Noyes et al. (1991) |
| Single-leg squat and single-leg calf raise | Single-leg strength and control | Reconstruction | At or above 80% | LE template |
| Countermovement jump (CMJ), dual force plate | Jump output and phase-specific force asymmetry | Reintegration | Asymmetry and output reviewed against the athlete's baseline (Section 7.3) | LE template; Jordan et al. (2015) |
| Drop jump | Reactive strength (RSI) and landing asymmetry | Reintegration | Reviewed against baseline (Section 7.3) | LE template; Kotsifaki et al. (2023) |
| Single-leg jump (SLJ), force plate | Single-leg jump output and asymmetry | Evaluation | Reviewed against baseline and the uninvolved side | LE template |
| 10-yard sprint | Acceleration | Evaluation | Compared with the athlete's pre-injury value | LE template |
| 10-5 change-of-direction test | Change-of-direction ability, each direction | Evaluation | Within 90% of the 10-yard acceleration reference (see Section 7.3) | LE template; Nimphius et al. (2013) |
| Subjective questionnaire (Lower Extremity Functional Scale or equivalent) | Athlete-reported function | Evaluation | Reviewed by the lead clinician | Outline V3; Binkley et al. (1999) |

Y-Balance is scored on the anterior reach only. The working group chose anterior reach as the most informative direction (Outline V2), and anterior reach asymmetry is the direction most linked to injury in Division I athletes (Smith et al., 2015).

The Nordic hamstring test, IMTP, FMS and rebound jump are also collected at intake (Section 6.5). After a hamstring injury, the Nordic test is added as a Reconstruction and Reintegration milestone (Section 7.3).

## 4.2 Rehabilitation Progression and Decision Framework

**Purpose.** The rehabilitation progression guides each decision with objective information and tested methods. The LE Rehab Program Template sets out the phases, the training blocks within each phase, their goals and weekly plans, and the milestones that must be met before the athlete moves on. Block durations are left open on purpose: the physician's protocol and the lead clinician set them for each injury, and clinical judgment can adjust the plan for each athlete.

The template opens with the athlete's details (sport, injury, date of injury or surgery, physician and lead practitioner) and a single checklist that dates each milestone. The fillable template is kept as a separate editable file, and the completed checklist is saved in the athlete's injury folder (Section 9.1).

**Milestone checkpoints.** Every Tier 3 case, and every Tier 2 case where they apply, includes:

- Mental health check-in at the initial evaluation (Healing), mid-rehabilitation and before clearance (Evaluation)
- Nutrition check-in at the same points
- Collection of outside records, especially from outside surgeons: surgical reports, imaging and physician notes (Healing)
- Physician clearance (Evaluation)
- Subjective questionnaire (Evaluation)

Workload reintegration (Section 3.3) begins in Reintegration. The full return-to-competition decision follows Section 8.4.

# 5. Upper Body RTP Protocol

DRAFT FOR JEREMY AND JACOB/JOSH REVIEW

Owner: Jeremy | Co-Pilot: Jacob/Josh

Upper body cases follow the same six phases as lower body cases. The upper body battery is smaller by design. Range-of-motion targets are less prescriptive because demands differ widely between sports: a pitcher and an offensive lineman need very different shoulders.

## 5.1 Testing Battery

| Test | What it measures | Phase | Passing result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Range of motion | Shoulder motion compared with the uninvolved side | Healing, Foundation | Within normal limits and symmetrical | UE template |
| Daily activities | Pain with daily tasks | Foundation | Pain-free | UE template |
| Functional Movement Screen | Whole-body movement quality | Foundation | Composite score above 14 | UE template; Kiesel et al. (2007) |
| Hand-held dynamometry | Rotator cuff and grip strength | Reconstruction | LSI at or above 90% | UE template |
| Athletic Shoulder (ASH) test, I, T and Y positions | Long-lever isometric shoulder force (N/kg) and symmetry | Reconstruction | At or above 90% of the uninvolved side | UE template; Ashworth et al. (2018) |
| Upper Quarter Y-Balance | Closed-chain upper body stability and reach | Reconstruction | At or above 85% symmetry | UE template; Westrick et al. (2012) |
| Plyometric push-up (force plate) | Upper body power and landing asymmetry | Reintegration | Asymmetry reviewed against baseline (Section 7.3) | UE template; Bohannon et al. (2020) |
| Throwing progression (throwing athletes) | Distance, velocity and tolerance | Reintegration, Evaluation | Full distance at 75–85% velocity (Reintegration); 100% velocity and distance pain-free (Evaluation) | UE template |
| Upper-limb function questionnaire (DASH) | Athlete-reported function and disability | Evaluation | Criterion under review (Open Item O6) | UE template; Hudak et al. (1996) |
| Shoulder psychological readiness scale (SIRSI) | Psychological readiness to return | Evaluation | At or above 85 | UE template; Gerometta et al. (2018) |

The working group removed the closed kinetic chain upper extremity stability test (CKCUEST) from the battery, and tabled the push-up and row endurance test because the functional trainer's force readings were unreliable (Outline V2–V3). Neither is a milestone. A force plate symmetry check in Evaluation is under review (Open Item O2). The plyometric push-up serves as both the intake baseline and the return-to-play measure.

## 5.2 Rehabilitation Progression and Decision Framework

**Purpose.** The UE Rehab Program Template guides upper body cases the same way the lower body template guides lower body cases (Section 4.2). It sets the phases, training blocks, goals, weekly plans and milestones, and leaves block durations to the physician's protocol and the lead clinician.

**Milestone checkpoints** are the same as for lower body cases: mental health and nutrition check-ins at the initial evaluation, mid-rehabilitation and before clearance; collection of outside records; physician clearance; and the subjective questionnaire. Workload reintegration follows Section 3.3. The upper body template sets the workload checkpoint at 80% at the end of Reintegration and 100% in Evaluation.

**Non-throwing athletes.** For a non-throwing athlete, once the strength criteria are met and the physician has cleared the athlete, the remaining steps are the subjective questionnaires and workload reintegration, moving from non-contact to contact work.

**Physician-specific testing (Biodex).** Some physicians require isokinetic (Biodex) testing before they clear an athlete. This is handled under the physician clearance checkpoint, not as part of the standard battery. If the physician has not cleared the athlete, the protocol is not complete, whatever the other results show. Isokinetic testing capacity on campus is limited, so the athletic trainer schedules it as soon as the physician's requirement is known (Open Item O13).

## 5.3 Sport-Specific Pathways (Throwing, Contact, Overhead)

**Throwing pathway.** Throwing athletes follow a structured interval throwing program that increases distance, then effort, then volume (Reinold et al., 2002). The UE template sets two checkpoints: full distance at 75–85% velocity in Reintegration, then 100% velocity and distance, pain-free, in Evaluation. At the later stages expertise shifts to the coaching staff, who track velocity, spin rate and location. Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance work with the coaches to compare these markers with the athlete's own pre-injury data (Open Item O3). In Competition, pitch and throw counts are monitored. Coaching staff have observed that some pitchers throw harder after elbow reconstruction, which can raise the risk of shoulder internal impingement, especially in athletes with a history of shoulder problems. Velocity gains are monitored with that risk in mind (Open Item O14).

**Contact pathway.** For upper body injuries in contact sports such as football, the athlete first meets the strength criteria, then moves from non-contact to contact work: individual drills, then controlled contact, then live contact. Each step is agreed by the athletic trainer, the Athletic Performance coach and the position coach.

**Overhead (non-throwing) pathway.** Overhead athletes in sports such as volleyball, tennis and swimming follow the same strength criteria. They then progress sport-specific overhead actions (serving, hitting, stroking) from reduced volume and effort to full volume and effort, using the same Load Steps (Section 3.3). Swimming is listed for completeness; it is not in the Section 6.5 intake matrix. Tennis players may use a sport-specific interval program (Reinold et al., 2002).

# 6. Testing Program

Owner: Eric Rash | Co-Pilot: Jeremy

## 6.1 Purpose Statement and Justification

Testing gives every practitioner the same objective information, so that each clearance decision rests on evidence that anyone on the care team can read and question. Testing does four jobs:

- **Baseline.** Intake testing records what each athlete can do while healthy. After an injury, that baseline is the most useful comparison, more useful than a population norm or the other limb alone.
- **Progress.** Repeat tests during rehabilitation show whether the plan is working and which quality is lagging: strength, power, speed or control.
- **Asymmetry.** Comparing the injured and uninjured sides finds deficits that are hard to see in practice. Force plate testing can find asymmetries that remain after an athlete has passed traditional hop tests (Kotsifaki et al., 2022; Kotsifaki et al., 2023).
- **Decision support.** At clearance, test results are one part of the decision, alongside physician clearance, psychological readiness and workload tolerance. No single test decides readiness; the decision weighs several sources together (Ardern et al., 2016; Creighton et al., 2010; Yung et al., 2022).

Testing also supports the athlete. Objective, trackable numbers show progress and explain why a step is or is not yet complete.

## 6.2 Literature Review

This section summarizes the evidence for each test domain. Full references are in Section 12.

**Return-to-sport decision making.** The 2016 international consensus statement describes return to sport as a continuum with three stages: return to participation, return to sport and return to performance. It recommends that decisions be shared between the athlete and the care team (Ardern et al., 2016). Decision models weigh the athlete's health status, the risk of participating and contextual factors such as timing and competitive pressure (Creighton et al., 2010; Yung et al., 2022). This manual's six phases and shared clearance (Section 8.4) follow that model.

**Strength and limb symmetry.** Criterion-based return after ACL reconstruction commonly requires quadriceps strength and hop tests at or above 90% of the uninvolved limb. Brinlee et al. (2022) list at least 9 months after surgery, 90% or better quadriceps strength symmetry, 90% or better on all hop tests and 80% or better on the ACL-RSI scale as minimum criteria. In the Delaware-Oslo cohort, athletes who met strength and hop criteria before returning had a lower reinjury rate, and each month of delay up to 9 months lowered the rate further (Grindem et al., 2016). Strength relative to body mass also matters, not only symmetry (Simonson et al., 2023). The 80% Reconstruction checkpoint in the templates is a mid-rehabilitation milestone set by the working group, not a return-to-sport criterion.

**Limits of symmetry.** A limb symmetry index compares one limb with the other. If both limbs have lost strength, the index can look normal while both limbs are weak (Jordan & Bishop, 2024). Asymmetry also varies by test and by metric, so a single threshold does not transfer between tests (Bishop, 2021; Philipp et al., 2022). For this reason the manual compares results with the athlete's own baseline and with normative data (Section 7.2), as well as with the other limb.

**Power: countermovement jump and drop jump.** Dual force plates measure each limb's force during a two-leg jump. Skiers with ACL reconstruction showed larger eccentric (braking) and concentric (push-off) impulse asymmetries than uninjured skiers (Jordan et al., 2015), and these measures tracked recovery during the return to sport (Jordan et al., 2020). At return to sport, athletes who had passed traditional discharge criteria still showed concentric impulse and landing force asymmetries and lower jump heights than controls (Kotsifaki et al., 2023). Hop distance symmetry can hide deficits in how the knee and hip produce the hop (Kotsifaki et al., 2022). Force plate CMJ and IMTP metrics have good within-session reliability when the protocol is standardized (Merrigan et al., 2020; Brady et al., 2020).

**Hop tests.** The single-leg hop tests (single hop, triple hop, crossover hop and 6 m timed hop) were developed to measure functional limitation after ACL injury (Noyes et al., 1991). They remain a standard part of return-to-sport batteries. Because distance alone can hide deficits, this manual pairs them with force plate testing (Kotsifaki et al., 2022).

**Balance.** The Y-Balance test's anterior reach is the direction most associated with injury. In Division I athletes, an anterior reach difference of 4 cm or more between limbs was associated with higher injury risk (Smith et al., 2015). The upper quarter version measures closed-chain shoulder stability and reach (Westrick et al., 2012). Reach is normalized to limb length so athletes of different sizes can be compared (Plisky et al., 2009). Normative values exist for collegiate volleyball players (Hudson et al., 2016).

**Movement quality.** In professional football, a Functional Movement Screen composite score of 14 or less was associated with serious injury (Kiesel et al., 2007). A later meta-analysis found that the composite score predicts injury poorly (Moran et al., 2017). The manual therefore uses the FMS as a movement-quality milestone in Foundation, not as a predictor of injury.

**Hamstring strength.** Lower eccentric hamstring strength measured during the Nordic exercise was associated with higher hamstring injury risk in elite Australian football (Opar et al., 2015).

**Upper body strength.** The Athletic Shoulder test measures long-lever isometric shoulder force in three positions on a force plate. It showed excellent reliability in elite rugby players (intraclass correlations 0.94–0.98; Ashworth et al., 2018). Force plate push-up tests are reliable between sessions (Bohannon et al., 2020).

**Speed and change of direction.** Total time on a change-of-direction test mixes straight-line speed with turning ability. The change-of-direction deficit isolates turning ability by subtracting the athlete's straight-line split time over the same distance. In Division I football players this was measured against the 10-yard split (Nimphius et al., 2013). The template's 10-5 test and its 10-yard reference follow this logic.

**Psychological readiness.** Psychological factors, including fear of reinjury and confidence, are associated with whether athletes return to sport (Ardern et al., 2013). The ACL-RSI scale measures psychological readiness after knee surgery (Webster et al., 2008). The SIRSI scale does the same after shoulder instability (Gerometta et al., 2018).

**Nutrition.** Disuse quickly reduces muscle protein synthesis, and injury can speed muscle loss beyond rest alone (Stokes et al., 2020). Energy and protein intake during rehabilitation affect recovery (Papadopoulou et al., 2022). This is the basis for the nutrition check-ins.

**Workload and progression.** Rehabilitation drills should move from controlled to chaotic as the athlete recovers (Taberner et al., 2019, 2020, 2023; Allen et al., 2021). Planned load progressions help the athlete tolerate the demands of competition (Taberner et al., 2022; Blanch & Gabbett, 2016).

## 6.4 Standard Operating Procedures

### 6.4.1 General Testing Guidelines

These rules apply to every test.

**Before testing**
- Confirm the athlete is cleared by the athletic trainer for the tests planned, given the injury and phase.
- Use the same warm-up for each test session. The warm-up for force plate testing is set by the Athletic Performance coach for that sport and recorded, so repeat sessions match.
- Test at a similar time of day and at a similar point in the training week as the baseline, when possible.
- Record body mass on the day of testing. Force plate metrics are normalized to body mass.

**Environment and equipment**
- Force plates sit on a flat, rigid floor. Zero the plates before each athlete, with no one on them.
- Check calibration and firmware on the schedule set by the manufacturer. Log each check.
- Use the same equipment for repeat tests on one athlete. A dual plate system can misread asymmetry if one plate is faulty, so check plates against each other before testing (Jordan et al., n.d.).

**During testing**
- Use the standard verbal cues for each test (Sections 6.4.2 and 6.4.3).
- Record the number of trials completed and discard trials that fail the test's quality checks.
- Stop the test if the athlete reports pain above the level the athletic trainer has set.

**Recording**
- Export force plate data from the VALD system and file it the same day (Section 9.1).
- Record any modification or regression as "modified" in the testing record (Section 6.6).

**Quality assurance**
- **Inter-rater reliability.** New testers are trained by an experienced tester and observed on at least one full session before testing alone. Each year, two testers run the same athletes on the same day for one test session and compare results.
- **Equipment maintenance.** Maintenance and calibration checks are logged for each device.
- **SOP review.** These SOPs are reviewed each year as part of the manual review (Section 11), or sooner if equipment or software changes.

## 6.6 Standardized Fallback and Regression Options

Some athletes cannot do a standard test because of pain, surgical restrictions, equipment access or a physician's instructions. A standard fallback keeps the data comparable. Any substitution is discussed with the supervising athletic trainer or Athletic Performance coach before the test, and is recorded as "modified" in the testing record.

| Standard test | Fallback or regression | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| Plyometric push-up | Modified plyometric push-up from the knees | Insufficient upper body strength or a restriction on full push-up |
| HHD knee extension (open chain) | Closed-chain isometric squat test | Open-chain extension causes pain; supervisor approval required |
| IMTP | Isometric belt squat | Grip, upper body or back restriction |
| Countermovement jump (two legs) | Squat assessment on force plates | Jumping not yet cleared |
| Single-leg jump | Two-leg CMJ with asymmetry metrics | Single-leg landing not yet cleared |
| Drop jump | Rebound jump from the floor, or delay the test | Drop landing not yet cleared |
| Hop battery | Single-leg squat and calf raise; delay hops | Hopping not yet cleared |
| Nordic hamstring test | Isometric hamstring HHD | Eccentric loading not yet cleared |
| Y-Balance, anterior reach | Single-leg stance balance | Single-leg reach not yet tolerated |
| Upper Quarter Y-Balance | Delay the test; use HHD and ASH | Weight bearing through the arm not yet cleared |
| ASH test | HHD in matching positions | Long-lever position not yet tolerated |
| 10-yard sprint, 10-5 test | Delay; use the speed hop and hopscotch | Sprinting or cutting not yet cleared |
| Physician-specific isokinetic (Biodex) test | No substitute | Required by the physician; see Section 5.2 |

## 7.2 Normative Data and Benchmarks

**Data sources, in order of use**

- **Primary: VALD published normative reports.** These are larger, de-identified Division I datasets. Available sports include football, men's and women's basketball, baseball, softball, women's volleyball, soccer, and track and field. Access is through VALD Hub, Normative Reports.
- **Secondary: internal Baylor data.** Internal data are strong for the CMJ across most sports and limited for other tests, including rebound jump and strength tests.
- **Published research norms** fill gaps: RSI-modified for Division I athletes (Sole et al., 2018), CMJ for Division I men's basketball (Berberet et al., 2024) and Y-Balance for collegiate women's volleyball (Hudson et al., 2016).

VALD data are the primary benchmark. Internal data are used for comparison until internal datasets are large enough across all tests and sports.

**Update cycle.** Norms are updated each year. VALD typically publishes updated reports each summer from data collected that year, and internal norms are refreshed on the same cycle. Yearly updates matter because collegiate rosters change quickly. A request to VALD for fuller sport-specific datasets was made in April 2026; its status is [CONFIRM: Eric].

**Clinical use.** Normative data add context; they do not gate clearance. For example, if an athlete's asymmetry is above the threshold but both limbs score above the normative benchmark, that context can support clearance. Norms are not used to hold an athlete out when every other criterion is met. They also protect against the opposite problem: two limbs that are symmetrical but both weak (Jordan & Bishop, 2024). Sport-specific tables are in Appendix C.

## 7.3 Asymmetry Thresholds

The thresholds below are **interim**. They come from the RTP Working Group templates and are supported by the sources listed. An external collaboration with Kitman Labs was set up to develop asymmetry thresholds from Baylor data; its current status is [CONFIRM: Eric]. If it does not proceed, the working group will review these thresholds internally at the annual update (Section 11).

| Test or metric | Phase | Interim threshold | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| HHD, IMTP, hop battery, SL squat and calf raise (lower body) | Reconstruction | At or above 80% of the uninvolved side (20% or less asymmetry) | LE template (working group mid-rehabilitation milestone) |
| HHD, IMTP, hop battery (lower body) | Reintegration | At or above 90% (10% or less asymmetry) | LE template; Brinlee et al. (2022); Grindem et al. (2016) |
| SLSB, Y-Balance anterior reach, squat competency | Foundation | At or above 90% | LE template; for Y-Balance see note below |
| FMS composite | Foundation | Above 14 | LE and UE templates; Kiesel et al. (2007) |
| HHD (upper body), ASH test | Reconstruction | At or above 90% | UE template |
| Upper Quarter Y-Balance | Reconstruction | At or above 85% symmetry | UE template (Open Item O7) |
| SIRSI | Evaluation | At or above 85 | UE template (Open Item O8) |
| CMJ, single-leg jump, drop jump, plyo push-up asymmetries | Reintegration, Evaluation | No fixed cutoff. Compared with the athlete's baseline and the test's normal variation | Bishop (2021); Kotsifaki et al. (2023); Jordan et al. (2015) |
| Nordic | Intake, hamstring cases | Working group target: 1.75 × body weight | RTP Working Group assessment protocol (Open Item O9); see Opar et al. (2015) |
| 10-5 change of direction | Evaluation | Within 90% of the 10-yard acceleration reference | LE template (Open Item O10); method from Nimphius et al. (2013) |

**What exceeding a threshold means.** An asymmetry above the threshold means the injured side is not yet doing its share. It is a reason to look closer and target the lagging quality, not an automatic stop. The lead clinician reviews the result alongside the athlete's baseline, the normative data, the other tests and how the athlete moves in practice. For example, a high concentric impulse asymmetry with a normal jump height suggests the uninjured leg is compensating (Kotsifaki et al., 2023).

**Why force plate asymmetries have no fixed cutoff.** Asymmetry depends on the test and the metric, and it varies from day to day (Bishop, 2021). A single percentage applied to every metric would flag normal variation in some tests and miss real deficits in others. Until Baylor-specific thresholds exist, each force plate asymmetry is judged against the athlete's own intake values.

**Y-Balance note.** The published injury-risk finding is a difference of 4 cm or more in anterior reach (Smith et al., 2015). The template uses 90% symmetry instead. Which form to use is Open Item O11.

**Report color bands.** Athlete reports color-code asymmetry at 5%, 10% and 15% to help the eye. These bands are a display aid, not decision thresholds (Section 9.2).

| Sport coach (head or position coach) | Practice planning during workload reintegration; return to competition. | Competition readiness, with input from the athletic trainer and Athletic Performance |
| Athletic Medicine supervisor | Oversight of cases and folders; second-level folder owner. | Escalation decisions; case reassignment |
| Health & Wellness leadership | Policy, approvals and resources for the HPI. | Mandating meeting structures; physician documentation standards |

**Who leads each phase.** The rehab templates name a primary and a secondary stakeholder for each phase. In the RACI terms the templates were converted from, primary means Responsible or Accountable and secondary means Consulted or Informed. The team physician is accountable for medical clearance in every phase.

| Phase | Primary | Secondary |
|---|---|---|
| Healing | Athletic trainer, physical therapist | Nutrition, Mental Health, Athletic Performance |
| Foundation | Athletic trainer, physical therapist, Athletic Performance | Nutrition, Mental Health |
| Reconstruction | Athletic Performance, athletic trainer, physical therapist | Nutrition, Mental Health, sport coach |
| Reintegration | Athletic Performance, athletic trainer or physical therapist, sport coach | Nutrition, Mental Health |
| Evaluation | Sport coach, Athletic Performance | Athletic trainer, Nutrition, Mental Health |
| Competition | Sport coach | Athletic Performance, Nutrition, Mental Health |

Source: LE and UE Rehab Program Templates, Appendix 1.

In short: the athletic trainer leads early rehabilitation, Athletic Performance leads late rehabilitation and return to training, and the sport coach decides game readiness with input from both.

## 8.2 Communication Flow

Information moves at fixed points. Each point has a sender, a receiver and a record.

| Trigger | Sender | Receiver | What is shared | Record |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Injury and initial evaluation | Athletic trainer | Team physician, sport coach, Athletic Performance | Injury, tier, initial restrictions | AT note; injury folder opened |
| Physician visit or surgery | Athletic trainer | Care team | Restrictions, protocol, outside records | Surgical report and imaging in folder |
| Each phase milestone met | Athletic trainer (to Reintegration), Athletic Performance (after) | Care team | Milestone date and test results | Template checklist; testing record |
| Each Load Step | Athletic Performance coach | Athletic trainer, sport coach | Load completed and tolerated; next step | Case notes |
| Mental health or nutrition check-in | Athletic trainer (referral) | Mental health provider, sports dietitian | Referral only | Checkbox and date; clinical details stay with the provider |
| Physician clearance | Team physician | Athletic trainer | Written clearance | Clearance document in folder |
| Return to competition | Sport coach, with athletic trainer and Athletic Performance | Care team, athlete | Decision and any limits | Clearance sign-off form (Section 10.2) |

**Weekly updates.** Active cases are reviewed in the weekly care team meeting (Section 8.3). Between meetings, each sport has a Microsoft Teams channel where the care team, including dietitians and physical therapists, can post notes on a case.

**Physician profiles.** Athletic Medicine will keep a short profile for each team and consulting physician: how that physician handles post-operative care, rehabilitation, restrictions (range of motion, weight bearing, bracing, movement and locomotion) and clearance, including any required tests. The profiles give staff who are new to a physician a clear starting point.

**Escalation triggers.** The athletic trainer raises a case with the Athletic Medicine supervisor and the care team when:

- A milestone is missed by more than one planned block, or the athlete regresses
- Symptoms return or a new injury occurs during progression
- A mental health or nutrition check-in has not happened by its planned point
- The athlete, a parent or a coach disagrees with the plan or timeline
- A physician's requirement cannot be met on campus (for example, isokinetic testing)

## 8.3 Care Team Meetings and Sport Performance Meetings

Two meeting types serve different purposes.

| | Care team meeting | Sport performance meeting |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | What is going on. Awareness-level updates across medical, academic, mental health and character formation. | How it is being done. Periodization, nutrition planning, technology, workload management and rehabilitation details. |
| Scope | Broad. Connects issues across areas (for example, academic stress and practice behavior). All athletes. | Deep. Mid- to long-term cases, plus training for healthy athletes. |
| Attendees | Athletic trainer, Athletic Performance, Mental Health, Nutrition, Academics, Character Formation, sport coach representative | Athletic trainer, Athletic Performance, Nutrition, sport coach (position or event coach as needed) |
| Format | Roster review with brief updates per athlete. No deep dives. | Structured agenda: injury report (mid- and long-term only), training status, action items, follow-up from the last meeting |
| Frequency | Weekly (established) | Weekly or every other week (proposed) |
| Status | Established by administration | Proposed, pending leadership approval [CONFIRM: Eric] |

The working group recommends sport performance meetings but does not have the authority to require them. The proposed structure is presented to Health & Wellness leadership for approval. Football already holds a weekly meeting of this kind.

**Proposed sport performance meeting structure**

- Clear objectives for each meeting, not open discussion
- Standard agenda: mid- and long-term injury updates (short-term cases stay in the care team meeting), training program, technology and data review, action items
- 30 to 45 minutes at most, depending on roster size
- Notes and action items recorded and reviewed at the next meeting
- Works for a 12-athlete roster such as tennis and a 120-athlete roster such as football

## 8.4 Clearance Authority and Procedures

Clearance is a shared decision. The sign-offs required depend on the tier.

| Tier | Required sign-off |
|---|---|
| Tier 1 | Athletic trainer. Team physician if the physician was involved in the case. |
| Tier 2 | Athletic trainer and team physician. Athletic Performance confirms the testing and workload results. |
| Tier 3 | Athletic trainer, team physician, Athletic Performance and the Athletic Medicine supervisor. The sport coach confirms competition readiness. |

**Two separate milestones**

- **Physician clearance** is clearance to begin participating and progressing back to full participation. It is not clearance for unrestricted competition.
- **Return to competition** is decided by the athletic trainer and Athletic Performance with the sport coach, after physician clearance and after the Evaluation milestones are met.
- Physician-specific test requirements, such as isokinetic testing, are handled under the physician clearance checkpoint. If the physician has not cleared the athlete, the protocol is not complete.

**Physician clearance documentation**

Documentation should look the same for every physician. This manual sets one standard:

- **Outside physicians** already provide written clearance on their letterhead. This continues.
- **Team physicians** provide a written note, a dictated visit note or a signed form documenting clearance. A verbal instruction alone is not enough for the record.
- Health & Wellness leadership will confirm this standard with the physician group before the manual goes to the wider staff. Status: proposed, pending leadership [CONFIRM: Eric].
- The clearance sign-off form (Section 10.2) will be reviewed and approved through the appropriate channels before use.

**Mental health in the clearance process**

- Mental health check-ins are milestone checkpoints. The checklist records that the check-in happened and the date.
- The outcome is recorded in the mental health provider's own records, separate from athletic training files. The clearance process documents that the check-in occurred, not the clinical details.
- If a mental health concern affects readiness, it is raised in the care team meeting and handled through the physician, within the existing clinical care structure.

**Nutrition**

Nutrition follows the same model. The checklist confirms that the referral was made and the meeting happened, and the care team meeting holds everyone accountable. No separate referral form is used.

## 8.5 Athlete and Parent Communication

**At the start of rehabilitation**, the athletic trainer explains to the athlete that physician clearance and return to competition are separate milestones. The physician clears the athlete to begin the return-to-sport progression; the care team decides together when the athlete is ready for unrestricted competition. The athletic trainer notes in the record that this conversation happened.

**Parents.** Federal privacy rules (FERPA and HIPAA) govern what staff can share. With the athlete's written consent, staff may explain the clearance process to parents early, which helps avoid the common confusion of "the doctor said I'm cleared, so why can't I play?" Staff explain the process and the milestones; they do not share clinical details beyond what the athlete has consented to. Questions about consent or legal limits go to Health & Wellness leadership.

**During the case**, the athlete sees test results at each milestone, with an explanation of what improved and what still needs work.

# 9. Data Repository and Visualization

Owner: Eric Rash

## 9.1 Data Collection, Storage and Folder Ownership

**From test day to the repository**

1. The tester runs the test and exports the session from the VALD system (ForceDecks or NordBord) as a CSV file the same day.
2. Applied Performance loads new files into the master database. A script checks for duplicates, standardizes column names, adds the file to the database and archives the original.
3. Hand-scored tests (FMS, Y-Balance, hop tests, HHD) are entered in the HPI data workbook, one sheet per test.
4. Applied Performance produces the athlete's progress report (Section 9.2) and saves it to the injury folder.

**Where it lives.** Injury folders are kept on Box [CONFIRM: Eric], within each sport's Athletic Medicine directory. Force plate data live in the Applied Performance master database. Access follows the folder hierarchy below.

**Naming conventions**

- Athlete folder: `Lastname_Firstname`
- Injury folder: `YYYY-MM-DD_BodyRegion_Injury` (date of injury)
- Files: `YYYY-MM-DD_TestName` (date of test)

**Folder ownership**

- Level 1: Team athletic trainer (primary owner)
- Level 2: Athletic Medicine supervisor (co-owner)
- Level 3: Department-level administrator (master access, for exceptional situations such as turnover of a whole sport's staff)

**Injury folders**

- Each injury gets its own folder inside the athlete's directory.
- Resolved injuries move to an archive folder.
- A flare-up or re-aggravation soon after return continues in the existing folder.
- A re-injury after a long gap (for example, a freshman-year injury that recurs as a senior) gets a new folder and is treated as a new case.

**Data protection.** Testing data are health-related and are shared only with staff who need them for the athlete's care or training. Data are not shared outside the care team without the athlete's consent.

## 9.2 Athlete Profile Template

The athlete profile is a one-page summary of an RTP case. It is the document brought to a meeting when leadership or the care team asks where an athlete stands. The layout follows the current production report:

- **Header:** athlete name, sport, position, injury, current phase and a return-to-play status banner
- **Summary cards:** key outputs (for example jump height, RSI-modified and power), each with the latest value, the change from baseline and a small trend line
- **Two-leg CMJ panel:** a table for each metric showing session, value, change from baseline and change from best
- **Single-leg panel:** paired left and right bars for each single-leg metric
- **Asymmetry panel:** asymmetry for each metric, color-coded (5% or less, 5–10%, 10–15%, above 15%) as a display aid, with the phase threshold from Section 7.3 shown alongside
- **Metric groups:** Output, Driver, Strategy and Asymmetry (Section 7.1)

A plain-language metric guide goes with every report so readers without a biomechanics background can read it.

## 9.3 Load Monitoring Integration

Sports that use wearable tracking (Catapult) add load data to the RTP picture.

- **Baseline.** Before the injury, the athlete's typical practice load for the position and training day is taken from the tracking system. This is the 100% reference for the Load Steps (Section 3.3).
- **Load Steps.** During reintegration, each session's load is reported as a percentage of that reference, using the sport's main load measures (for example total distance, high-speed distance and accumulated load). Each sport's Athletic Performance coach sets the measures for that sport (Open Item O18).
- **Clearance.** At Evaluation, the record shows the athlete has completed full practice loads (100%) without symptoms. Load data are one input to the decision, not a gate on their own.
- **Football and similar sports** track live reps or snaps alongside wearable data.
- **Sports without wearables** use session duration and session rating of perceived exertion, as recorded by Athletic Performance.

Weekly CMJ monitoring (Section 6.5) adds a neuromuscular check alongside load.

# 11. Audit, Review and Continuous Improvement

Owner: Eric Rash

A written process only helps if someone checks that it is followed. Each component below has an owner, a schedule and a measure.

| Component | Owner | When | What is checked | Measure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Post-case review | Athletic trainer and Applied Performance | After each Tier 3 case reaches full return | Every milestone completed and documented; outcome | Share of Tier 3 cases with a complete record |
| Care team accountability | Athletic Medicine supervisor | Monthly, for each open mid- to long-term case, in the care team meeting | Mental health and nutrition check-ins happening on schedule | Share of check-ins completed by their planned point |
| Athlete survey | Applied Performance | At the end of each Tier 2 and Tier 3 case | Whether the athlete felt informed and that everyone involved was included | Share of athletes answering yes |
| Periodic audit | Applied Performance with the Athletic Medicine supervisor | Each semester | A sample of closed cases across sports | Gaps found and fixed |
| Testing process audit | Applied Performance | Each semester | Testers following the SOPs; equipment checks logged | Inter-rater agreement; checks on schedule |
| Manual review | Eric Rash, with section owners | Each year, before the start of the academic year | Audit findings, new evidence, updated norms | New version issued with a revision history entry |

The care team accountability check exists because long-term cases can drift: an athlete in a long rehabilitation can go many months without a nutrition or mental health visit unless someone checks.

## Appendix A: NCAA Performance Technology Recommendations

The NCAA Sport Science Institute convened experts on performance technology and published consensus recommendations. Performance technology is defined broadly: anything that collects biometric or performance data, including cameras, surveys and apps, not only wearables. The recommendations put student-athlete rights (informed consent, data privacy, compliance) at the center and note possible harm, including anxiety, fixation on numbers and body image concerns. The original NCAA document is to be cited directly; location: [CONFIRM: Eric].

| NCAA recommendation | What it asks | Where this manual meets it |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Policy | A written plan, built by a multidisciplinary team and reviewed regularly | This manual is the written plan for RTP testing. It was built by the RTP Working Group across Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, Applied Performance, Nutrition and Mental Health, and is reviewed each year (Section 11). |
| 2. Education | Training at least once a year, tailored by audience | Staff training on the manual and SOPs (Section 6.4.1, Appendix B); athlete communication at the start of each case (Section 8.5). |
| 3. Data management | Clear data ownership, storage, access and use; a plan for transfers | Folder ownership levels, naming and access (Section 9.1); data shared only with the care team. |
| 4. Technology selection | Evaluate accuracy, reliability and validity before adoption; cross-functional decisions | Each test is backed by reliability and validity evidence (Section 6.2); fallbacks keep data comparable (Section 6.6). |
| 5. Continuous improvement | Regular feedback from athletes, coaches and staff | Athlete survey, audits and the annual review (Section 11). |

# 1. Executive Summary

Owner: Eric Rash

The High Performance Initiative (HPI) brings Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, Applied Performance, Nutrition and Mental Health together around one goal: every Baylor student-athlete who is injured returns to competition healthy, prepared and confident. This manual is the operating guide for that return. It describes how an injured athlete moves from the athletic training room back to full competition, who is responsible at each step, which tests show readiness, and how each decision is recorded.

The manual applies to every sport, every injury and every length of time lost. A two-week ankle sprain and a nine-month knee reconstruction follow the same six-phase framework (Section 3.1). What changes is the pace and the depth of testing, which scale with the injury tier (Section 3.2).

A shared framework does three things. It gives the athlete a clear, predictable path and the same standard of care in every sport. It gives practitioners a common language, objective criteria and a written record of the decisions they make. It gives the department a documented, evidence-based process that holds up to review. Clinical judgment stays central. The manual standardizes the framework and the documentation, not the clinician's decisions inside it.

The manual follows the NCAA Sport Science Institute recommendations on performance technology: a written plan, staff education, clear data ownership, evidence-based test selection and regular review (Appendix A).

The manual takes effect on [CONFIRM: Eric]. Full operation, including all forms and reports, is planned for [CONFIRM: Eric]. Appendix B records the rollout to date.

# 2. Purpose Statement

Owner: Eric Rash

Every injured athlete at Baylor goes through the same evidence-based process before returning to competition. Injury severity, sport and the pressure of the calendar change the pace of that process. They do not change whether it happens.

**What this manual addresses.** Returning an athlete to sport involves several professionals, often working in different buildings and on different schedules. This manual gives them one plan to work from. The plan starts from the demands of the sport: what the athlete must be able to do and withstand to compete safely. It then works backward to the testing and training that build and confirm that capacity. Each phase has named milestones, each milestone has an owner, and each decision is documented.

**Why now.** Health & Wellness leadership has directed that post-injury testing apply to every injury type and duration. The department now has the tools to do this well: force plates, a shared data repository and an established care team structure. A written framework turns those tools into a consistent process.

**What success looks like.** Before every athlete is cleared, physical, mental health and nutritional readiness have all been checked, and the record shows it. Clearance decisions rest on objective data that any member of the care team can read. Handoffs between athletic training, Athletic Performance and the sport coach happen on schedule and in writing. Section 11 describes how the department will measure this.

# 3. Return-to-Performance (RTP) Protocol Framework

DRAFT FOR JEREMY REVIEW

Owner: Jeremy | Co-Pilot: Eric Rash

This section sets out the framework every RTP case follows: six phases, three injury tiers and a four-step workload reintegration model. Sections 4 and 5 apply it to lower and upper body injuries.

## 3.1 Stage Overview

Every case moves through the same six phases. The phases are the same for every injury; the pace is not. An athlete moves forward when the milestones for the current phase are met, not when a set number of days has passed. Block durations within each phase are set by the physician's protocol and the lead clinician for that injury.

| Phase | Focus | What happens | Milestones to move forward (summary) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Healing | Prepare for activity: recovery | Control pain and swelling, restore range of motion within the physician's protocol, restore muscle activation. Aerobic conditioning and training of uninjured regions begin. Surgical reports and imaging are collected. First mental health and nutrition check-ins. | Pain below 3/10; range of motion progressing per protocol; muscle activation; swelling graded |
| 2. Foundation | Prepare to train: range of motion and movement quality | Restore full range of motion, normal gait or pain-free daily activity, balance and basic loading. | Range of motion symmetrical to the uninvolved side; movement screen and balance criteria (Sections 4.1, 5.1) |
| 3. Reconstruction | Prepare for practice: strength, symmetry, fitness | Rebuild strength and symmetry, return to the weight room, introduce low-level plyometrics and, for upper body cases, throwing or hitting progressions. | Strength and functional symmetry at or above 80% (lower body) or 90% (upper body) of the uninvolved side |
| 4. Reintegration | Prepare for game speed: rate of force development, change of direction, technical skill | Agility, cutting, reactive plyometrics, sport-specific work and non-contact practice. Workload reintegration (Section 3.3) begins. | Strength and hop symmetry at or above 90%; force plate jump testing; workload checkpoint |
| 5. Evaluation | Prepare for competition: maximal and sustained outputs | Full practice, game-like demands, psychological readiness. Final testing, subjective questionnaire, physician clearance, final mental health and nutrition check-ins. | Speed and change-of-direction tests; workload at 100%; questionnaire; physician clearance |
| 6. Competition | Maintenance and load management | Return to competition with ongoing monitoring of soreness, swelling and load. | Competition tolerated without pain or swelling |

Source: Baylor LE and UE Rehab Program Templates (phase names, focus and milestones).

The progression from controlled work to unpredictable, game-like work follows the control-chaos continuum (Taberner et al., 2019). Drills move from high control (planned, closed, low intensity) to high chaos (reactive, open, game speed) as the athlete progresses. The lower body template marks these steps: high to moderate control in Reconstruction, moderate control to moderate chaos in Reintegration, and moderate to high chaos in Evaluation.

## 3.2 Injury Classification and Tiered Response

The injury tier sets how much testing and documentation a case needs. The athletic trainer assigns the tier at the initial evaluation, based on expected time lost. If the expected time changes, the tier changes with it.

| Tier | Expected time lost | Testing response | Justification |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 1: Abbreviated | Less than 2 weeks | If still training: movement quality and visual assessment in practice. If not training: a quick strength screen. | Short absences cause little deconditioning when the athlete keeps training. Disuse without training causes measurable muscle loss within one week (Stokes et al., 2020). |
| Tier 2: Standard | 2 to 4 weeks | If training: force plate data plus visual assessment. If not training: the expanded objective battery for the injured region. | Cardiovascular deconditioning can be expected within 4 weeks of reduced training, and athletes show declines in function within 5 weeks of reduced training (Stokes et al., 2020). Objective testing is needed to see these changes. |
| Tier 3: Comprehensive | More than 4 weeks, or any surgery | Full protocol. Every milestone checkpoint, including mental health, nutrition, physician clearance and the complete testing battery. | Tendon and ligament strength declines within a month of detraining, on top of muscle and cardiovascular losses (Stokes et al., 2020). Psychological factors also shape return after longer absences (Ardern et al., 2013). Full documentation is required. |

Tier boundaries of 2 and 4 weeks were set by the RTP Working Group (Outline V2–V3). The cited evidence explains why deconditioning grows with time away; it does not set the exact cut points.

**Tier 1.** Most Tier 1 cases keep training in some form. Their return is judged mainly by how the athlete moves in practice. If the athlete could not train at all, a short strength screen of the injured region confirms readiness. The athletic trainer's note records the tier and the result.

**Tier 2.** Tier 2 calls for more judgment. If the athlete trained throughout, force plate jump data combined with practice observation is usually enough. If the athlete could not train, the athlete completes the objective tests for the injured region from Section 4.1 or 5.1. Mental health and nutrition check-ins are offered and recorded.

**Tier 3.** Tier 3 cases complete the full protocol with no shortened steps. They have checkpoints at the beginning, middle and end of rehabilitation, and mandatory mental health and nutrition check-ins at each. Outside surgeons' records, including the surgical report, imaging and physician notes, are collected in the Healing phase. Every Tier 3 case receives a post-case review (Section 11).

The longer supporting classification document is held by Athletic Medicine. Location: [CONFIRM: Eric].

## 3.3 Workload Reintegration Guidelines

Workload reintegration applies to both upper and lower body cases. It begins in the Reintegration phase and moves the athlete from controlled, predictable work into full participation with its unplanned demands. The steps below are called Load Steps so they are not confused with the six rehabilitation phases.

| Load Step | Target workload | Setting | Typical phase |
|---|---|---|---|
| Load Step 1 | About 70% | Controlled, sport-specific activity only. No live or unpredictable scenarios. | Reintegration |
| Load Step 2 | About 90% | More volume and intensity in controlled settings. Limited live scenarios introduced. | Reintegration to Evaluation |
| Load Step 3 | About 110% controlled, about 80% live | Overload in the controlled setting to build a reserve. Drop to about 80% when the athlete enters full, unpredictable participation such as scrimmages. | Evaluation |
| Load Step 4 | 100% | Unrestricted participation and competition, with ongoing monitoring. | Competition |

Source: RTP Working Group model (Outline V2–V3), based on professional team workload practice. The step percentages have no published source yet (Open Item O12).

Workload is expressed as a percentage of the athlete's typical pre-injury practice load for the same position and training day. The workload milestones in the rehab templates are checkpoints within these steps: 80% at the end of Reintegration (upper body) and 100% in Evaluation (both). The general principle, that an athlete returning to play needs enough recent training load to tolerate competition, is supported in the literature (Blanch & Gabbett, 2016; Taberner et al., 2022). The acute:chronic workload ratio that Blanch and Gabbett proposed has since been criticized on statistical grounds (Impellizzeri et al., 2019). This manual therefore uses it only as one input to the decision, never as a gate.

**Who leads.** The athletic trainer leads through the early phases. Athletic Performance staff take primary ownership of workload from Reintegration onward. The sport coach decides competition readiness, with input from the athletic trainer and Athletic Performance.

**Handoffs at each step.** At each Load Step the athletic trainer, the Athletic Performance coach and the sport coach agree on the next step's target and record it in the athlete's case notes. The athletic trainer confirms there are no new symptoms. The Athletic Performance coach confirms the load was completed and tolerated. The sport coach confirms which practice activities fit the next step.

**Sports measured in reps or snaps.** In football and similar sports, workload is managed in live reps or snap counts rather than a percentage of practice volume. Where wearable data are available, they are used alongside rep counts (Section 9.3).

## 4.2 Rehabilitation Progression and Decision Framework

**Purpose.** The rehabilitation progression guides each decision with objective information and tested methods. The LE Rehab Program Template sets out the phases, the training blocks within each phase, their goals and weekly plans, and the milestones that must be met before the athlete moves on. Block durations are left open on purpose: the physician's protocol and the lead clinician set them for each injury, and clinical judgment can adjust the plan for each athlete.

The template opens with the athlete's details (sport, injury, date of injury or surgery, physician and lead practitioner) and a single checklist that dates each milestone. The fillable template is kept as a separate editable file, and the completed checklist is saved in the athlete's injury folder (Section 9.1).

**Milestone checkpoints.** Every Tier 3 case, and every Tier 2 case where they apply, includes:

- Mental health check-in at the initial evaluation (Healing), mid-rehabilitation and before clearance (Evaluation)
- Nutrition check-in at the same points
- Collection of outside records, especially from outside surgeons: surgical reports, imaging and physician notes (Healing)
- Physician clearance (Evaluation)
- Subjective questionnaire (Evaluation)

Workload reintegration (Section 3.3) begins in Reintegration. The full return-to-competition decision follows Section 8.4.
